Peer-reviewed work finds the benefits tilt toward higher earners. As a transfer, each $1 is worth $1 to borrowers but costs taxpayers $1 or more plus the economic drag of raising it, so the ratio runs from about -1.39 to 0.67.

policies.title: Block Social Security/Medicare age or benefit changes
policies.bcr_basis: Blocking any rise in eligibility ages or cut in benefits means paying scheduled benefits after the trust funds run out (OASDI 2034, HI 2033), so the extra money must be raised by taxes or borrowing. Benefits are a transfer, valued at $1 per $1 to retirees, so the net-damage form of the UBI entry applies: ratio = (1 - excess burden x net fiscal cost) / net fiscal cost, where net fiscal cost includes administration and the fiscal externality (FE) of lower work. FE from age changes: CBO (2012) finds raising the full retirement age from 67 to 70 cuts Social Security spending about 13% and enlarges the economy by slightly more than 1% in the long run; 13% of today's 5.3%-of-GDP programme (2026 Trustees) is 0.69% of GDP; CBO's rule of thumb (as reported by CRFB) is about 0.25 of extra GDP returning as revenue (0.5% of GDP on 2% more GDP), so blocking the age rise forgoes 0.25 x 1.0 = 0.25% of GDP of taxes per 0.69% of GDP of benefits kept: FE = 0.36. Mastrobuoni (2009, JPubE) confirms the behaviour: when the 1983 law raised the normal retirement age, mean retirement ages rose by about half the increase. Administration adds 0.53% of benefits. HIGH = 0.66: blocking across-the-board benefit-formula cuts (little labour-supply response, FE about 0) with the Ballard-Shoven-Whalley central excess burden of 0.33: (1 - 0.33 x 1.0053) / 1.0053 = 0.66. LOW = -1.27: blocking an age rise (FE 0.36, net fiscal cost 1.365) financed at Feldstein's (1999) nearly $2 marginal deadweight loss: (1 - 2.0 x 1.365) / 1.365 = -1.27. Middle case (age rise blocked, BSW 0.33): (1 - 0.33 x 1.365) / 1.365 = 0.40. The financing deadweight is subtracted in the ratio and the work-loss effect enters through the FE, so neither is added again; the GDP-loss figure in cost_components is output, which overstates the welfare loss. The choice of cost base (75-year gap, current annual deficit or post-2034 shortfall) changes cost_bn but not the ratio. Poverty-reduction value (Engelhardt & Gruber) is not weighted.
policies.grade_reason: Combines a peer-reviewed natural experiment on retirement behaviour (Mastrobuoni 2009, JPubE), CBO macro estimates and the Trustees' official fiscal gap, with peer-reviewed excess-burden estimates (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). No published benefit-cost ratio exists for keeping current-law benefits, and the labour-supply feedback is from CBO's model rather than a measured welfare change, so the grade is below B+.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: the 2026 Trustees' 75-year actuarial deficits (OASDI 4.42% and HI 0.56% of payroll) come to about 1.67% of GDP, ~$535bn a year. Administration: SSA spends 0.4% of OASDI cost on administration (CY2025, $6.95bn) and Medicare HI 1.3% ($5.9bn of $444.2bn, CRS 2026); applied to the extra benefits that is about $2.8bn a year (an upper bound). Private compliance: none identified. GDP loss: (a) CBO (2012) finds raising the full retirement age to 70 would enlarge the economy by slightly more than 1%, so blocking it gives up about $320bn a year of output (output, not welfare, since retirees gain leisure); (b) the excess burden of the taxes needed at Feldstein's ~$2 per $1, $1,070bn a year. cost_bn = 535 + 2.8 + 1,390 = $1,927.8bn a year (75-year average). With only the 2026 cash deficit (0.8% of GDP) and Ballard-Shoven-Whalley's 33 cents, the total would be far smaller (about $340bn).
policies.difficulty_reason: Keeping current benefit rules needs no change, but paying full scheduled benefits after 2034 (OASDI) and 2033 (HI) needs ordinary legislation to raise payroll taxes or transfer general revenue; Congress has done this before (1977 and 1983 amendments). No constitutional change.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits go to nearly all retirees and disabled workers; Engelhardt & Gruber find a roughly unitary elasticity of elderly poverty with respect to benefits, so cuts would raise poverty, which favours the poor. But benefits rise with lifetime earnings and the cost falls on current workers through payroll taxes, so the net effect is broad rather than clearly pro-poor.
policies.summary: This policy blocks any rise in the Social Security or Medicare eligibility ages and any cut in scheduled benefits, so the trust-fund shortfalls must be filled with new taxes or borrowing. It is among the most popular ideas tested: 87.5% of US GSS/ISSP respondents say government should provide a decent living for the old, and protecting both programmes from cuts or age increases had net support of +72 in a 2024 YouGov poll of 4,038 voters. The 2026 Trustees put the gap at about $535bn a year on average over 75 years; at the high end, the taxes to fill it and the work forgone could cost the economy more than twice that again. As a transfer, each $1 is worth $1 to retirees, but raising it costs $1 plus the drag of higher taxes, and blocking higher retirement ages also forgoes extra work and tax revenue. The ratio runs from about -1.27 to 0.66.

policies.title: Globally Strict Border Controls
policies.bcr_basis: Global accounting: the net benefit of restriction to everyone affected, including the people kept out, per migrant kept out, divided by enforcement spending per migrant deterred, in the same net-damage form as the other rules. Dollars are 2012-2024 as published (not harmonised); a 20-year working life is discounted at 3% (annuity factor 14.88). Terms. US natives (Allen, Dobbin & Morten 2024): low-skill workers +$9/yr x 47.6m, high-skill -$21/yr x 78.7m (BLS 2009), over 311,000 deterred: +$20,500 and -$79,000 per migrant. Migrant's lost earnings (Clemens, Montenegro & Pritchett 2019): lower bound on the Mexico place premium PPP$10,523/yr (2000 dollars) x 14.88 = $156,600; at 2024 prices (CPI-U x1.82) $285,200. Remittances are part of these earnings, so not added again; sending-country brain-drain effects for low-skill Mexican flows are small and of uncertain sign (Docquier & Rapoport 2012), so set to zero. Fiscal: a saving of $231,000 per migrant kept out (Heritage reading of NAS 2017) in the case most favourable to restriction, or a forgone fiscal contribution of $57,000 (Cato update of NAS) in the least favourable. Enforcement per migrant deterred: $10,600 for the 2006-10 wall (Allen et al.) to $533,400 under H.R. 1 ($170.7bn / CBO's 320,000 fewer residents in 2035; CBO counts removals and may understate deterrence). Before the lost-income mortality step: case most favourable to restriction (cheapest enforcement, Heritage fiscal reading) = (231,000 + 20,500 - 79,000 - 156,600) / 10,600 = 1.50; least favourable case (H.R. 1 enforcement, Cato fiscal reading) = (20,500 - 79,000 - 57,000 - 285,200) / 533,400 = -0.75. Lost-income mortality: income lost to a policy costs lives. Broughel & Viscusi (Mercatus 2017) put it at about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed; valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m, each $1 of net income lost carries 13.1/99.3 = $0.132 of mortality cost (and each $1 gained saves the same). Migrants' lost earnings are lost income, so the step is applied here directly, to the net income change per $ of enforcement: (20,500 - 79,000 - 156,600 - 10,600) / 10,600 = -21.3 in the first case and (20,500 - 79,000 - 285,200 - 533,400) / 533,400 = -1.64 in the second. LOW = 1.50 - 0.132 x 21.3 = -1.31. HIGH = -0.75 - 0.132 x 1.64 = -0.97. The low end comes from the case most favourable to restriction: cheap enforcement keeps out many migrants per dollar, and their lost earnings (and the deaths that lower income causes) outweigh the fiscal saving. Poor-country infant deaths from lower world income use Baird, Friedman & Schady (REStat 2011): +0.24 to 0.40 infant deaths per 1,000 births per 1% fall in GDP per person, on ~119.9m births a year in low- and middle-income countries (World Bank). Not counted: migrants' non-wage welfare, long-run variety gains to natives (di Giovanni et al. 2015, +5-10%), and the world-GDP upper bounds (Clemens 2011, +50-150% of world GDP; Kennan 2013, Review of Economic Dynamics, gains like doubling incomes in poor countries). All of these would lower the ratio further.
policies.grade_reason: The deciding term is the migrant's lost earnings. That comes from a peer-reviewed, tightly estimated lower bound (Clemens, Montenegro & Pritchett 2019, REStat) and is backed by quantified peer-reviewed global models (Clemens 2011 JEP; Kennan 2013 RED; di Giovanni et al. 2015 JEEA). The native labour-market inputs come from a working-paper spatial model that agrees with peer-reviewed natural experiments (Clemens, Lewis & Postel 2018 AER; East et al. 2023 JOLE). The fiscal term still relies on think-tank readings of the NAS model, but under global accounting it does not change the sign of the result, so the grade is B. No peer-reviewed benefit-cost study of restriction itself exists, so it is not A-level.
policies.cost_basis: Full annual cost = $59.9bn public outlay (H.R. 1 2025 reconciliation enforcement money $38.9bn/yr plus the 2026 Secure America Act $21.0bn/yr) + $1.3bn administration (DOJ immigration judges and prosecutions, border processing) + private compliance (no estimate, null) + $82.2bn lost global output (Brookings US GDP effect of $90-180bn x the 0.61 place-premium share; range $55-110bn) = about $143bn/yr. Detention ($45bn, about $10.6bn/yr) sits inside the H.R. 1 total. AIC (2024) estimates a full mass-deportation programme of 1m removals a year at $88bn/yr, which is a higher outlay scenario.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: ordinary legislation and executive action in one country, and it has just been done (H.R. 1 in 2025). Fully stopping unauthorized entry has no modern precedent at the US-Mexico border.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The largest losers are would-be low-skill migrants from poorer countries, who give up at least 2.6 times their home real wage (Mexico) and 3.95 times at the median origin country, or at least PPP$10,500-13,600 a year (Clemens et al. 2019). Their families lose remittances: Mexico received $66bn in 2023 (World Bank). Within the US, the only gainers are low-skill workers (+$9/yr), while high-skill workers lose (-$21/yr; Allen et al.). The gains are tiny and go to people far richer than the losers.
policies.summary: Globally strict border controls means every major destination country adopting enforcement on the scale of the 2025-26 US build-up (H.R. 1 and the Secure America Act), scored per migrant kept out using the US evidence; the cost total shown is the US share. Counting everyone affected, including the people kept out, the benefits to some native workers and to the budget are far smaller than the losses: migrants forgo earnings several times higher than at home, high-skill natives lose, and enforcement costs up to about $533,000 per person deterred. Lower income costs lives, so each dollar of enforcement destroys about 97 cents to $1.31 of value.

policies.title: Medicare for All (single payer)
policies.bcr_basis: No published BCR exists for single payer. It is scored in the same transfer form as the UBI and Social Security entries: new federal spending replaces premiums and out-of-pocket costs, so it counts $1 to households per $1 in both benefit and cost; the excess burden of tax financing and the waiting-time cost are subtracted from benefits; the cost base adds any rise in national health spending. Life-years are valued at ICER's $100,000-150,000 per QALY thresholds. Financing at this scale: at the peak of the Laffer curve the US can raise at most about 7.4% of GDP in extra tax revenue and the EU-14 about 3.1% (Trabandt & Uhlig 2012, Table 7). New tax-financed outlays larger than that cannot be raised at the 34-cent marginal burden measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985); near or past the peak the marginal burden rises without limit (Browning 1987: up to more than 300% of marginal revenue). Policies whose new tax-financed outlays exceed 7.4% of GDP therefore use Feldstein's (1999) estimate, which 'may exceed $2 per $1 of revenue', at both ends of the range. New federal spending of $1.5-2.8T is 5-10% of US GDP, at or beyond the 7.4% maximum, so both ends use Feldstein's $2 per $1. The CEA's (2018) estimate that tax financing would cut GDP by 9% ($2,778bn at 2025 GDP) measures the same tax distortion and is not added; it is an output measure and assumes about $2.4T of new taxes in 2022. Waiting: Blahous (2019 testimony) notes that first-dollar coverage would raise demand by about 11% for the privately insured and 16% for the uninsured while provider payments would be cut by more than 40% in the lower-bound design, the setting in which queues arise. Canada's single-payer system had a median wait of 30.0 weeks from GP referral to treatment in 2024 (Fraser Institute, Waiting Your Turn), and Moir & Barua (Fraser Institute 2024) value patients' lost time at C$10.6bn a year (all waking hours). Scaled per person to the US and converted at 1.3494 C$ per US$: $67.3bn a year, subtracted at both ends. LOW = -0.77: Urban Institute (2019) finds its comprehensive single payer raises national health spending by $720bn and federal spending by $2.8T in 2020 (administration is inside these figures). Lives saved: Galvani's 1.73m life-years at $100,000 = $173bn, which generously assumes Galvani's mortality gain. LOW = (2,800 + 173 - 2.0 x 2,800 - 67.3) / (2,800 + 720) = -0.77. HIGH = -0.57: Galvani et al. (2020, Lancet) estimate single payer saves 13%, about $450bn a year (net of single-payer administration), and 1.73 million life-years (68,000 lives) a year, valued at $150,000 = $259.5bn; federal cost $1.5T, the low end of CBO's 2030 range for new federal subsidies (which includes administration). HIGH = (1,500 + 450 + 259.5 - 2.0 x 1,500 - 67.3) / 1,500 = -0.57. CBO's five options span national-spending changes of -$0.7T to +$0.3T in 2030, which falls between these cases. Blahous (Mercatus 2018) puts added federal spending at $32.6T over 2022-31 and says even that assumes providers accept payment cuts of more than 40%, which points to the low end; his alternative estimate without provider cuts ($38.8T) is an outlay figure, a transfer in this ratio, so it does not change the ends. Not priced: health losses from delayed treatment (no published US-applicable dollar estimate found) and physician-supply responses to 40% payment cuts (Blahous: 'We do not know how providers would respond'), both of which would lower the ends further. Benefit and cost years differ (2017-2030 dollars); that is a stated simplification. Lost-income mortality: income lost to a policy costs lives. Broughel & Viscusi (Mercatus 2017) put it at about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed; valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m, each $1 of net income lost carries 13.1/99.3 = $0.132 of mortality cost (and each $1 gained saves the same). This adjustment is applied to every policy after the range shown here is computed. Poor-country infant deaths from lower world income use Baird, Friedman & Schady (REStat 2011): +0.24 to 0.40 infant deaths per 1,000 births per 1% fall in GDP per person, on ~119.9m births a year in low- and middle-income countries (World Bank).
policies.grade_reason: The range rests on official CBO estimates and think-tank models (Urban Institute, Mercatus), plus one peer-reviewed modelling study (Galvani et al., Lancet) whose savings CBO and Urban do not replicate. Health effects of coverage are backed by quasi-experimental and randomized evidence (Miller et al. 2021 QJE; Oregon experiment), but no peer-reviewed BCA of single payer exists. The waiting-list cost is a think-tank estimate for Canada applied by analogy.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: CBO (Dec 2020) finds federal subsidies rise by $1.5-3.0T in 2030; the design closest to current bills (Option 5) is about $3.0T, used here (Urban Institute: +$2.8T in 2020; Blahous 2018: $32.6T over 2022-31). Most of this replaces private premiums and out-of-pocket spending (a transfer). Administration: shown separately within the $3.0T, at Medicare fee-for-service's ~2% administrative rate, about $60bn (CBO assumes 1.5-1.6%; critics say that is too low, supporters say billing savings shrink total admin). Private compliance: provider billing is inside national health spending, already in the ratio. GDP loss: the CEA (2018) estimates tax-financed Medicare for All would cut GDP by 9%, about $2,778bn a year at 2025 GDP, the high-end published estimate. Private cost of waiting: Canada's waiting-list time cost (Fraser Institute 2024, all waking hours, C$10.6bn) scaled per person to the US, $67.3bn a year. cost_bn = 2,940 + 60 + 67.3 + 2,778 = $5,845.3bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate by the rubric: ordinary federal legislation, with modern precedents abroad (e.g., Canada, Taiwan's 1995 single payer). Politically it is near the hard end, because it replaces employer insurance for about 150 million people and needs roughly $1.5-3T a year in new federal revenue.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Gains go mostly to the uninsured and underinsured, who are disproportionately low-income: covering low-income adults through Medicaid cut their mortality (Miller, Johnson & Wherry 2021) and cut their medical debt (Oregon experiment). Financing through broad taxes is typically more progressive than premiums.
policies.summary: Medicare for All would replace private insurance with one government plan covering everyone. It is popular, with 66% support in the CES 2022. Official and think-tank estimates agree it would add $1.5-3.0 trillion a year in federal spending, but they disagree about whether total national health spending would rise or fall, and one government estimate says the taxes to pay for it could shrink GDP by 9%. If US waiting lists grew to Canadian levels (a 30-week median wait), patients' lost time would cost about $67bn a year. Counting lives saved, waiting time and the economic drag of the extra taxes leaves each $1 destroying 0.57 to 0.77 dollars of value, because taxes on this scale sit at or past the peak of the Laffer curve: the optimistic end uses a Lancet study projecting $450bn in savings and 68,000 lives saved a year, and the pessimistic end uses an Urban Institute estimate that national spending rises by $720bn, with taxes on this scale costing about $2 of lost output per $1 raised (Feldstein 1999).

policies.title: Universal basic income (global)
policies.bcr_basis: Treated as a full, permanent, tax-financed global UBI. Net-damage construction per $1 paid out: BCR = (value to recipients - excess burden x net fiscal cost) / net fiscal cost. Value to recipients: $1 (a transfer is worth its face value to the person receiving it). Net fiscal cost = $1 + the fiscal externality of reduced earnings + delivery cost. Fiscal externality: the NBER version of the OpenResearch trial (Vivalt et al. 2024, w32719) finds treated households received an extra $950 a month ($11,400 a year) over the control group; household income excluding transfers fell by $4,215 a year in the raw survey measure (0.37 per $1) and by $3,228 in the authors' preferred adjusted measure (0.28 per $1); partners cut hours about as much as participants. Daruich & Fernández find a labour-tax-financed UBI raises the average labour tax from 22% to about 27.8%. Delivery cost per $1 delivered (excluded from the ILO costing): $0.041 (PROGRESA, Caldes, Coady & Maluccio) to $0.25 (GiveDirectly). Financing at this scale: at the peak of the Laffer curve the US can raise at most about 7.4% of GDP in extra tax revenue and the EU-14 about 3.1% (Trabandt & Uhlig 2012, Table 7). New tax-financed outlays larger than that cannot be raised at the 34-cent marginal burden measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985); near or past the peak the marginal burden rises without limit (Browning 1987: up to more than 300% of marginal revenue). Policies whose new tax-financed outlays exceed 7.4% of GDP therefore use Feldstein's (1999, REStat) estimate, which 'may exceed $2 per $1 of revenue', at both ends of the range. A global UBI costs about 32.7% of world GDP, so both ends use $2 per $1. HIGH: preferred household response 0.28 at the pre-reform 22% rate, FE = 0.28 x 0.22 = 0.062; net fiscal cost = 1.062 + 0.041 = 1.103; BCR = (1 - 2.0 x 1.103) / 1.103 = -1.09. LOW: raw household response 0.37 at the post-reform 27.8% rate, FE = 0.370 x 0.278 = 0.103; net fiscal cost = 1.103 + 0.25 = 1.353; BCR = (1 - 2.0 x 1.353) / 1.353 = -1.26. A universal, untargeted government scheme would probably deliver at nearer PROGRESA's 4 cents, which would give a low end of about -1.13. A global scheme costing 32.7% of world GDP would need far higher tax rates than Daruich & Fernández's US scheme, so the low end's fiscal externality is likely understated. The Daruich-Fernández GDP loss is the output counterpart of the excess-burden term already in the ratio, so it is reported in cost_components but not subtracted again. Cross-checks: Hendren & Sprung-Keyser (2020, QJE) score the randomized US Negative Income Tax at an MVPF of -0.01; Daruich & Fernández's dynamic GE model finds a labour-tax-financed UBI cuts steady-state GDP 12.9% and costs future generations over 9% of lifetime consumption, i.e. net damage. Excluded (the counter-evidence list): the GiveDirectly Kenya UBI RCT (Banerjee et al. 2023), which is donor-funded with no financing distortion; the Kenya local multiplier (~2.4) for a one-off transfer into poor villages, and Finland's unemployed-only pilot, neither of which is a permanent tax-financed universal payment.
policies.grade_reason: Built from a modern RCT (Vivalt et al. 2024), a peer-reviewed MVPF for the randomized NIT experiments (Hendren & Sprung-Keyser 2020, QJE) and peer-reviewed excess-burden and dynamic GE estimates (Feldstein 1999; Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Daruich & Fernández 2024); no study scores a global UBI directly.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: ILO (Ortiz et al. 2018) puts a global poverty-line UBI at 32.7% of GDP, about $34.3T a year at ~$105T world GDP; the ILO excludes administration. Administration: delivery costs per $1 delivered range from $0.041 (PROGRESA's steady-state cost-transfer ratio, Caldes, Coady & Maluccio) to $0.25 (GiveDirectly, ~80% of large-programme spending reaching recipients; GiveWell finds ~83% overall); the high end gives $8,575bn a year. Private compliance: none identified. GDP loss: Daruich & Fernandez's dynamic model finds a labour-tax-financed UBI cuts steady-state GDP 12.9%, $13,545bn a year on world GDP. cost_bn = 34,300 + 8,575 + 13,545 = $56,420bn a year (with low-end admin, $35,706bn before GDP loss).
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: a global scheme needs binding commitments across many countries, and the ILO puts a poverty-line UBI at 32.7-39.4% of GDP on average and 62-79% of GDP in low-income countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Payments go to everyone rather than being targeted, so most spending reaches the non-poor, and financing creates high implicit marginal tax rates on middle earners (Henderson 2019). Daruich & Fernandez (2024) find the long-run losses fall on future generations through lower capital and human capital.
policies.summary: A universal basic income pays every adult a regular, unconditional cash amount. It splits opinion: 45% of Americans favoured a $1,000-a-month UBI in Pew's 2020 survey, while 68% of EU respondents said they would vote for one in Dalia's 2017 poll. A randomized US trial (OpenResearch) found every $1 paid out cut recipients' household earnings by 28-37 cents, with partners cutting work as much as recipients, and delivering the money costs about 4-25 cents per $1 on top. Once that and the excess burden of the taxes needed to fund it are counted, each $1 returns between about minus $1.26 and minus $1.09, because a scheme costing a third of world GDP is far beyond what taxes can raise without very large losses, and a dynamic model finds such a scheme would shrink GDP by about 13%. Kenya's 12-year GiveDirectly UBI trial shows strong local gains in poor villages, but it is donor-funded, so the ILO's estimate of roughly a third of world GDP for a global poverty-line UBI (before delivery costs) is the relevant scale.

policies.title: Digital ID mandate worldwide
policies.bcr_basis: Built from the two randomized evaluations of biometric ID in welfare delivery (both Muralidharan, Niehaus & Sukhtankar, India). LOW (-1.0): making Aadhaar biometric authentication compulsory for food rations in Jharkhand (NBER 2020; RESTAT 2025). Benefit = change in leakage, which rose by an insignificant Rs 14 per ration card per month. Cost = extra transaction costs to government, dealers and beneficiaries, Rs 13.6 per card per month (+7.8%). BCR = -14 / 13.6 = -1.03, about -1.0. HIGH (1.1): the Andhra Pradesh biometric smartcard payment system (AER 2016), which was rolled out carefully alongside the old system. Beneficiaries' time savings alone (Rs 26 crore) exceed the programme cost (Rs 24 crore), so BCR = 26/24 = 1.08, about 1.1. Its large leakage reductions (Rs 197 crore) are mostly a transfer from corrupt officials to the state and are not counted. The spread reflects the authors' own conclusion that results depend on how the mandate and transition are managed. Platform costs: the Jharkhand low end already counts the extra costs to government, ration dealers and beneficiaries of compulsory authentication; adding the platform's own running cost to the denominator would mechanically pull a negative ratio toward zero, which would understate the harm, so it is not done. The Andhra Pradesh high end compares time savings with the smartcard system's full delivery cost, which paid for enrolment and payments through the bank commission; a share of a national ID platform's recurrent cost (0.06-0.1% of GDP) is not included and would lower the high end somewhat. Exclusion: in the Jharkhand trial the 23% of households not 'seeded' at baseline lost Rs 49 a month (12.6%), an average of 0.23 x 49 = Rs 11.3 per ration card a month, and nearly 300,000 people lost benefits; but value received by the average household was unchanged and disbursement rose slightly, so these losses are already inside the measured Rs 14 rise in leakage (disbursed minus received), and adding them again would double count. With an equity weight on excluded poor households (losses not offset by small gains to others), they would add, giving -(14 + 11.3) / 13.6 = -1.86. Not priced: surveillance and data-breach risk (Cato, EFF) and business identity-verification (KYC) costs; no published estimate attributes these to a digital ID mandate per $1 of programme cost, and all would lower both ends. Excluded (the counter-evidence list): McKinsey's 3-13% of GDP projection for consent-based 'good ID'; India's correlational DBT savings claim; and Defra's 2008 appraisal of carbon-allowance tracking (BCR 0.07-0.22), which applies only if the ID is used for personal carbon tracking.
policies.grade_reason: Both ends are converted directly from peer-reviewed randomized evaluations (RESTAT 2025; AER 2016) that report costs and benefits. Applying evidence from Indian welfare delivery to a worldwide mandate is by analogy, and the two trials point in opposite directions, so the grade is B+ rather than A.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, illustrative global extrapolation. Build/enrolment: the World Bank's ID4D cost-driver report cites enrolment and credential costs of about $4-11 per registrant; at the high end for ~8.0bn people, amortised over 10 years, $8.8bn a year. Operation and administration: recurrent costs of about 0.06-0.1% of GDP in the countries studied; at the high end on ~$105T of world GDP, $105bn a year. Cross-check: the OBR's provisional UK cost (GBP 1.8bn over three years, ~GBP 0.6bn a year) scales per person to ~$90bn a year globally. Private compliance: no published estimate. GDP loss: none published. cost_bn = 8.8 + 105 = $113.8bn a year. If the ID were also used for personal carbon-allowance tracking, Defra's GBP 52 per person a year implies about $420bn more.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: a worldwide mandate needs action in nearly every country and enrolment of billions of people. Even a single rich democracy retreated: the UK dropped compulsory right-to-work use in January 2026, and the incoming prime minister moved to scrap the scheme in July 2026.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Exclusion risk falls on the poor. About 45% of the poorest quintile in low-income countries lack ID, against 28% of the richest (ID4D 2019), and 1.5-2 million Indian welfare beneficiaries lost access at some point during the biometric authentication rollout (Muralidharan, Niehaus & Sukhtankar 2025).
policies.summary: A digital ID mandate would require everyone to hold and use a government digital identity. Public support is lukewarm: a September 2025 YouGov poll found 42% of Britons for and 45% against the UK plan. The best evidence comes from two randomized trials in India. When biometric checks were made compulsory for food rations, corruption did not fall, costs rose about 8% and hundreds of thousands of legitimate recipients lost benefits, a return of about minus $1 per dollar. A carefully managed biometric payment system in Andhra Pradesh roughly paid for itself through time savings alone (about $1.10 per $1). The range is therefore about -1.0 to 1.1, before counting privacy and surveillance risks.

policies.title: Medicare drug-price negotiation
policies.bcr_basis: Lower negotiated prices are mainly a transfer from drug makers to Medicare and its enrollees. They are scored in the same form as the other transfer policies: savings to taxpayers and enrollees, plus health gains from lower out-of-pocket costs, are the benefit; lost innovation is subtracted as a health harm; the transfer from manufacturers plus administration is the cost base. BCR = (savings + health gains - lost innovation) / (manufacturer revenue loss + administration). Savings: CBO puts negotiation's deficit reduction at $98.5bn over 2022-31 and $25bn in 2031, which is also the manufacturers' revenue loss. Cogan, Heil & Mulligan (Hoover 2025) model a fully phased-in IRA in which brand revenue falls $10.9bn a year after manufacturers' launch-price response. Administration: the $3bn appropriation spread over 10 years is $0.3bn a year; manufacturer reporting (about $0.013bn a year) does not change either end at two decimals. Lost innovation: CBO expects 13 fewer of about 1,300 new drugs over 30 years (about 1%), or 0.43 a year; valuing each lost drug at the $2.5bn of revenue needed to bring one new chemical entity to market (Dubois et al. 2015, peer-reviewed) gives $1.1bn a year. This treats revenue as the value of a drug, a floor, since patients usually gain more than the seller's revenue. The Hoover paper's own (Mulligan) method gives $4.5bn a year. The Philipson & Durie method ($196.3bn a year; 135 fewer drugs and 331.5m US life-years lost through 2039 under H.R. 5376) implies about ten times CBO's projected loss of drugs and is not used. Health gains: lower out-of-pocket costs keep patients on their medicines. Chandra, Flack & Obermeyer (2024, QJE) find Medicare patients facing smaller drug budgets 'consume fewer drugs and die more: 0.0164 percentage points per month (13.9%) for each $100 per month budget decrease', i.e. about one death per $610,000 of out-of-pocket cost (1.64e-4 / $100 a month). CMS estimates enrollees save $1.5bn in out-of-pocket costs in 2026 on the first 10 drugs and $685m in 2027 on the next 15 ($2.185bn a year). $2.185bn / $610,000 = 3,583 deaths averted a year, valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m = $46.9bn. Chandra et al. study a sharp loss of coverage at age 65; applying it to lower negotiated prices is an extrapolation. LOW = (10.9 - 4.5) / (10.9 + 0.3) = 0.57, with no health gains, because CBO has not assessed patients' health outcomes. HIGH = (25 + 46.9 - 1.1) / (25 + 0.3) = 2.80. Without the health gains the high end would be (25 - 1.1) / (25 + 0.3) = 0.94. Lost innovation is valued as a health harm, so the lost-income mortality adjustment applies only to the administration cost.
policies.grade_reason: The high end rests on official CBO and CMS estimates, converted with peer-reviewed estimates (Dubois et al. 2015, RAND Journal, for the value of a lost drug; Chandra, Flack & Obermeyer 2024, QJE, for health gains, applied by extrapolation). The low end rests on think-tank modelling (Hoover), so the best sources are official estimates, which makes it B-.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, US$bn a year: administration $0.3bn (IRA appropriation of $3bn over 10 years) + manufacturer reporting $0.013bn + lost innovation $4.5bn a year (Cogan, Heil & Mulligan 2025, Mulligan method; CBO's projection of ~13 fewer drugs in 30 years implies about $1.1bn a year at Dubois et al.'s $2.5bn per new drug). Lower prices are a transfer of about $10.9-25bn a year from manufacturers to Medicare and enrollees, so they are not a cost to society.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: it needed ordinary federal legislation (the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022) and is now run by CMS. Expanding the number of drugs, or extending negotiation to commercial insurance, would again need legislation.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Savings are spread across Medicare enrollees and taxpayers. Hoover's modelling finds Part D households save about $51 (middle income) to $65 (upper income) a year, under 0.1% of income. Costs from fewer future drugs fall on future patients generally.
policies.summary: Medicare negotiates prices for some high-spend drugs, and about 85% of Americans support it (KFF 2024; CES 2022 85.9%). Lower prices move money from drug makers to Medicare and its enrollees, and enrollees save about $2.2bn a year out of pocket on the first 25 drugs (CMS). A Quarterly Journal of Economics study finds Medicare patients who face higher drug costs take fewer medicines and die sooner; applied to these savings, that is about 3,583 deaths averted a year. Against CBO's small estimated loss of new drugs (13 of 1,300 over 30 years), each $1 returns between 57 cents and $2.80.

policies.title: Childhood immunization
policies.bcr_basis: All figures are aid-programme scale-ups in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The Copenhagen Consensus 2023 'Halftime' package raises 2022 coverage to 2030 targets for 9 vaccines (pentavalent, HPV, JE, measles, MR, MenA, PCV, rotavirus, yellow fever) in 80 LMICs; Patenaude, Sriudomporn & Mak (2023, JBCA) give benefits $762.2bn / costs $7.58bn (present value, 8% discount, VSLY valuation) = 100.5, reported as 101 in Best Things First. Ozawa et al. (2016, Health Affairs) find a return of 16 times cost for 10 vaccines in 94 LMICs when only cost of illness (treatment costs and lost productivity) is counted; their full-income value of life gives 44. Sim et al. (2020, Health Affairs) get 19.8 (cost of illness) and 52.2 (value of statistical life) for 2021-30. The Post-2015 Consensus panel gave expanded immunization $60 per $1, and Copenhagen Consensus 2012 (Jamison et al.) gave 20. Cost-of-illness methods therefore give 16-26 and value-of-life methods 44-101. US programme studies (BCR 7.5-10.9) are a different setting and are listed as counter-sources. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 13.6: Ozawa et al. 16 / 1.178 = 13.6 (all of its cost is programme spending, so the full 17.8% Gavi non-direct share is added). HIGH = 94 (lower overhead rate): CCC 100.5 / (1 + 0.075 x 0.882) = 94.3, rounded 94, where 0.882 = 1.5/1.7 is the programme (non-time) share of the CCC cost. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Several independent peer-reviewed benefit-cost/ROI studies (Patenaude et al. 2023 JBCA; Ozawa et al. 2016 and Sim et al. 2020 in Health Affairs) agree that benefits are many times costs, and each vaccine's efficacy rests on randomized controlled trials. The results are consistent across methods, datasets and decades.
policies.cost_basis: Copenhagen Consensus Best Things First leaflet (2025 web version): $1.7bn a year, of which $0.2bn is parents' time. The government/donor programme cost is therefore about $1.5bn a year; parents' time belongs inside the BCR, not in cost_bn. Cross-check: Patenaude et al. (2023) give a present-value cost of $7.58bn for 2023-2030 (8% discount), about $0.95bn a year in discounted terms. GiveWell's New Incentives programme costs about $146 per vaccinated infant at the margin in northern Nigeria, which shows the last children are expensive to reach. cost_bn = public outlay $1.5bn + administration/overhead $0.27bn + private (household) cost $0.2bn = $1.97bn/yr. Patenaude et al. (2023) cost vaccines (procurement, injection supplies, freight) plus immunization delivery costs that explicitly include labour, cold chain and its overheads, transport, buildings/utilities overheads and 'program management, short-term training, IEC/social mobilization, disease surveillance' (Section 4.1.1); Ozawa/Sim also cost vaccines, supply chain and service delivery. Country-level administration is therefore already included. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Gavi: Secretariat implementation, partners' (WHO/UNICEF/CSO) technical assistance and overhead). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: a sustained donor and government funding scale-up through national immunization programmes on the proven Gavi model. Nothing new has to be invented, but global DTP3 coverage has stalled at 85% with 14.3 million zero-dose infants in 2024 (WHO/UNICEF), and those children are in conflict-affected and remote areas.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Zero-dose children are concentrated in the poorest households and fragile states (WHO/UNICEF 2025). The averted deaths, which dominate the benefits, are mostly young children in low-income countries (Patenaude et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Paying for routine childhood vaccines (measles, pneumococcal, rotavirus, HPV and others) in poor countries is one of the best-documented high-return investments in health. Every major study finds benefits far above costs: about 16-26 times when only medical costs and lost work are counted, and 44-101 times when lives saved are valued. The Copenhagen Consensus 2023 package costs about $1.5bn a year in programme spending and saves about 523,000 lives a year. The hard part is reaching the last 10-15% of children in conflict zones and remote areas. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $1.97bn a year and the ratio range is 13.6-94.

policies.title: Blood-pressure and heart-disease drugs (aspirin, antihypertensives, polypill)
policies.bcr_basis: WHO 'Saving lives, spending less' (2018), using the Bertram et al. (2018, Lancet) method, gives $3.29 per $1 for drug therapy and counselling for people at high cardiovascular risk in low- and lower-middle-income countries. This counts only economic output and averted health spending, not the value of lives saved, so it is a floor. Nugent's Post-2015 paper gives 3-17 for multi-drug secondary prevention (DALY at $1,000 vs $5,000, 3% discount). The Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 expert panel put aspirin therapy for heart attacks at $63 per $1. The same panel gave high-blood-pressure medication $47 and a stroke/heart-attack pill (polypill) $7. Nugent's Post-2015 assessment gives aspirin for heart attack 31-153 and hypertension management 7-34. The full 'best investment' NCD package scored 23. So cheap acute aspirin is the top item, routine antihypertensives sit around 7-47, and multi-drug or polypill regimens sit lowest (3-17). Before overhead, the policy's components span 3.3-63. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 3.1: WHO 3.29 / 1.08 = 3.05, rounded 3.1. HIGH = 59 (lower overhead rate): Post-2015 panel 63 / 1.07 = 58.9, rounded 59. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Watkins et al. 2023 in JBCA; Bertram et al. 2018 in the Lancet; Nugent & Brouwer 2015 in Global Heart), with effect sizes taken from randomized-trial meta-analyses of aspirin, antihypertensives and statins, and polypill RCTs (TIPS-3, PolyIran). It is not A+ because the published BCRs for each component vary by an order of magnitude and depend heavily on the DALY value.
policies.cost_basis: Watkins, Ahmed & Pickersgill (2023, JBCA): scaling up the 'best-investment' NCD interventions in LICs and LMCs (including aspirin for heart attack, CVD primary prevention and heart-failure care in LMCs, plus near-zero-cost taxes and regulations) costs US$19bn over 2023-2030, about US$2.4bn a year. This is used as the annual government cost for the CVD drug scale-up. It is a rough proxy: it also covers a few non-CVD clinical items (e.g., early breast cancer, epilepsy) but leaves out lower-BCR CVD drugs. Cross-checks: the WHO HEARTS package costs about US$18-44 per person treated per year (Moran et al. 2022). The CCC NCD bundle is $4.4bn/yr (leaflet), and Nugent's five Post-2015 NCD interventions cost about $8.5bn/yr. cost_bn = public outlay $2.4bn + administration/overhead $0.19bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $2.59bn/yr. Watkins et al. (2023) clinical unit costs already carry a 17% above-facility (programme management) markup plus ancillary facility costs (replication data: cost-adjustment multipliers 1.17, 1.257 and 1.488 by platform). WHO's $3.29 return uses the OneHealth Tool, which costs drugs/supplies plus related health-system costs (WHO/UNDP 2019 guidance note). A larger programme markup (70% of direct service costs, used for TB by Pretorius et al. 2023) was not applied because it is specific to vertical TB programmes. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UN agency (WHO/UNICEF/UNDP) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs a sustained funding scale-up of primary-care hypertension and CVD treatment, with precedent in the WHO HEARTS programme in dozens of countries. The drugs are generic and cheap. The hard parts are screening, follow-up and adherence (in TIPS-3, 43% of participants had stopped taking the pill by the end of the trial).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits go to adults with hypertension or heart disease across all income groups in LICs and LMICs. Programmes funded by government or donors help poorer patients who cannot pay for drugs, but diagnosis and continuing care reach better-off, urban patients first, so the sources do not show the benefits are concentrated on the poorest.
policies.summary: Cheap generic drugs (aspirin at the time of a heart attack, blood-pressure pills, and combination 'polypills' with a statin) prevent heart attacks and strokes, now the leading killers in many poor countries. Copenhagen Consensus panels put aspirin for heart attacks at about $63 per $1 and blood-pressure medication at about $47. WHO's narrower economic-only estimate is $3.29, and long-term multi-drug regimens score lower (about 3-17). A primary-care scale-up costs roughly $2.4bn a year across poor countries. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $2.59bn a year and the ratio range is 3.1-59.

policies.title: Malaria: bed nets, seasonal chemoprevention, treatment
policies.bcr_basis: Shretta & Anye (2023, JBCA) cost a 10-percentage-point scale-up of insecticide-treated nets in 29 African countries at $5.7bn present value (8% discount) for 2023-2030. Benefits are $275.3bn (mortality $225.9bn, productivity $41.7bn, health-system savings $7.7bn), giving BCR 48, which is the Copenhagen Consensus 2023 figure. Middle: the Post-2015 Consensus panel put 'halve malaria infections' at $36 per $1, and Copenhagen Consensus 2012 (Jamison, Jha, Laxminarayan & Ord) gave the ACT treatment subsidy a BCR of about 35. Hallett et al. (2025, Lancet) find that an optimal HIV/TB/malaria investment returns up to $19 of health value per $1. This is a whole-portfolio figure across three diseases, so it is a conservative floor for malaria's highest-value tools. The same paper gives $3.50 if only direct economic benefits are counted (see counter-sources). Seasonal malaria chemoprevention has no published BCR in these sources. Its cost-effectiveness is similar to nets: GiveWell estimates about $4,000 per life saved for SMC versus $5,500 for nets. ACCESS-SMC (2020, Lancet) found 88% protective effectiveness within 28 days at about $3.63 per child per season. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 17.4: Hallett et al. 19 / 1.090 = 17.4. HIGH = 45 (lower overhead rate): Shretta & Anye 48 / 1.067 = 45.0. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Shretta & Anye 2023 in JBCA; Hallett et al. 2025 in the Lancet) built on randomized-trial evidence for nets, SMC and ACTs, with large-scale observational confirmation (Bhatt et al. 2015; ACCESS-SMC 2020). It is not A+ because there is essentially one BCA per component rather than several independent BCAs.
policies.cost_basis: Costed scale-ups behind the BCRs: Copenhagen Consensus 2023 net scale-up $1.1bn a year (leaflet), plus about $0.3bn a year for the ACT treatment subsidy (Jamison et al. 2012) = about $1.4bn a year. SMC adds little: about $3.63 per child per season (ACCESS-SMC). The full funding gap is larger: WHO World Malaria Report 2025 says US$3.9bn was spent in 2024 against a US$9.3bn target, a shortfall of about US$5.4bn a year. Filling all of it would likely have a lower marginal BCR than the costed scale-ups. cost_bn = public outlay $1.4bn + administration/overhead $0.13bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $1.53bn/yr. Shretta & Anye (2023) cost nets, their distribution and social-behaviour-change communication from country and literature unit costs (Table 3); the authors state that active-surveillance costs are not included. Jamison et al. (2012) price the ACT subsidy at delivered cost. National programme management is not itemised separately, so only the funder overhead is added. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Global Fund Secretariat operating expenses). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: a sustained donor funding scale-up (only 42% of the required funding was attained in 2024) through proven channels: the Global Fund, PMI, national malaria programmes, AMF and Malaria Consortium. Precedent: SMC grew from 170,000 to 54 million children per cycle between 2012 and 2024, and several countries have been certified malaria-free.
policies.who_benefits_reason: About 95% of malaria deaths are in the WHO African Region and about 75% of those are children under five (World Malaria Report 2025). The burden falls on the poorest rural households. Sarma et al. (2019) find larger income effects from reduced malaria in poorer, high-burden countries.
policies.summary: Insecticide-treated bed nets, seasonal preventive drugs for young children in the Sahel, and cheap combination treatment are the core tools against malaria, which still kills about 610,000 people a year, mostly African children. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies put the return at about $19-48 per dollar when lives saved are valued, and GiveWell estimates $4,000-5,500 per life saved. Costed scale-ups need about $1.4bn a year, while the global funding gap is about $5.4bn a year. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $1.53bn a year and the ratio range is 17.4-45.

policies.title: Micronutrients
policies.bcr_basis: Component BCRs: (1) Multiple micronutrient supplements (MMS) replacing iron-folic acid for pregnant women: BCR 37.5 at 8% discount (Larsen, Hoddinott & Razvi 2023, JBCA). This sets the high end. MMS plus calcium is 19-24 (the CCC leaflet's nutrition item), and the whole CCC nutrition package (MMS, calcium, complementary feeding, SQ-LNS) is 18. (2) Staple-food fortification: iron fortification of flour about 8 (Horton, Alderman & Rivera 2008: 8 at 3% discount, 7 at 6%; Copenhagen Consensus guide: $1,336M benefits / $167M cost = 8.0). Horton & Ross (2003, Food Policy) give a median of 6 for iron fortification counting physical productivity only, which sets the low end, rising to 36 with cognitive benefits. Salt iodization is about 30 ($570M / $19M; GAIN cites 28). GAIN (Garrett et al. 2019) gives 27 for fortification overall. (3) Child vitamin A supplementation: no published BCR was found. A Cochrane review of 19 trials (Imdad et al. 2022) shows 12% lower all-cause child mortality, and GiveWell estimates about $3,500 per life saved, its most cost-effective top charity. The Post-2015 panel's 45 for 'reduce child malnutrition' is a broader stunting package and is not used. Before overhead the range is 6 (iron fortification, productivity only) to 37.5 (MMS). Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 5.6: Horton & Ross 6 / 1.08 = 5.6. HIGH = 35 (lower overhead rate): Larsen et al. 37.5 / 1.07 = 35.0. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Larsen et al. 2023 in JBCA; Horton & Ross 2003 in Food Policy) backed by randomized trials and meta-analyses (Cochrane review of vitamin A supplementation, 19 trials, 1.2 million children, high-certainty evidence). It is not A+ because a large trial (DEVTA) found a non-significant mortality effect for vitamin A, and no BCA covers the exact iron-zinc-vitamin A fortification bundle.
policies.cost_basis: Sum of costed components: iron flour fortification at 50% coverage in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa $167M/yr, plus salt iodization at 80% coverage $19M/yr (Copenhagen Consensus guide), plus MMS for pregnant women about $84M/yr and calcium about $216M/yr (Larsen et al. 2023). Total = 0.167 + 0.019 + 0.084 + 0.216 = $0.486bn, rounded to $0.5bn a year. Not included: zinc/vitamin A in fortification (no separate cost found) and scaling up child vitamin A supplementation (~$2 per child-year per GiveWell; existing programmes already reach many children). Much of fortification's cost is borne by millers and passed to consumers rather than paid by government. The CCC nutrition package as a whole is $1.4bn/yr including $0.2bn of time costs. cost_bn = public outlay $0.5bn + administration/overhead $0.04bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $0.54bn/yr. Larsen, Hoddinott & Razvi (2023) include an incremental delivery cost of US$0.50-1.45 per pregnant woman for MMS through antenatal care. The fortification cost lines (Copenhagen Consensus guide; Horton et al. 2008) are total resource costs, including the share borne by millers and salt producers, so industry compliance cost is already counted in public outlay rather than added again. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UN agency (UNICEF/WFP/WHO) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Easy: one health ministry or food regulator can mandate fortification under existing food-standards law, and over 60 countries already have 70%+ household coverage of iodized salt. Supplements in pregnancy and vitamin A capsules can be funded by a single donor or health ministry through existing antenatal and child-health days. The total cost is about $0.5bn a year.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Micronutrient deficiency is concentrated among poor households that rely on cheap, nutrient-poor staples. 80% of undernourished children are in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa (Copenhagen Consensus), and vitamin A and pregnancy supplements are delivered through public programmes that reach low-income mothers and children.
policies.summary: Adding iron, zinc and vitamin A to flour, salt and oil, giving pregnant women a daily multiple-micronutrient tablet, and giving young children vitamin A capsules all cost cents to a few dollars per person a year. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies put the return at about 6-8 per dollar for iron fortification counting only productivity, about 30 for iodized salt, and about 37 for prenatal multiple micronutrients. Vitamin A capsules cut child deaths by about 12% in trials and are among GiveWell's most cost-effective programmes. The costed package is about $0.5bn a year. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $0.54bn a year and the ratio range is 5.6-35.

policies.title: Tobacco and alcohol excise taxes
policies.bcr_basis: HIGH = 100: Watkins, Ahmed & Pickersgill (2023, JBCA, Copenhagen Consensus Halftime), replication data, 8% discount, 2023-30, LICs+LMCs: tobacco excise tax gross benefits $51.31bn PV against incremental implementation cost $0.045bn and a forgone-consumer-surplus charge of $0.462bn = 101.2 (LMCs 102, LICs 94). Alcohol excise tax: $2.94bn / ($0.029bn + $0.026bn) = 53.3 (LICs 53). The implementation cost includes tax administration (WHO/UNDP 2019 costing convention: programme costs at the administrative level), and the marginal administrative cost of raising an existing excise rate is reported to be small (India: US$5.7m/yr), so no further cost is added at the high end. Without any consumer-surplus charge the tobacco BCR would be 620 (LICs) to 1,300 (LMCs); that is not used. Middle: the Post-2015 panel gave 'increase tobacco prices 125%' $22 per $1; Nugent (Post-2015) gave tobacco tax 10-52; WHO 'Saving lives, spending less' (2018) gives $7.43 (tobacco package) and $9.13 (alcohol) counting only output and averted health spending. LOW = 2.9: base-case tobacco-tax benefits reduced by 10% for illicit substitution (World Bank 2019: illicit trade is about 10% of global consumption; tax increases add little to it) divided by Watkins' cost and surplus charge plus the upper-bound annual costs in cost_components (collection $0.80bn + enforcement $0.45bn + secure stamps $1.21bn = $2.46bn/yr) over 8 years: 0.9 x 51.31 / (0.045 + 0.462 + 6.206 x 2.46) = 46.18 / 15.79 = 2.9. WHO's 7.4 lies inside the range. Note on the consumer-surplus charge: the paper text describes offsets of 0.9 (tobacco/alcohol) and 0.5 (salt) of health benefits, but the replication code applies 0.009 and 0.001; if the paper's stated 90% offset were subtracted from benefits, the tobacco BCR would be 0.1 x 1,134 = 113, above the published 101, so the high end is not overstated on that account. Tax revenue is a transfer and is not a benefit. Elasticities behind the health effects: tobacco about -0.4 (Jha & Peto 2014); alcohol -0.51 (Wagenaar et al. 2009).
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Watkins et al. 2023 in JBCA; Bertram et al. 2018 in the Lancet, underlying WHO's ROI figures), built on price elasticities from meta-analyses of many quasi-experimental and econometric studies (Wagenaar et al. 2009; Jha & Peto 2014). It is not A+ because the BCR depends heavily on how lost consumer surplus is treated (100 vs 1,300) and no RCTs exist.
policies.cost_basis: cost_bn = public outlay $0 + administration/enforcement $1.26bn + industry compliance $1.21bn = $2.47bn/yr (upper bound; details in cost_components). Tax revenue is a transfer, so only administrative, enforcement and compliance costs count. Watkins et al. (2023) put full implementation of India's tobacco tax increase at US$5.7m a year, and their replication data give a PV implementation cost of $0.045bn (tobacco) + $0.029bn (alcohol) for all LICs and LMCs over 2023-30 (~$0.012bn/yr). Chisholm et al. (2018) put alcohol excise tax implementation below I$0.10 per capita. Tax collection, illicit-trade enforcement and secure tax stamps are costed from WHO (2021) and World Bank (2019) ratios. Funding status: tax administration and enforcement are carried out and paid for by national governments; donors (e.g., Bloomberg Philanthropies, WHO FCTC programmes) fund technical assistance. Costs here are government administration plus industry compliance.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs ordinary tax legislation in each country, with many precedents (the Philippines, Turkey, South Africa and others have raised tobacco excise sharply). Industry lobbying and smuggling concerns are the main obstacles. Progress on tobacco taxes has stalled partly because of tobacco-industry political influence.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Global Tobacco Economics Consortium (2018, BMJ): in 13 middle-income countries, a 50% cigarette price rise gives the poorest 20% 6.7 times more life-years than the richest 20%, averts 8.8 million men's falls into extreme poverty, and the poorest pay only about 10% of the extra tax. Measured as a share of cash spent, the tax is regressive for poor smokers who do not quit (Remler 2004).
policies.summary: Raising excise taxes on cigarettes and alcohol pushes up prices, which cuts smoking and heavy drinking, especially among the young and the poor, and raises revenue. Copenhagen Consensus analysis puts the return at about 53-100 per dollar of social cost; WHO's narrower economic-only estimates are $7.43 for tobacco and $9.13 for alcohol. Counting the full cost of collecting the tax, policing smuggling and secure tax stamps (up to about $2.47bn a year across poor countries) and a 10% loss of benefit to illicit cigarettes lowers the bottom of the range to about 2.9. Jha and Peto estimate that doubling real cigarette prices could cut smoking by about a third.

policies.title: School-based deworming
policies.bcr_basis: LOW = 6: Copenhagen Consensus best-practice paper (Hall & Horton), 'each dollar spent results in about $6 of benefits' for preschool children. HIGH = 100: DCP3 (Ahuja et al., Vol. 8 Ch. 29) reports the long-run benefits from the Kenyan Primary School Deworming Project (Baird et al. 2016, QJE) as 'more than 100 times the cost', with an annualised internal rate of return of 32-51%; Copenhagen's own high-prevalence figure is 'up to 60 times' the costs. The 20-year follow-up (Hamory et al. 2021, PNAS) finds an annualised social internal rate of return of 37% at a 10% discount rate, with a social net present value of US$ PPP 231-468 per child. Cost is about $0.30 per child per treatment; treating most of the 870 million at-risk children costs under $0.3bn a year (DCP3 p. 419). The evidence is disputed: the Cochrane review (Taylor-Robinson et al. 2015) finds no effect on many outcomes from mass drug administration, which is why the low end uses the conservative Copenhagen figure.
policies.grade_reason: Built on a long-run cluster-randomized trial with peer-reviewed economic returns (Baird et al. 2016, QJE; Hamory et al. 2021, PNAS) and a Copenhagen Consensus best-practice paper, but the wider trial evidence is contested (Cochrane review), so B+ rather than A.
policies.cost_basis: About $0.30 per child per treatment; under $0.3bn a year to treat most of the 870 million at-risk children in low- and middle-income countries (DCP3 Vol. 8 Ch. 29, p. 419). Drugs are largely donated.
policies.difficulty_reason: Delivered through existing schools once or twice a year with cheap, largely donated drugs.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Children in poor, high-infection areas; the Kenyan trial's long-run gains in earnings and consumption accrue to them as adults.
policies.summary: Giving schoolchildren a cheap pill once or twice a year clears intestinal worms that sap nutrition and school attendance. A long-running randomized trial in Kenya found the treated children earned and consumed more as adults twenty years later, an annual social return of 37%, and the development-economics handbook DCP3 puts the long-run benefits at more than 100 times the cost. Copenhagen Consensus's conservative figure is about $6 per $1. The wider evidence is disputed, so the range is wide, but at about $0.30 per child the whole programme costs under $0.3bn a year.

policies.title: Contraception & family planning
policies.bcr_basis: Main policy = universal access to modern contraception. Kohler & Behrman (Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015) give 120 for meeting the unmet need of 214 million women at ~$3.6bn/yr; about 40 of this comes from health benefits (640,000 fewer newborn and 150,000 fewer maternal deaths a year) and the rest from a $288bn/yr demographic dividend (Lomborg 2019). Madise et al. (2023, JBCA, 8% discount) give 22 for the 'family planning' package alone in 55 LICs/LMICs (Figure 3). In between, Ghana Priorities (Amporfu et al. 2020, 8%) gives 33.6 (married women, +10 pp contraceptive prevalence) and 29.3 (unmarried women). The spread reflects how much demographic-dividend benefit is counted and the discount rate (Post-2015 work used lower rates than the 8% of the Halftime/Ghana studies). Sub-policy (girls' full secondary education) is not folded into the range because its returns are lower and differently measured: the Ghana scholarship RCT (Duflo, Dupas & Kremer 2021; Duflo, Dupas, Spelke & Walsh 2026, AER) gives a conservative $4.1 per $1 of long-run government cost, rising to 10-110x when targeted at girls and counting their children's survival (VoxDev summary); Copenhagen Post-2015 puts secondary completion at ~4 and girls' schooling/later marriage programmes at ~5. If the sub-policy were bundled at its cost (~$15bn/yr upper bound) the combined ratio would fall to roughly (3.6x22 + 15x4.1)/18.6 = 7.6 at the low end and (3.6x120 + 15x10)/18.6 = 31 at the high end. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 20.4: Madise et al. 22 / 1.08 = 20.4. HIGH = 112 (lower overhead rate): Kohler & Behrman 120 / 1.07 = 112.1, rounded 112. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimate including family planning (Madise et al. 2023, JBCA) consistent with Copenhagen Post-2015 and Ghana Priorities BCRs, backed by quasi-experimental evidence (Matlab, Bangladesh: Joshi & Schultz 2013 Demography; Colombia: Miller 2010 Economic Journal). The girls'-education sub-policy rests on a 15-year randomized trial with a peer-reviewed BCR (Duflo et al. 2026, AER).
policies.cost_basis: $3.6bn a year to provide modern contraception to the 214 million women with unmet need (Kohler & Behrman, Copenhagen Consensus, as reported by Lomborg 2019); donor funding for family planning was only ~$1.27bn in 2017. Funding: government/donor spending. The girls' secondary-education sub-policy is costed separately and not included: ~$505 per girl for four years of senior high school including forgone wages (VoxDev summary of the Ghana trial) = ~$126/yr; x 122 million out-of-school girls (UNESCO) = ~$15bn/yr, an upper bound since many are primary-age. cost_bn = public outlay $3.6bn + administration/overhead $0.29bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $3.89bn/yr. The $3.6bn/yr Kohler & Behrman figure comes from the Guttmacher 'Adding It Up' costing, whose method adds 'programs and systems costs' (program management, supervision, M&E, training, outreach, supply systems, HMIS) to direct costs; Madise et al. (2023) cost staff, consumables, overheads and supervision. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UNFPA standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs a sustained donor/government funding scale-up (~$3.6bn a year vs ~$1.27bn donor funding in 2017; Lomborg 2019) with working precedents, e.g. Bangladesh's Matlab outreach programme (Joshi & Schultz 2013) and Colombia's Profamilia (Miller 2010). The girls'-education sub-policy is a larger, budget-heavy scale-up with a tested model in Ghana's scholarships.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Unmet need is concentrated among poorer women in high-fertility low-income countries (Kohler & Behrman; Madise et al. 2023 cover 55 LICs/LMICs). Matlab showed long-run gains in women's and children's health in rural Bangladesh (Joshi & Schultz 2013). The Ghana scholarships were means-tested; female recipients gained 20-30% in earnings and their children's mortality fell (J-PAL; Duflo et al. 2026).
policies.summary: Fund modern contraception (pills, injectables, implants, IUDs, counselling) for the roughly 214 million women in poor countries who want to avoid pregnancy but lack access, at about $3.6bn a year. Copenhagen Consensus estimates $22-120 of benefit per $1, depending on how much of the 'demographic dividend' from smaller families is counted; health benefits alone give about $40. A sub-policy, paying for girls to finish secondary school, is backed by a 15-year randomized trial in Ghana (Duflo, Dupas, Kremer and co-authors): it delayed childbearing, raised women's earnings and halved infant mortality among their children, returning at least $4 per $1 of government cost, more if targeted at girls. The headline ratio is for family planning; the schooling sub-policy is valuable but lower-return and costs far more. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $3.89bn a year and the ratio range is 20.4-112.

policies.title: Maternal & newborn care: cut neonatal deaths 65% via basic hospital upgrades
policies.bcr_basis: To avoid double counting with #27, this item is defined as facility obstetric and newborn care only (no family planning). Madise et al. (2023, JBCA, 55 LICs/LMICs, 8% discount, coverage raised from 68% to 90%) report by package (Figure 3): BEmONC alone = 83 and comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care (CEmONC, adds caesarean capacity) = 65; these set the high and low ends before overhead. The CCC headline of 87 (Lomborg 2023; leaflet) is BEmONC + family planning and includes a $25bn/yr demographic dividend, so it is not used. Wider packages score lower (entire continuum of care 36; antenatal 7) and are reported as counter-evidence. Benefits are mostly newborn lives: the BEmONC+FP package averts 1.20m newborn and 161,000 maternal deaths a year (newborn lives worth $238bn of $281bn benefits, VSLY $2,983). Valuing stillbirths averted would raise the bundle's BCR to 159. On the '65%' target: universal coverage of existing interventions would avert 71% of neonatal deaths, 82% of that through facility-based care (Bhutta et al. 2014); Madise's 1.2m of 2.16m LIC/LMIC neonatal deaths is about 56%. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 62: 65 / (1 + 0.08 x 0.571) = 62.2, rounded 62, where 0.571 = 2.8/4.9 is the financial share of the CCC cost (the rest is mothers' time). HIGH = 80 (lower overhead rate): 83 / (1 + 0.07 x 0.571) = 79.8, rounded 80. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis (Madise et al. 2023, JBCA; Lomborg 2023 JBCA summary) whose intervention effects come from the trial-based Lives Saved Tool evidence summarised in the Lancet Every Newborn series (Bhutta et al. 2014).
policies.cost_basis: Lomborg (2023) Table 3.1 / CCC leaflet: maternal & newborn package costs $4.9bn/yr (2023-30 average), of which $2.1bn is mothers' time (non-financial), leaving $2.8bn of financial (government/donor) cost. That package includes family planning; Madise et al. (2023) Table 2 costs FP at 68.6m extra women x ($2.89 + $2.14 + $0.65 + $0.75 = $6.43) = ~$0.44bn/yr. Facility care excluding FP therefore ~$2.8bn - $0.4bn = ~$2.4bn/yr (approximate, since it mixes 2020 and 2023 dollar bases). Cross-check: Bhutta et al. (2014) put facility-based care at $3.66bn of a $5.65bn/yr incremental running cost for universal coverage. cost_bn = public outlay $2.4bn + administration/overhead $0.19bn + private (household) cost $2.1bn = $4.69bn/yr. Madise et al. (2023) include provider costs (staff, consumables, equipment, overheads), a 15% supervision add-on, beneficiary costs (travel) and demand-generation costs. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UN agency (UNICEF/UNFPA/WHO) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs a sustained government/donor scale-up to staff, equip and supply birth facilities in 55 countries (Madise et al. 2023), plus demand-generation payments for facility births on the model of India's Janani Suraksha Yojana, which Madise et al. use for costing. Precedent exists, but it is a health-system build-out, not a single-agency switch.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The 55 low- and lower-middle-income countries modelled carry about 90% of global maternal and neonatal deaths; the welfare loss from these deaths is ~5.5% of their GDP (Madise et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Upgrade basic hospitals and health centres in poor countries so every birth has trained staff, clean delivery, drugs to stop bleeding, antibiotics, newborn resuscitation and steroids for preterm labour. Peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus analysis finds $65-83 of benefit per $1 for these facility packages, mainly from newborn lives saved, at roughly $2.4bn a year in public cost. Existing interventions could prevent about 71% of newborn deaths, most of them through better care at birth. The often-quoted ratio of 87 also includes family planning, which is counted separately under policy 27. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $4.69bn a year and the ratio range is 62-80.

policies.title: Scale up tuberculosis diagnosis + treatment by 90%
policies.bcr_basis: Pretorius et al. (2023, JBCA, Copenhagen Consensus Halftime) cost-benefit analysis of the Stop TB Global Plan 2023-2030 (modern diagnostics, screening, treatment, prevention) in LICs/LMICs, without new vaccines, vs standard baseline, 8% discount, effects to 2050: incremental costs $56.4bn and benefits $2,595bn (PV, 2020 US$) = 46.0; 27.3m deaths averted (~1m/yr) at ~$2,063 per death averted. The paper's own sensitivity range is 28-84: about 28 with vaccines and R&D costs included (27.7) and about 84 against the disruption baseline at a 5% discount (83.9); these set the low and high ends before overhead. Other cells: 55.4 at 5%, 36.6 at 12%, 34.0 including R&D, 71.0 vs the COVID-disruption baseline. Consistent with Copenhagen Post-2015 (Vassall): cut TB deaths 95% and incidence 90% for $8.1bn/yr, BCR 43. The older World Bank estimate of 9-15 (Laxminarayan et al. 2007) is below this range and listed as counter-evidence. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 26: 27.7 / (1 + 0.090 x 0.839) = 25.8, rounded 26, where 0.839 = 5.2/6.2 is the financed share of the total cost. HIGH = 79 (lower overhead rate): 83.9 / (1 + 0.067 x 0.839) = 79.4, rounded 79. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost analysis (Pretorius et al. 2023, JBCA), consistent with Post-2015 (43) and with positive older World Bank estimates, built on the trial-established efficacy of standard TB treatment and diagnostics.
policies.cost_basis: Lomborg's Best Things First Table 3.1 lists TB 'Total cost $6.2 billion' and, in a separate column 'whereof non-financial cost', '$1.0 billion enabler cost'. Total social cost = $6.2bn/yr (2023-30 average; used in the BCR) and the part that governments/donors must finance = $6.2bn - $1.0bn = $5.2bn/yr. This matches Pretorius et al.'s year-by-year incremental costs: $4.4bn in 2023, peaking at $7.1bn in 2027, $5.2bn in 2030. Post-2015 (Vassall) costed a 95%-death / 90%-incidence target at $8.1bn/yr. cost_bn = public outlay $5.2bn + administration/overhead $0.47bn + private (household) cost $1.0bn = $6.67bn/yr. Pretorius et al. (2023) state that costs 'include health system costs and substantial markups beyond patient costs such as program costs and enablers'; programme (above-patient) costs are a 70% markup on direct service costs, based on expenditure data reported to WHO. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Global Fund Secretariat operating expenses). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with precedent: national TB programmes already treat 8.3m people a year with 88% success for drug-susceptible TB, but only US$5.9bn was available in 2024 against a US$22bn annual target for 2027 (WHO 2025).
policies.who_benefits_reason: TB deaths (over 1.2m in 2024; WHO 2025) are concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and the modelled ~1m deaths averted a year are in LICs/LMICs (Pretorius et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Find and treat far more TB cases in poor countries: rapid molecular tests, screening of high-risk groups, full treatment courses, prevention for contacts, and work with private clinics. A peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus study puts the return at about $46 per $1 (range 28-84), saving close to a million lives a year at roughly $2,000 per death averted. Governments and donors would need to find about $5.2bn a year (about $6.2bn including patients' non-financial costs). Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $6.67bn a year and the ratio range is 26-79.

policies.title: HIV prevention (voluntary medical male circumcision)
policies.bcr_basis: Geldsetzer, Bloom, Humair & Bärnighausen (2015, Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015) model raising male circumcision coverage to 90% of HIV-negative adult men in the five hyperendemic countries (Botswana, Lesotho, South Africa, Swaziland, Zimbabwe), 2015-2030. Their BCR tables: 7.4 (5% discount, $1,000 per life-year), 11.3 (3%, $1,000), 37.0 (5%, $5,000) and 56.4 (3%, $5,000); the lowest and highest set the range before overhead. The Copenhagen summary headline is 28 (annual benefits $818m / annual costs $30m = 27.3). These value only life-years gained; health-system savings alone are also large: scaling VMMC to 80% in 13 countries costs $2bn (2011-2025) and yields $16.51bn net savings in averted HIV care (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011), and each circumcision at age 20 in South Africa saves a net $617 at 5% (Haacker et al. 2016). Returns fall as HIV incidence falls: a five-model comparison found continued VMMC cost-effective in 68% of settings (Bansi-Matharu et al. 2023), so the low end is the safer guide where incidence is now lower. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 6.8: Geldsetzer et al. 7.4 / 1.090 = 6.8. HIGH = 53 (lower overhead rate): Geldsetzer et al. 56.4 / 1.067 = 52.9, rounded 53. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed economic evaluations (Njeuhmeli 2011 and Haacker 2016, PLOS Medicine; Bansi-Matharu 2023, Lancet Global Health) and a Copenhagen Consensus BCR, all built on randomized controlled trials showing ~60% protection against HIV acquisition (Auvert et al. 2005, ANRS 1265; Kenya and Uganda trials).
policies.cost_basis: Copenhagen Post-2015 summary: $30m a year (outcome document $35m). Geldsetzer et al. (2015) Table 1: additional cost over maintaining current coverage = $451.9m (3% discount) to $524.7m (5%) over 2015-2030, i.e. ~$30-35m a year. Unit cost $65.85-$95.15 per circumcision (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011). Funding: government/donor spending (PEPFAR, Global Fund). cost_bn = public outlay $0.03bn + administration/overhead $0.0027bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $0.033bn/yr. Njeuhmeli et al. (2011) unit costs, used by Geldsetzer et al. (2015), include direct costs (consumables, staff, training) and indirect costs (capital, maintenance, utilities, support overhead and management overhead) plus waste-management and supply-chain costs; they exclude demand-creation costs, for which no global estimate was found. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Global Fund Secretariat operating expenses (used as the rate for the PEPFAR/Global Fund channel)). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained donor-funded scale-up with precedent (national VMMC programmes across 13 eastern and southern African countries modelled by Njeuhmeli et al. 2011). Cost is small, but prevention depends on aid: international assistance funds 80% of HIV prevention programmes in LMICs, and 2025 cuts put it at risk (UNAIDS 2025). Demand creation among adult men is the practical bottleneck.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Targets hyperendemic Southern African countries (adult HIV prevalence >15%) where HIV is a leading cause of lost life and income; women also benefit over time as fewer male partners are infected (Geldsetzer et al. 2015).
policies.summary: Offer free, voluntary medical circumcision to HIV-negative adult men in the Southern African countries with the highest HIV rates. Three randomized trials found it cuts men's risk of acquiring HIV by about 60%, and it is a one-off procedure costing under $100.
