Copenhagen Consensus puts the return at about $28 per $1 (range 7-56 depending on discount rate and how a life-year is valued), for only $30-35 million a year; it also saves more on future HIV treatment than it costs. Returns are falling where HIV incidence has declined. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $0.033bn a year and the ratio range is 6.8-53.

policies.title: Privatize Social Security into personal accounts
policies.bcr_basis: The ratio compares what later generations gain from funded personal accounts with what the transition generations pay to keep honouring benefits already promised. HIGH = 2.0: Feldstein & Samwick (1998, NBER volume Privatizing Social Security) simulate a shift to Mandatory Individual Retirement Accounts. In the long run, about 2.04-2.1% of payroll in accounts replaces the 12.4% payroll tax, and deadweight loss falls by 1.57% of payroll (a combined gain of 11.92% of payroll). In the early decades, workers pay an extra 0.82% of payroll in year 1, rising to 1.58% by year 15. In their worked family example (3% discount rate), two 45-year-old parents lose $11,680 in present value and their two children gain more than $23,000: 23,000 / 11,680 = 1.97, rounded to 2.0. Feldstein (1996, AER P&P) puts the net present-value gain above $15 trillion, about 3% of future GDP a year. LOW = 1.0: Geanakoplos, Mitchell & Zeldes (1998) show that once the debt to current retirees and workers is paid (about a permanent 3% of payroll), the higher return on accounts disappears; without extra saving, privatization moves money between generations rather than creating it. Kotlikoff (1998) finds the pure efficiency gain, after fully compensating transition generations, ranges from 7.23% of lifetime income (cold-turkey) and 4.33% (consumption-tax financing) down to 1.08% (payroll-tax financing). It turns into a 1.22% loss with income-tax financing and strong benefit-tax linkage, so the ratio can dip slightly below 1 under some designs. Caveats: Feldstein & Samwick credit accounts with the return on capital, and their own sensitivity case (5.4% return) raises the long-run contribution to 3.31% of payroll. Feldstein & Samwick also find the summed present value for everyone aged 20-65 at the switch is negative, so the gains go mainly to the young and the unborn. Both ends already include the costs counted in cost_bn. The transition financing is the denominator of the high end (the parents' $11,680 present-value loss in Feldstein & Samwick's worked example) and of the low end (Geanakoplos, Mitchell & Zeldes net the legacy debt out of the account return). Feldstein & Samwick also deduct account administration: they assume a 9.0% return against the 9.30% actually reported, i.e. 0.30 points of assets a year for administrative costs. Diamond's $40-50 per worker is a level estimate of the same cost and is not added again. A discussant of the Feldstein & Samwick chapter notes that Latin American account systems cost at least 1% of assets; that higher cost is not modelled in the published family example and is a downside risk to the high end.
policies.grade_reason: The numbers come from published theory quantified in peer-reviewed or academic-press models: Feldstein (1996, AER P&P); Feldstein & Samwick and Kotlikoff (1998, University of Chicago Press/NBER); Kotlikoff, Smetters & Walliser and Cooley & Soares (1999, Review of Economic Dynamics). They are supported by a historical case (Chile 1981; Schmidt-Hebbel 1998 credits the reform with about a quarter of Chile's growth increase). It is not B+ because no peer-reviewed natural experiment measures the gain and turns it into a BCR. The rate-of-return gain is also disputed in peer-reviewed-quality work (Geanakoplos, Mitchell & Zeldes).
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: transition financing of 0.82-1.58% of taxable payroll (Feldstein & Samwick 1998) on 2025 taxable payroll of about $10,670bn (2026 Trustees Report) = $87-169bn a year; the $169bn high end is used. This is the extra amount current workers pay while benefits already promised (closed-group unfunded obligation $55.6 trillion in present value, Trustees Table VI.F2) continue; much of it is saving credited to their own accounts. Administration: Diamond (1999) puts a government-organised account system at $40-50 per worker per year; inflated to 2025 prices and applied to 185 million covered workers this is $14.3-17.9bn a year ($17.9bn used). Private compliance: none identified. GDP loss: no published estimate. cost_bn = 169.0 + 17.9 = $186.9bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate under the rubric: it needs ordinary federal legislation, and full or partial privatization has precedents (Chile 1981 and other Latin American countries, World Bank 2005). It is politically among the hardest moderate items: the 2005 US personal-accounts proposal never reached a vote, and Cooley & Soares (1999) find no majority supports a transition in its first periods.
policies.who_benefits_reason: In the long run, gains reach all income classes. Kotlikoff (1998) finds poorer classes gain more (about 10.1%) than richer ones (about 8.1%) under consumption-tax financing. The transition generations lose, though: without compensation, the oldest cohorts lose up to about 26% of remaining lifetime welfare, and all those aged 20-65 lose in aggregate (Feldstein & Samwick). Without a progressive floor, the loss of Social Security's progressive benefit formula and coverage gaps (World Bank 2005, Latin America) could make the outcome regressive for low earners.
policies.summary: This policy would replace pay-as-you-go Social Security with funded personal retirement accounts, phasing the old system out. Simulation studies find large long-run gains: about 2% of payroll in accounts eventually replaces the 12.4% payroll tax, and the economy's capital stock and wages rise. Those gains go mostly to young and future workers, while today's workers must also keep paying for benefits already promised. Counting both sides gives roughly $1.00 to $2.00 of benefit per $1 of transition cost, and critics argue that the higher return is mostly a transfer rather than a net gain.

policies.title: Abolish the income tax
policies.bcr_basis: The ratio is the benefit to taxpayers per $1 of income-tax revenue given up, assuming the revenue is replaced by cutting government (the 'shrink the size of government' sub-policy) and the forgone spending is valued at $1 per $1: BCR = 1 + DWL/R (deadweight loss removed per $) + C/R (compliance cost removed per $). Revenue at stake is FY2025 individual income tax $2,656bn plus corporate $452bn = $3,108bn, 59% of federal receipts ($5,235bn) or 44% of outlays ($7,010bn) (CBO). C/R counts the full avoided income-tax compliance cost (Tax Foundation 2024, from OIRA/IRS paperwork-burden estimates) plus avoided IRS administration A/R (0.59 x $19.0bn FY2025 IRS operations = $11.2bn). LOW = 1.24: DWL/R = 0.13, the lower bound of Ballard, Shoven & Whalley's (AER 1985) gain from replacing the whole tax system with lump-sum taxes (13-22 cents per $). C/R = $328.9bn income-tax forms (individual $145.4bn + business income-tax returns $118.9bn + depreciation $25.4bn + estates and trusts $20.2bn + QBI deduction $19.0bn) / $3,108bn = 0.106; A/R = 11.2 / 3,108 = 0.004. 1 + 0.13 + 0.106 + 0.004 = 1.24. HIGH = 3.2: DWL/R = 2.0, Feldstein's (1999, REStat) 'nearly two dollars' of deadweight loss per extra $ raised by a proportional rate rise. C/R = $501.3bn (all federal tax paperwork $546.1bn less the $44.8bn employer quarterly return still needed for payroll taxes) / $3,108bn = 0.161; A/R = 0.004. 1 + 2.0 + 0.161 + 0.004 = 3.17, rounded to 3.2. The high end applies a marginal figure to the whole tax (an upper bound). Central: Saez, Slemrod & Giertz's (JEL 2012) illustrative $0.38 excess burden gives 1 + 0.38 + 0.134 (midpoint compliance, $415bn / $3,108bn) + 0.004 = 1.52, between Hendren & Sprung-Keyser's (QJE 2020) MVPFs of 1.16 and 1.85. Corporate sub-policy: Chodorow-Reich, Zidar & Zwick (JEP 2024) find the 2017 cut lowered corporate revenue about 40% (0.63% of GDP a year) and raised long-run GDP about 0.9% and labour income by under $1,000 per worker. Output per $ of revenue: 0.9/0.63 = 1.4 long-run, 0.44/0.63 = 0.7 in the first decade. Shrinking government: Bergh & Henrekson (2011) find that 10 points more government size goes with 0.5-1 pp slower growth in rich countries. If cut spending is worth over $1 per $, the ratio falls toward 1.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed welfare-cost estimates: natural-experiment MVPFs (Hendren & Sprung-Keyser 2020, QJE); a quasi-experimental study of the 2017 corporate cut (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar & Zwick 2024, JEP); Feldstein's TAXSIM deadweight-loss estimate (1999, REStat); and Ballard-Shoven-Whalley general-equilibrium results (AER 1985). These are converted into a BCR and extrapolated to full repeal, which no study observes, so it is not A-range.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Repealing a tax needs no new spending, and revenue returned to taxpayers is a transfer; the fiscal hole is $3,108bn a year (FY2025 individual $2,656bn + corporate $452bn, CBO), closed under the headline sub-policy by shrinking government (44% of FY2025 outlays of $7,010bn). Administration: no new bureaucracy; about $11.2bn a year of IRS income-tax administration is avoided (0.59 x $19.0bn FY2025 IRS operations). No published one-time wind-down cost was found. Private compliance: none created; $328.9-501.3bn a year of income-tax compliance is avoided (Tax Foundation 2024, OIRA/IRS paperwork-burden data). These avoided costs enter the ratio's numerator. If a replacement tax were used instead (a revenue-neutral FairTax needs a 27.8%+ tax-inclusive rate, American Action Forum 2023), its collection and compliance costs would offset part of this saving. cost_bn = 0 + 0 + 0 = $0.
policies.difficulty_reason: Repealing the 16th Amendment needs a constitutional amendment (two-thirds of both Houses and three-fourths of states, Article V). The revenue to replace is about 59% of federal receipts, which means either cutting spending by about 44% or adopting a large new tax, with no modern precedent in a large economy.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The income tax is the progressive part of the federal system. Tax Foundation finds a FairTax replacement less progressive than current law, and Altig et al. (2001) find that removing progressivity lowers the welfare of the poorest. Chodorow-Reich, Zidar & Zwick (2024) find that most of the corporate cut's gains went to capital, with labour income up under $1,000 per worker. Jokisch & Kotlikoff (2007) find a prebated consumption tax could still leave the poor better off in the long run, so the design of the replacement matters.
policies.summary: This policy would abolish the personal income tax (via repeal of the 16th Amendment) and the corporate income tax, replacing about $3.1 trillion a year mainly by shrinking government. Economists estimate that each dollar of income tax costs between about 13 cents and 2 dollars extra in lost work, saving and investment. Filing and paperwork add another $329-501bn a year (11-16 cents per dollar raised), and the IRS spends about $11bn a year on the income taxes; repeal removes both. Repeal therefore returns about $1.24-3.20 per dollar of revenue given up (central about $1.50). The 2017 corporate tax cut raised investment and long-run GDP by about 0.9%, but recovered little of its revenue cost.

policies.title: Privatize government land, parks and natural resources
policies.bcr_basis: No study computes a welfare BCR for selling all federal land, so the headline range uses published revenue-per-management-dollar ratios for land run for income rather than by federal agencies. Both published ratios count annual management costs but not the one-time cost of transferring title, which is added at the measured 3.3% of sale value (GAO 2008, BLM FLTFA sales: $3.17m administration / $95.7m proceeds). Land value is taken as what a buyer would pay, the present value of net income: V = 12.46 x (R - C) (20 years at 5%). Ratio = 12.46R / (12.46C + 0.033 x 12.46 x (R - C)) = R / (C + 0.033(R - C)). LOW = 1.66: in the peer-reviewed Utah transfer model (Jakus et al. 2017, Land Economics; figures from Stambro 2014), Utah manages 31.2m acres and bears all federal costs; in the high-energy-price case, $422.0m revenue / $248m cost = 1.70 before transaction costs; with them, 422.0 / (248 + 0.033 x 174.0) = 422.0 / 253.7 = 1.66. HIGH = 10.0: in Fretwell & Regan (PERC 2015, 2009-2013 averages), Montana, Idaho, New Mexico and Arizona trust lands earn $14.51 per $1 of management cost, vs $0.73 for the Forest Service and BLM; with transaction costs, 14.51 / (1 + 0.033 x 13.51) = 14.51 / 1.446 = 10.0. Transaction costs lower the high end most because trust-land management costs are small relative to the land's value. Sensitivity at FLTFA's 20% statutory ceiling: 1.49 and 3.9. In the low-price Utah case the ratio is 0.72, shown in the counter list. Spectrum sub-policy (not in the headline because it is extrapolated): Hazlett & Munoz (2009, RAND J. Econ.) estimate that 60 MHz more licensed mobile spectrum in the US cuts prices about 8% and raises consumer surplus about $8.8bn a year. The real cost of freeing spectrum, scaled from the 2021 C-band auction (280 MHz; $3.3bn relocation + $9.7bn accelerated-clearing payments), is 13.0 x 60/280 = $2.8bn per 60 MHz. Ten years of benefit at 5% (annuity factor 7.72): 8.8 x 7.72 = $68bn; 68 / 2.8 = 24. Using only relocation costs ($0.71bn per 60 MHz) gives about 96. Hazlett & Munoz also find consumer-surplus losses from withholding spectrum are 15-20 times the social value of auction revenue (Belgium, Greece). Not netted out in the land ratio: non-market recreation and existence value. Haefele, Loomis & Bilmes (2016) value the National Park Service at $92bn a year, and outdoor recreation is $639.5bn of value added (BEA). Private and trust owners can keep much of this value, but no source measures how much.
policies.grade_reason: The low end comes from a peer-reviewed fiscal model (Jakus et al. 2017, Land Economics) and the high end from PERC's think-tank comparison of official agency accounts. Property-rights theory of resource management in academic books (Anderson & Leal) and peer-reviewed spectrum welfare estimates (Hazlett & Munoz 2009, RAND J. Econ.; Hazlett 2008, JEP) support them. No study prices full privatization including non-market values, so it is not higher.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: none net; sales raise money (the 2021 C-band auction alone brought $80.9bn in clock-phase bids, MITRE 2021), and the policy ends federal land-agency net losses (BLM/NPS/FWS spent $7.8bn vs $5.2bn revenue in 2010; Edwards & O'Toole 2012). Administration: the measured cost of running federal land sales is 3.3% of proceeds (GAO 2008: BLM FLTFA administration $3.17m on $95.7m of sales). Applied to BEA's $1.8 trillion value of federal land (Larson 2015, 2009 values) this is $59.4bn one-time, or $3.0bn a year over an assumed 20-year disposal programme. Private compliance and GDP loss: no published estimates (null). cost_bn = 0 + 3.0 = $3.0bn a year. Spectrum relocation costs are paid by buyers and sit inside the spectrum ratio.
policies.difficulty_reason: It dismantles the federal land agencies, which manage about one-third of US land, with no modern precedent; Cato's own blueprint phases auctions over 20-40 years (Anderson, Smith & Simmons 1999). The spectrum part alone would be moderate, since the FCC has run auctions since 1994 and has flexible-use licences, but full property rights in all bands, including government bands, would need major legislation.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Under the Anderson-Smith-Simmons (Cato 1999) design, every citizen gets equal 'public land share certificates', spreading the gains. A plain auction would favour wealthy and extractive buyers and could cut free recreational access. Spectrum gains go mostly to consumers through lower wireless prices (Hazlett & Munoz: consumer surplus at least 10 times producer surplus).
policies.summary: This policy would sell or transfer federal land, parks and natural resources to private (or trust) owners and give radio spectrum full, tradable property rights. Land run for income earns far more than federal land: four western states earn $14.51 per $1 of management cost on trust lands, against 73 cents for the Forest Service and BLM. Counting the cost of running the sales (3.3% of proceeds in BLM's recent land sales) as well as management, the ratio is about 1.7 (a Utah takeover bearing every federal cost, high energy prices) to 10. Spectrum liberalization looks even better: 60 MHz more mobile spectrum is worth about $8.8bn a year to US consumers. The main uncounted cost is recreation and conservation value (the national parks alone are valued at about $92bn a year).

policies.title: Tradable fishing quotas (ITQs)
policies.bcr_basis: Built from the World Bank's 'Sunken Billions Revisited' (2017) global bio-economic model (5% discount rate, 20 years). Benefit = PV of fishery net benefits on a reform path minus the current path (2012 effort held constant: PV $514bn). Cost = transition losses plus PV of the public cost of running a rights-based management regime, which the report puts at 1-14% of the value of landings; optimal landings revenue is $140.6bn a year (Table 3.1), and the 20-year annuity factor at 5% is 12.46. LOW = 2.8 (moderate path, effort cut 5% a year): PV $1,196bn - $514bn = $682bn gain; first-year loss $0.3bn; management at 14%: 0.14 x 140.6 = $19.7bn/yr x 12.46 = $245bn. 682.3 / (0.3 + 245) = 2.8. HIGH = 16 (rapid path, effort cut sharply until stocks recover): PV $1,465bn - $514bn = $951bn net, after a $44bn cumulative loss in the first four years; management at 1%: $1.4bn/yr x 12.46 = $17.5bn. (951 + 44) / (44 + 17.5) = 16.2. The annual prize is $83.3bn (95% CI $49.7-104.9bn): net benefits rise from $3.0bn to $86.3bn as effort falls about 44%. Cross-checks: Costello et al. (2016, PNAS) find rights-based reform raises 2050 profits by $53bn a year over business-as-usual, with the median fishery recovering in under 10 years. Costello, Gaines & Lynham (2008, Science) find catch-share fisheries were about half as likely to collapse across more than 11,000 fisheries. The World Bank does not prescribe ITQs specifically; it lists catch shares among tools that work, sometimes alongside community management. So this ratio applies to ITQ-type reform as the main route to the effort cut. The ratio is global; US federal fisheries already use catch shares widely, so the US increment is smaller. Both ends include the components counted in cost_bn: the low end uses the 14% management cost and the moderate path's transition loss; the high end uses the 1% management cost and the rapid path's $44bn transition loss. Combining the worst of each (rapid-path loss with 14% management) gives (951 + 44) / (44 + 245) = 3.4, inside the range.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed natural comparisons measure the gain from catch shares: Costello, Gaines & Lynham 2008, Science, on collapse across 11,000+ fisheries; Grafton, Squires & Fox 2000, J. Law & Econ., on the BC halibut natural experiment. A peer-reviewed global model gives the size of the prize (Costello et al. 2016, PNAS: +$53bn/yr profit). The BCR itself is built from the World Bank's official model (B- on its own). There is no peer-reviewed BCR, so it is not A-.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, global. Administration and enforcement: World Bank (2017) puts fisheries governance costs (science, management, monitoring, control and surveillance, public and fisher-borne) at 1-14% of landings value; the 14% high end on the optimal $140.6bn of global landings is $19.7bn a year. Private compliance: inside the World Bank range (null). GDP loss: temporary catch cuts while stocks rebuild, $44bn over four years on the rapid path = $11.0bn a year during the transition ($0.3bn in year 1 on the moderate path). Public outlay: none beyond management. cost_bn = 19.7 + 11.0 = $30.7bn a year (transitional years; $19.7bn a year thereafter).
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary legislation or regulation in one country, with many precedents (New Zealand, Iceland, US catch-share programmes such as BC/Alaska halibut). Globally, though, it requires fishing effort to fall about 44% (World Bank 2017), with 'very high adjustment costs' for displaced fishers.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The World Bank (2017) notes the benefits concentrate on the relatively few fishers who stay in, while displaced vessel owners and crews bear most adjustment costs and the public sector bears much of the management cost. Pinkerton & Edwards (2009) find quota leasing transfers rents from active fishers to quota owners. Auctioned or community-held quotas could make it broad, but the evidence here is for grandfathered ITQs.
policies.summary: Tradable fishing quotas give fishers a secure, sellable share of the total allowed catch, ending the race to fish. Across more than 11,000 fisheries, those with catch shares were about half as likely to collapse. The World Bank estimates that cutting global fishing effort to a sustainable level would raise fishery net benefits by about $83bn a year. Counting the temporary catch cuts and the cost of running the system, each $1 of cost returns about $2.80 to $16.

policies.title: End the Fed & Implement Neutral Reserve Currency
policies.bcr_basis: Abolish central-bank fiat money and return to a neutral reserve standard (gold, bitcoin or a floating commodity basket) with free banking, adopted by the major economies. All figures are % of US GDP a year; the perspective is global, so the exorbitant privilege the US earns on dollar reserves and lower interest paid to foreign lenders are transfers between countries rather than gains or costs to the world. Benefits come through four channels. (1) Inflation: a sustained 4% inflation costs 0.41% of output a year when money is currency (Dotsey & Ireland 1996, JME); Lagos & Wright (2005, JPE) find 3-5% for 10% inflation, scaled to the Fed-era average of about 3.4% (a 24-fold price rise 1913-2008; Selgin, Lastrapes & White 2012) = about 1.0%; and the interaction of inflation with the tax code adds about 1% of GDP a year going from 2% inflation to price stability (Feldstein 1997, 1999). (2) Banking crises: crises since 1973 have been twice as frequent as under the classical gold standard (Bordo, Eichengreen, Klingebiel & Martinez-Peria 2001); halving the Basel Committee's 4.5% annual crisis probability, at 0.2-0.6% of output per point (BCBS 2010), is worth 0.45-1.35% of GDP. (3) Trade: countries sharing the gold standard traded 18-57% more with each other (Mitchener & Weidenmier 2008, Economic Journal), 60% more in Lopez-Cordova & Meissner (2003, AER), and adopting gold raised trade about 42% (Estevadeordal, Frantz & Taylor 2003, QJE; applying the 1913 standard in 1870 would have raised trade volumes about 30%). On the US trade share of 25.0% of GDP (World Bank 2024), an 18% rise adds 4.5 points of trade and a 30% rise 7.5 points; at Frankel & Romer's (1999) lower bound of 0.5% of income per point, that is 2.25-3.75% of GDP. (4) Borrowing costs: gold adherence lowered sovereign spreads by about 40 basis points (Bordo & Rockoff 1996; Obstfeld & Taylor 2003: 40-60 bp before 1914); on foreign-held federal debt of 29.3% of GDP that is 0.12% of GDP. Cost is the real resource cost of the commodity or free-banking system (Watts & Snyder 2015, Cato Journal): Meltzer 0.5% of GDP; the measured US classical gold standard 1879-1913, 0.249%; White's free banking with 2% gold reserves, 0.05%. Fiat money carries its own resource cost in private gold hoarding (Friedman 1986), measured at 0.014% of GDP a year since Bretton Woods (Watts & Snyder 2015, Table 1), which is netted off. LOW = (inflation 0.41 + crises 0.45 + trade 2.25 + borrowing 0) / (0.5 - 0.014) = 3.11 / 0.486 = 6.4. HIGH = (inflation 1.0 + tax interaction 1.0 + crises 1.35 + trade 3.75 + borrowing 0.12) / 0.05 = 7.22 / 0.05 = 144. With the measured classical gold-standard cost the central case is about 25. Downside risks kept in the counter-evidence: the IMF finds exchange-rate volatility has at most a small effect on trade (Clark, Tamirisa & Wei 2004), which with no trade gain gives (0.41 + 0.45) / 0.486 = 1.8; Friedman's (1960) 2.5%-of-GDP cost for a full 100% commodity standard gives about 0.3; output growth was more volatile under the classical gold standard (Bordo 1981); and countries that left gold early in the 1930s recovered faster (Bernanke 1995).
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed historical estimates of the gold standard's effects on trade (Lopez-Cordova & Meissner 2003 AER; Estevadeordal, Frantz & Taylor 2003 QJE), borrowing costs (Bordo & Rockoff 1996 JEH; Obstfeld & Taylor 2003 EJ), crises (Bordo et al. 2001) and inflation (Lagos & Wright 2005 JPE; Lucas 2000 Econometrica), combined in published monetary theory (Selgin & White 1994 JEL). Not tried in a modern economy, and the Depression-era evidence cuts the other way, so B.
policies.cost_basis: Public outlay and administration: $0; closing the Fed needs no budget outlay, supervision passes to existing regulators, and lost seigniorage is a transfer. Private resource cost of holding commodity reserves: Meltzer's 0.5% of GDP (the high end of the estimates reviewed by Watts & Snyder 2015, Cato Journal) x 2025 GDP $30,861bn = $154.3bn a year; the measured 1879-1913 US gold standard cost 0.249% ($76.8bn) and White's free banking 0.05% ($15.4bn). The ratio's denominator uses these same percentages of GDP.
policies.difficulty_reason: It dismantles a major entrenched institution with no modern precedent. No advanced economy has run without a central bank since Canada created the Bank of Canada in 1935 (Bordo, Redish & Rockoff 2015). The competing-currencies sub-policy alone would be moderate (ordinary legal-tender and tax changes; Utah 2011, El Salvador 2021 precedents).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Inflation is a tax on all money holders (Lucas 2000; Benati & Nicolini measure it as a share of everyone's consumption). Savers and cash-dependent households gain most; debtors and the Treasury lose the inflation and seigniorage transfer. Banking crises hit output and jobs economy-wide.
policies.summary: This policy would abolish the Federal Reserve and return money to a neutral standard (gold, bitcoin or a basket of commodities) issued by competing banks, the system most major economies used before 1914. Stable money removes the hidden tax of inflation and its interaction with the tax code, banking crises under the classical gold standard were half as frequent as since 1973, and countries sharing gold traded 18-60% more with each other, which raises incomes; governments that kept to gold also borrowed more cheaply. Counting those gains against the cost of holding gold or running free banks gives about $6.40 to $144 of benefit per dollar. The risk is a rigid money supply in a deep slump, as in the 1930s.

policies.title: End Bailouts and Deposit Insurance
policies.bcr_basis: Constructed from published inputs; no published benefit-cost ratio for abolishing deposit insurance exists. Benefit of abolition = crises avoided because guarantees no longer weaken market discipline. Cost = welfare lost from removing depositor protection (more runs and failures). HIGH = 5.5: Demirgüç-Kunt & Detragiache (JME 2002; IMF WP 00/3) estimate that cutting US deposit-insurance coverage to Swiss levels would have lowered the predicted probability of the 1980 US banking crisis from 4.3% to 2.5%, i.e. by 1.8 points a year. Laeven & Valencia (IMF WP 18/206) put the output loss of the 2007 US crisis at 30% of trend GDP. Expected avoided loss = 0.018 x 0.30 = 0.54% of GDP a year (about $167bn at 2025 GDP of $30.9tn, FRED). Cost: Dávila & Goldstein (JPE 2023) estimate that raising coverage from $100,000 to $200,000 was worth $13.2bn a year in 2008 (9.46 bp of $14tn bank assets), i.e. 13.2/14,770 = 0.089% of 2008 GDP; taking this as the welfare value of the first $100,000 of cover gives 0.54/0.089 = 6.1 before administration. Adding the operating cost of private replacement insurance, $2.9bn a year (0.248 NAIC expense ratio x $11.6bn FDIC 2024 assessments), in 2025 dollars (GDP $30,861bn, FRED): benefit 0.0054 x 30,861 = $166.6bn; cost 0.00089 x 30,861 + 2.9 = 27.5 + 2.9 = $30.4bn; 166.6 / 30.4 = 5.5. This is an upper bound: Dávila & Goldstein say marginal gains are highest at low coverage, so full abolition costs more, and DD find the destabilising effect is insignificant where institutions are strong, as in the US. LOW = 0.5: direct resolution costs that guarantees created since 1934, S&L crisis $153bn (Curry & Shibut 2000) + 2008 bailouts ~$500bn (Lucas 2019) + SVB/Signature $16.3bn (FDIC 2023) = ~$669bn over ~90 years = $7.4bn a year, against the same $13.2bn a year plus the $2.9bn private-insurance operating cost: 7.4 / (13.2 + 2.9) = 0.46, rounded to 0.5 (0.56 before administration). The sign is contested: Anginer, Demirgüç-Kunt & Zhu (2014) find deposit insurance raised risk before 2007 and lowered it during the crisis, with a net destabilising effect.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed cross-country panel (Demirgüç-Kunt & Detragiache 2002, JME), peer-reviewed historical studies (Calomiris & Jaremski 2019, JF; Calomiris 1990, JEH) and peer-reviewed models (Diamond & Dybvig 1983; Dávila & Goldstein 2023, JPE) quantify each input. The ratio itself is assembled here rather than published, and the inputs disagree on sign, so it cannot rate B+ or above.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Repeal needs no new public spending; the FDIC is premium-funded. Transition to private deposit insurance: private insurers' operating cost at the property-casualty underwriting expense ratio (24.8%, NAIC 2024) on premiums equal to the FDIC's 2024 assessment revenue ($11.6bn) = $2.9bn a year (FDIC's own 2024 DIF operating expenses were $2.43bn; not credited because supervision continues elsewhere). Private compliance and GDP loss: the welfare cost of weaker depositor protection and more runs (depositors lost about 30% in a typical pre-FDIC failure, Correia, Luck & Verner) is the ratio's denominator, not repeated here. cost_bn = 0 + 2.9 = $2.9bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: it dismantles a major federal institution in place since 1933 and ends the implicit too-big-to-fail guarantee (worth up to $70bn a year to US banks, IMF 2014). No large advanced economy runs without deposit insurance today. New Zealand, the last OECD holdout, introduced a NZ$100,000 Depositor Compensation Scheme on 1 July 2025.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Mixed. Ending bailouts removes transfers that mostly went to bank creditors and shareholders (Lucas 2019: ~$500bn in 2008-09) and the too-big-to-fail funding subsidy to large banks (IMF 2014). Ending deposit insurance shifts risk onto ordinary depositors, who are least able to monitor banks. Neither effect is clearly concentrated on the poor or the rich.
policies.summary: This policy would close federal deposit insurance and bar government rescues of failed banks, so that depositors and creditors carry their own risk. Cross-country evidence finds explicit deposit insurance makes banking crises more likely where institutions are weak, and historical US state schemes encouraged risk-taking that ended in collapse. Bank-run theory and a recent calibrated model, however, find deposit insurance very valuable, especially its first dollars of cover. Putting published crisis costs against the modelled value of insurance gives a ratio of about 0.5 to 5.5 once the running cost of private replacement insurance (about $2.9bn a year) is included, which straddles 1.

policies.title: Unilateral global free trade: zero tariffs, zero quotas
policies.bcr_basis: Both ends use Copenhagen Consensus estimates of full global liberalisation that include growth (dynamic) effects. LOW = 90: Anderson (2012, CC III), completing the Doha agenda gives PV benefits of $12-64tn against PV adjustment costs below $400bn; Anderson's reported global BCR is 90-180 (140-250 for developing countries), and 90 is the floor. HIGH = 2,800: Anderson (2015 Post-2015 Consensus; Cambridge UP 2018), Doha with growth effects, global BCR 1,300-2,800 at 5% and 3% discount rates (developing countries 2,100-4,700). Anderson & Winters (2008) give 269-1,121 with dynamic gains (17-80 without). The dynamic assumption rests on quasi-experimental evidence: liberalisers grew ~1.5 points a year faster (Wacziarg & Welch 2008), and a 1-point rise in trade share raises income per person 0.5-2% (Frankel & Romer 1999). One country acting alone captures a smaller share of these global gains. The narrow static Halftime estimate (Feyrer et al. 2023: global 11, high-income 5-7) is kept as counter-evidence. Sub-policies, reported but not averaged in: anti-dumping repeal 2-14 (USITC 1995; Gallaway, Blonigen & Flynn 1999 JIE) and trade facilitation 11-640 (Feyrer et al. 2023; WTO 2015 benefits vs OECD costs of EUR 3.5-19M per country). Current US stakes (2026): Tax Foundation (Sept 2026) finds remaining tariffs cut long-run GDP 0.4% (~$120bn a year) and cost $820 per household in 2026. Yale Budget Lab (Apr 2026) finds 0.1% lower GDP (~$30bn a year) and a $760-940 household loss. These are recurring losses that repeal removes at near-zero budget cost. Anderson's ratios already put the adjustment costs (the GDP-loss component of cost_bn) in the denominator, and trade-facilitation administration is inside the sub-policy ratio.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-edited Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost estimates (Anderson 2012, 2015; Cambridge UP 2018 chapter) backed by peer-reviewed quasi-experimental and instrumental-variable evidence on growth (Wacziarg & Welch 2008 WBER; Frankel & Romer 1999 AER; Fajgelbaum et al. 2020 QJE). Even the narrowest peer-reviewed estimate (Feyrer et al. 2023, JBCA) is above 1. The sub-policies rate B (anti-dumping: peer-reviewed GE model) and A- (trade facilitation: one peer-reviewed BCA).
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: $0; repealing tariffs and quotas needs no budget outlay, and lost tariff revenue is a transfer. Administration: trade facilitation about $0.02bn a year for the US (OECD, Moise 2013). Private compliance: no published estimate (null). GDP loss: adjustment costs for displaced workers and firms, below $400bn in present value for full global liberalisation (Anderson 2012), annualised over 20 years at 5% = $32.1bn a year (global). cost_bn = 0.02 + 32.1 = $32.1bn a year. These adjustment costs are already the denominator of the Copenhagen Consensus ratios, so they are not added again.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: one country acting alone needs only ordinary tariff legislation, with working precedents in Hong Kong (no tariff on any import or export, HK Trade and Industry Department), Singapore, New Zealand's unilateral tariff cuts and Britain's 1846 Corn Law repeal. Anti-dumping repeal needs Congress to repeal Title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930. Customs reform can be done under existing authority (WTO TFA in force since 2017). In Learning Resources v. Trump (20 Feb 2026) the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs, but other statutory authorities (Sections 122, 232, 301, 338) remain (Tax Foundation 2026).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Anderson (2015) finds developing-country BCRs of 2,100-4,700 versus 1,300-2,800 globally and ~160 million fewer people in extreme poverty by 2030; Feyrer et al. (2023) find ~100 for low/lower-middle-income countries versus ~5 for high-income; Fajgelbaum et al. (2020) show 2018 US tariffs fell fully on domestic buyers. In the US, tariffs act as a consumption tax ($760-940 per household, Yale Budget Lab 2026), so removing them helps lower-income households most relative to income.
policies.summary: Unilaterally abolishing all tariffs and quotas, repealing anti-dumping duties, and simplifying border paperwork is among the best-evidenced policies in economics. Copenhagen Consensus estimates for full trade liberalisation, counting growth effects, return about $90 to $2,800 per $1 of adjustment cost, and liberalisers grow about 1.5 percentage points a year faster. The sub-policies also pay: anti-dumping repeal returns about 2-14 to 1 and trade facilitation about 11-640 to 1. In 2026 the remaining US tariffs cost households $760-940 a year (Yale Budget Lab) and lower long-run GDP by 0.1-0.4%.

policies.title: Repeal the Jones Act
policies.bcr_basis: Benefit = present value of US national welfare gains from repealing the Jones Act's US-build, US-flag and US-crew rules for domestic shipping. Cost = one-time earnings losses of displaced maritime and shipbuilding workers. Repeal has no material budget cost. Benefits: USITC (2002, Pub. 3519) estimates a $656m/yr net welfare gain from complete liberalisation (1999 data). Cato PA 845 reports that USITC studies using different assumptions gave economy-wide costs of $656m to $9.8bn a year. PV over 20 years at 5% (annuity factor 12.46): $656m x 12.46 = $8.2bn and $9.8bn x 12.46 = $122bn. Costs: USITC (2002) projects ~7,700 FTE maritime and ~3,100 FTE shipbuilding job losses, 10,800 workers in total. BLS median water-transportation pay is $71,860 (May 2025). Davis & von Wachter (2011, BPEA) put a displaced worker's PV earnings loss at 1.4 years of pay (low unemployment) to 2.8 years (high unemployment). That gives 10,800 x $71,860 x 1.4 = $1.09bn and x 2.8 = $2.17bn. LOW = 8.2 / 2.17 = 3.8. HIGH = 122 / 1.09 = 112. Corroboration: Kellogg & Sweeney (2024, NBER WP 31938) find repeal would have raised US consumer surplus in petroleum markets alone by $769m/yr against $367m/yr of lost supplier profits (2018-19), a sector-specific ratio of about 2.1 per year before any PV. Caveat: the job-loss figures belong to the USITC $656m scenario; the $9.8bn upper estimate comes from an older USITC model with no matching job estimate, and GAO (1998, per Cato) warned that US tax and labour-law compliance by foreign carriers could shrink the gains. The only cost component found (displaced-worker earnings losses) is the denominator, and the compliance burden of the Act is the benefit measured by USITC.
policies.grade_reason: The ratio's inputs are official estimates (USITC CGE model, BLS pay) plus peer-reviewed displacement-cost evidence (Davis & von Wachter, BPEA). Price effects are confirmed by a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study (Olney 2020, JIE), an NBER structural study of petroleum markets (Kellogg & Sweeney 2024) and Cato studies. No peer-reviewed welfare estimate of full repeal exists, so the grade is B-.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay, administration and compliance: $0; repeal removes requirements rather than adding them, and the regulatory cost avoided (higher freight costs, $656m-9.8bn a year) is the ratio's benefit. GDP loss: one-time displaced-worker earnings losses of up to $2.17bn (USITC job losses, BLS pay, Davis & von Wachter), annualised over 20 years at 5% = $0.17bn a year. cost_bn = $0.17bn a year. This adjustment cost is already the ratio's denominator.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs ordinary legislation in one country, with a working precedent in New Zealand's Maritime Transport Act 1994 (s198), which lets foreign ships on international voyages carry domestic coastal cargo; the main obstacle is ~10,800 concentrated maritime jobs (USITC 2002).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Gains accrue to coastal and non-contiguous consumers generally (Olney 2020: 1.35% higher prices in coastal states), and are largest relative to income in Puerto Rico, where households bear $692m/yr, 1.1% of spending (Hillberry & Jimenez 2024).
policies.summary: The Jones Act (1920) requires goods shipped between US ports to travel on US-built, US-owned, US-crewed ships, which cost several times more to build and run than foreign vessels. Official USITC modelling finds repeal would raise US national welfare by $0.7-9.8 billion a year. Newer research shows the law raises prices in coastal states and East Coast fuel costs, and costs Puerto Rico households about $692 million a year. Against the one-time earnings losses of the roughly 10,800 workers expected to be displaced, repeal returns about $4-112 per $1.

policies.title: Deregulate the Economy (top ten)
policies.bcr_basis: One reform package of ten US deregulation items; the ratio is total yearly benefits over total yearly costs, $bn. (1) Occupational licensing: consumer costs of $184bn (Kleiner & Vorotnikov 2018) to $203bn (Kleiner 2015); forgone quality from Kleiner & Soltas's (2023, REStud) finding that buyers' willingness to pay offsets 80% of licensing-induced price increases and wages offset 60% of training costs: 184/1.25 = 147.2 and 203/1.67 = 121.6. (2) Minimum wage: reversing CBO's (2019) $15 scenario, upper-income families gain $30.5bn and lower-income families lose $21.9bn (2018$); low benefit 0.69 x 21.9 = 15.1 (Cengiz et al. 2019, QJE). (3) Zoning: Hsieh & Moretti (2019, AEJ: Macro) find US GDP in 2009 would be 3.7% higher with housing supply constraints eased in the most productive cities (imperfect mobility); on 2025 GDP of $30,861bn that is $1,142bn. Greaney (2026, AEJ: Macro) finds the gain about two orders of magnitude smaller, 0.037% of GDP or $11.4bn; Glaeser & Gyourko (2018, JEP) give 0.7-2% of GDP. These estimates are net of congestion and housing costs. (4) FDA drug approval: faster reviews under PDUFA added $14-31bn of social surplus (Philipson et al. 2008, J. Public Econ), $3.2bn a year at the low end; Peltzman (1973, JPE) finds the 1962 amendments act like a 5-10% tax on drug purchases, 10% x $467bn of 2024 drug spending (CMS) = $46.7bn; cost up to $1.0bn a year for the upper bound on safety harm. (5) Sugar program: consumers pay $2.5-3.5bn a year; net cost to the economy about $1bn (GAO). (6) Davis-Bacon: CBO's option saves $17.8bn over 2025-34, $1.78bn a year, mostly lower wages (a transfer). (7) Bank compliance: community banks spent $4.5bn on compliance in 2014 (St. Louis Fed/CSBS); CBO scores the 2018 relief act at $671m over ten years. (8) Sarbanes-Oxley 404(b): about $210,000 per issuer a year for about 500 issuers, $0.105bn (SEC 2020). (9) Employment-protection doctrines (Autor, Kerr & Kugler 2007) and (10) nuclear plant regulation (Eash-Gates et al. 2020) are not priced. Sums: benefits $222.6bn (low) to $1,432.0bn (high); costs $146.8bn (low) to $174.5bn (high). LOW = 222.6 / 174.5 = 1.28; HIGH = 1,432.0 / 146.8 = 9.75. Cross-checks on the federal regulatory stock as a whole: Coffey, McLaughlin & Peretto (2020, RED) find regulation slowed growth by about 0.8 percentage points a year after 1980, leaving GDP about $4 trillion (25%) lower in 2012; Dawson & Seater (2013, J. Econ. Growth) find larger losses. OMB's 2017 report finds major rules of 2006-16 had benefits of $287-911bn a year against costs of $78-115bn, mostly EPA air rules, which are not on this list.
policies.grade_reason: Most items rest on peer-reviewed natural experiments or structural models that measure the gain (Kleiner & Soltas 2023; Cengiz et al. 2019; Hsieh & Moretti 2019; Peltzman 1973; Philipson et al. 2008), with official estimates for the sugar program, Davis-Bacon and bank compliance (GAO, CBO, SEC). The largest item, zoning, rests on a model whose replication found much smaller effects, so B+.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, $bn a year (high end): forgone licensing quality 121.6-147.2 (Kleiner & Soltas 2023 ratios applied to $184-203bn of licensing costs), income lost by lower-income families after minimum-wage repeal 21.9 (CBO 2019), sugar producers' lost surplus 1.5-2.5 (GAO), Davis-Bacon wage transfer 1.78 (CBO 2024), FDA safety bound 0-1.0 (Philipson et al. 2008), bank-crisis risk 0.067 (CBO 2018). Low 146.8, high 174.5. Repealing the rules needs no new spending.
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs dozens of separate federal statutes plus pre-emption of state licensing and local zoning, against entrenched beneficiaries (incumbent homeowners, licensed professions, sugar growers, construction unions).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Zoning and licensing reform favour lower-income entrants and renters; FDA and sugar reform help consumers widely; minimum-wage and Davis-Bacon repeal lower some wages.
policies.summary: Ten federal, state and local regulations are removed together: occupational licensing, minimum wages, restrictive zoning, slow FDA drug approval, the sugar program, the Davis-Bacon Act, community-bank compliance rules, Sarbanes-Oxley audits for small firms, employment-protection doctrines and nuclear plant rules. Easing zoning in the most productive cities alone could raise US GDP by up to 3.7%, licensing costs consumers up to $203bn a year, and FDA delays act like a tax of up to 10% on drug purchases. Adding up the priced items gives $1.28 to $9.75 of benefit per dollar of cost; the spread depends mostly on how large the zoning gain really is.

policies.title: Secure Private Property Globally
policies.bcr_basis: Copenhagen Consensus analysis of land tenure security in Sub-Saharan Africa (Byamugisha & Dubosse 2023, Journal of Benefit-Cost Analysis; 8% discount rate, 30 years): rural titling benefits $395.71bn against costs $21.72bn (BCR 18); urban titling $236.93bn (average house price) or $159.89bn (population-weighted) against $5.29bn (BCR 45 or 30). Benefits rest on a 15% household wealth effect for rural land and a 25% rise in urban property values. HIGH = (395.71 + 236.93) / (21.72 + 5.29) = 23.4, shown as 23. The paper's headline is 21 (population-weighted urban prices). LOW = 6: urban benefits only, with rural benefits set to zero following the systematic reviews that find no consistent income or productivity effect of rural titling in Africa (Higgins et al. 2018; Lawry et al. 2017; Jacoby & Minten 2007), and all costs kept: 159.89 / 27.01 = 5.9. Quasi-experimental evidence on the mechanism: titling in Peru raised household work hours 17% and cut child labour 28% (Field 2007, QJE); titled families in Buenos Aires built 12% more and their children got 0.69 more years of schooling (Galiani & Schargrodsky 2010); Rwanda's land regularisation raised soil-conservation investment about 10 percentage points, 19 for female-headed households (Ali, Deininger & Goldstein 2014). Other Copenhagen Consensus country studies find higher ratios (Malawi 73, range 18-138).
policies.grade_reason: One peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis (Byamugisha & Dubosse 2023, JBCA) backed by quasi-experimental and natural-experiment studies (Field 2007; Galiani & Schargrodsky 2010; Ali, Deininger & Goldstein 2014); systematic reviews find mixed income effects, so A-.
policies.cost_basis: $82.4bn over 30 years for Sub-Saharan Africa (rural $68.6bn, urban $13.8bn, undiscounted; Byamugisha & Dubosse 2023, Table 4) = $2.7bn a year, mostly registry operation and upkeep. Per-parcel titling costs of $5-25 have been achieved in Rwanda, Malawi and Tanzania. A global programme would cost more; no sourced global total exists.
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs working land administration, protection against elite capture and long-term registry upkeep in many countries; customary systems complicate formal titling.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Targets squatters, smallholders and female-headed households, who gained most in Rwanda; about 1.1 billion adults report insecure land or property rights (Prindex).
policies.summary: Giving the world's poor formal, tradable titles to the land and homes they already occupy lets them invest, borrow against and sell what they own. A peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus analysis for Sub-Saharan Africa finds $18 back per dollar for rural titling and $30-45 for urban titling, at costs of $5-25 a parcel, and field studies find titled families work more, build more and keep children in school longer. Because reviews find weaker effects on rural incomes, the range runs from about $6 to $23 per dollar.

sources.title: Cash for carbon: A randomized trial of payments for ecosystem services to reduce deforestation
sources.reported_estimate: RCT in 121 Ugandan villages: tree cover fell 4.2% in treatment vs 9.1% in control villages; no evidence of leakage; value of delayed CO2 emissions 2.4 times programme cost.

sources.authors: Jayachandran, S.; de Laat, J.; Lambin, E. F.; Stanton, C. Y.
sources.title: Cash for Carbon: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Payments for Ecosystem Services to Reduce Deforestation (IPR Working Paper WP-16-25)
sources.venue: Institute for Policy Research, Northwestern University
sources.reported_estimate: Cost at scale ~$0.57 per tCO2 delayed; SCC $39; BCR ~2 in base case, 0.7 if immediate catch-up, 12.3 if permanent delay; take-up 32%; equity caveats (landless households).

sources.authors: Kindermann, G.; Obersteiner, M.; Sohngen, B.; Sathaye, J.; Andrasko, K.; Rametsteiner, E.; Schlamadinger, B.; Wunder, S.; Beach, R.
sources.title: Global cost estimates of reducing carbon emissions through avoided deforestation
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105(30):10302-10307
sources.reported_estimate: 10% cut in deforestation 2005-2030: 0.3-0.6 GtCO2/yr for $0.4-1.7bn/yr; 50% cut: 1.5-2.7 GtCO2/yr for $17.2-28.0bn/yr.

sources.authors: Assuncao, J.; Gandour, C.; Rocha, R.
sources.title: DETER-ing Deforestation in the Amazon: Environmental Monitoring and Law Enforcement
sources.reported_estimate: IV design using cloud cover: satellite-targeted monitoring and enforcement significantly reduced Amazon deforestation. CPI summary of the research: avoided ~59,500 km2 of clearing 2007-2011; any carbon price above $0.76/tCO2 covers the cost of monitoring and enforcement.

sources.title: How Better Monitoring and Law Enforcement Saved 60,000 km2 of the Amazon
sources.reported_estimate: DETER-based enforcement prevented clearing of over 59,500 km2 (2007-2011); break-even carbon price $0.76/tCO2.

sources.title: Biodiversity: Post-2015 Consensus
sources.reported_estimate: Reduce global forest loss by at least 50%: BCR ~10 (highlight); McVittie's re-estimate $2-3 per $1; Markandya's own assessment $30-100+.

sources.authors: Austin, K. G.; Baker, J. S.; Sohngen, B. L.; Wade, C. M.; Daigneault, A.; Ohrel, S. B.; Ragnauth, S.; Bean, A.
sources.title: The economic costs of planting, preserving, and managing the world's forests to mitigate climate change
sources.reported_estimate: Avoided tropical deforestation supplies 0.3-1.8 GtCO2/yr (2025-2055 average) and 30-54% of forest mitigation in 2055 at carbon prices $5-100/t; total forest-mitigation cost $2-393bn/yr by 2055.

sources.title: Social Cost of Carbon 101
sources.reported_estimate: US IWG interim SCC $51/tCO2; EPA (Nov 2023) $190/tCO2.

sources.reported_estimate: Synthetic-control evaluation of 18 voluntary REDD+ projects (26 sites): only ~6.1% of credits tied to additional emission reductions; 68% of credits from projects with no significant reduction.

sources.authors: Merger, E.; Held, C.; Tennigkeit, T.; Blomley, T.
sources.title: A bottom-up approach to estimating cost elements of REDD+ pilot projects in Tanzania
sources.reported_estimate: MRV and carbon-market compliance (transaction) costs: US$0.9/ha/yr or US$1.46/tCO2 (Masito Ugalla); US$0.3/ha/yr (Lindi); US$0.2/ha/yr or US$0.21/tCO2 (Kilosa).

sources.authors: Hu, J.; Jastad, E. O.; Bolkesjo, T. F.; Rorstad, P. K. (citing Gan, J. & McCarl, B. A. 2007, Ecological Economics 64(2):423-432)
sources.title: The Quantification and Tracing of Leakage in the Forest Sector in Nordic Countries
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Gan & McCarl (2007): 'between 42% and 95% of forest conservation efforts within a country or region may be redirected elsewhere'; other studies 50-100% for harvest reductions in the EU and Norway.

sources.authors: International Forest Industries (reporting the Eliasch Review, UK Government)
sources.title: Eliasch Review on international deforestation published
sources.reported_estimate: Capacity building for forest nations estimated at up to $4bn over five years for 40 forest nations; without action, deforestation could add climate damages of $1 trillion a year by 2100.

sources.authors: McVittie, A. (in Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 biodiversity assessment)
sources.title: Biodiversity Perspective / alternative estimate
sources.reported_estimate: Adjusted BCR for halving forest loss of only $2-3 per $1.
sources.why_excluded: Falls inside the adopted range; not a separate end point.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at a 2% near-term discount rate; used for the cross-check.
sources.why_excluded: Highest published social cost of carbon ($185/t); used only in the cross-check.

sources.title: Do Renewable Portfolio Standards Deliver Cost-Effective Carbon Abatement? (BFI Working Paper 2019-62, revised 24 June 2026)
sources.venue: Becker Friedman Institute / Energy Policy Institute, University of Chicago
sources.reported_estimate: June 2026 revision (SSRN abstract): electricity prices 11% higher seven years after RPS passage; CO2 emissions 8-17% lower; cost per abated tCO2 $86-211. The 2019 working-paper version (EPIC summary, https://epic.uchicago.edu/research/do-renewable-portfolio-standards-deliver): prices +11% after 7 years and +17% after 12; cost exceeds $130/t in all specifications, up to $460.

sources.authors: Abrell, J.; Kosch, M.; Rausch, S.
sources.title: Carbon abatement with renewables: Evaluating wind and solar subsidies in Germany and Spain
sources.reported_estimate: Short-run abatement cost of solar subsidies EUR 411-1,944/tCO2; wind EUR 82-276/tCO2; consumers bear 4-7x larger costs when solar is promoted and benefit when wind is promoted.

sources.authors: Bistline, J.; Mehrotra, N.; Wolfram, C.
sources.title: Economic Implications of the Climate Provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act (NBER WP 31267; Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2023)
sources.venue: NBER / Brookings Papers on Economic Activity
sources.reported_estimate: Power-sector average abatement cost of IRA tax credits $36-87/tCO2 with discounted costs and undiscounted emissions, $88-94 if both are discounted; 'would be higher if distortions associated with financing the incentives were included'; tax-credit expenditures to 2031 $244bn (lower), $781bn (central), $1,070bn (higher); total fiscal costs $365-1,190bn.

sources.title: Energy: Post-2015 Consensus
sources.reported_estimate: Doubling the share of renewables in the global energy mix: BCR below 1 (excessively costly until intermittency/storage solved); doubling energy RD&D: 11; phasing out fossil-fuel subsidies: 15.

sources.title: The Budgetary Cost of the Inflation Reduction Act's Energy Subsidies (Policy Analysis No. 992)
sources.reported_estimate: IRA energy subsidies $936bn-$1.97 trillion over 2025-2034 ($2.04-4.67 trillion through 2050); CBO/JCT ~$786bn over 2024-2033; also reports Goldman Sachs $1.2T and Penn Wharton just over $1T.

sources.title: 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' Brings Big Changes to Green Energy Tax Credits
sources.reported_estimate: Wind/solar 45Y/48E credits end unless construction begins by July 4, 2026 or in service by Dec 31, 2027; EV credits eliminated after 2025.

sources.title: The Distributional Effects of US Clean Energy Tax Credits
sources.venue: Tax Policy and the Economy 30 (NBER WP 21437)
sources.reported_estimate: Top income quintile received ~60% of clean-energy tax credits, bottom three quintiles ~10%; ~90% of EV credits went to the top quintile.

sources.title: Social Cost of Carbon 101
sources.reported_estimate: US IWG interim SCC $51/tCO2; EPA 2023 $190/tCO2.

sources.title: Levelized Full System Costs of Electricity
sources.reported_estimate: Introduces Levelized Full System Costs of Electricity (LFSCOE): the cost of serving an entire market with one source plus storage (abstract, RePEc); in Germany and ERCOT Texas, wind and solar LFSCOE exceed the most expensive dispatchable technology, and even a 90% fall in storage costs does not make them competitive. Fraser Institute commentary (2025) reports from a study in Energy that solar costs rise from $36/MWh to as much as $1,548/MWh and wind from $40 to up to $504/MWh on this basis.

sources.authors: Gowrisankaran, G.; Reynolds, S. S.; Samano, M.
sources.title: Intermittency and the Value of Renewable Energy
sources.reported_estimate: Southeastern Arizona: social cost of $138.4/MWh for 20% solar generation (excluding CO2 offset), of which intermittency overall accounts for $46 and unforecastable intermittency $6.1; 20% solar would be welfare neutral at $1.52/W installation cost and a $39/t CO2 social cost.

sources.title: Nonrefundable Tax Credits versus Grants: The Impact of Subsidy Form on the Effectiveness of Subsidies for Renewable Energy
sources.venue: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 6(3):433-460
sources.reported_estimate: Wind developers valued $1 of nonrefundable tax credits the same as $0.85 of a grant; credits favour incumbents with tax liability.

sources.title: Solar and wind power make electricity more expensive - that's a fact
sources.reported_estimate: Citing 'a recent study published in Energy' (the study is not named on the page): with full system costs, solar rises from US$36/MWh to as high as US$1,548 and wind from US$40 to up to US$504 per MWh.

sources.title: Goldman Sachs reviews Inflation Reduction Act's investment potential
sources.reported_estimate: Goldman Sachs estimates the IRA will provide 'an estimated $1.2 trillion of incentives by 2032'.

sources.title: United States Electricity Profile 2024; Revenue from Sales to Ultimate Customers by State (revenue_annual.xlsx)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024 US retail sales 3,975,381,832 MWh at an average 12.94 c/kWh (= ~$514bn revenue); state revenue file (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/state/revenue_annual.xlsx), 2020: US total $393.6bn, of which the 31 RPS jurisdictions listed in cost_components $276.0bn (70.1%).

sources.title: What does it cost the IRS to collect taxes?
sources.reported_estimate: IRS cost of collecting $100: 36 cents in FY2024; recent peak 53 cents in FY2010 (used as the administration rate).

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.reported_estimate: 'The SCC in the baseline run is $66/tCO2 for the 2020 period (in 2019 international $).'

sources.title: The Cost of Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions
sources.reported_estimate: Static policy costs: RPS $0-190/t, solar PV subsidies $140-2,100/t (Table 2); argues actions with high static costs can have low dynamic costs via learning (solar panels, EVs).
sources.why_excluded: Learning-by-doing spillovers may raise the true ratio above static estimates, but the paper does not quantify a BCR; the table values overlap the adopted range.

sources.authors: Dayaratna, K. D.; McKitrick, R.; Michaels, P. J.
sources.title: Climate sensitivity, agricultural productivity and the social cost of carbon in FUND
sources.reported_estimate: Abstract: with updated climate-sensitivity and CO2-fertilisation parameters in FUND, 'the lower bound of the social cost of carbon is likely negative' and 'the upper bound is much lower than previously claimed'; body: $19.33-27.06/tCO2 at 3% for 2020-2050, $1.61 with Lewis-Curry sensitivity.
sources.why_excluded: An SCC below the US IWG and Rennert values used across this dashboard; using it would put every ratio here near zero (19.33/2,138 = 0.009 at the low end; 19.33/86 = 0.22 at best). A published Comment in the same journal disputes the paper. Reported for transparency.

sources.authors: Wiser, R.; Mai, T.; Millstein, D.; Barbose, G.; Bird, L.; Heeter, J.; Keyser, D.; Krishnan, V.; Macknick, J.
sources.title: Assessing the costs and benefits of US renewable portfolio standards
sources.reported_estimate: Existing RPS: system costs up to $31bn (PV 2015-2050); health benefits $97bn and climate benefits $161bn (central); lower bounds $48bn and $37bn. Expanded RPS: costs $23-194bn, health $558bn, climate $599bn (central). Authors: RPS not the most cost-effective route but cost-effective nationally once externalities counted.
sources.why_excluded: Modelled ex ante by DOE national laboratories (LBNL, NREL), which also carry out DOE renewable-energy programmes; uses projected costs from the laboratories' own capacity-expansion model rather than observed prices, and its ratio is driven by health co-benefits; ex-post studies of the same mandates (Greenstone & Nath) find higher costs per tonne. Kept as the optimistic counter-estimate (8.3; 2.7 with lower-bound benefits).

sources.authors: Millstein, D.; Wiser, R.; Bolinger, M.; Barbose, G.
sources.title: The climate and air-quality benefits of wind and solar power in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: 2007-2015 cumulative air-quality benefits $29.7-112.8bn and climate benefits $5.3-106.8bn; 3,000-12,700 avoided premature deaths; 2015 marginal benefits 7.3 c/kWh wind, 4.0 c/kWh solar.
sources.why_excluded: DOE national-laboratory (LBNL) model estimate of air-quality and climate benefits per MWh; benefit-side mechanism only, no cost comparison; treated as optimistic counter-evidence.

sources.authors: Barbose, G. et al. (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)
sources.title: State Electricity Resource Standards: 2025 Data Update
sources.reported_estimate: RPS compliance costs averaged roughly 4% of retail electricity bills across states (less than 1% in 5 states, more than 10% in 3), based on REC prices and utility/PUC data.
sources.why_excluded: DOE-laboratory estimate built from REC prices and utility-reported compliance costs, which omit wider price effects; Greenstone & Nath's observed 11% retail-price effect is used for the private-compliance component (LBNL's 4% would give ~$14.4bn/yr).

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413), 2% discount rate.
sources.why_excluded: Highest published social cost of carbon ($185/t); the range uses DICE-2023 ($66/t) as the upper carbon value.

sources.title: Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience
sources.venue: Global Center on Adaptation / World Resources Institute
sources.reported_estimate: $1.8tn invested 2020-2030 in five areas yields $7.1tn net benefits; BCRs 2:1 to 10:1; 24 hours' warning cuts damage 30%; $800m on EWS in developing countries avoids $3-16bn/yr; EWS benefits at least 10x cost; mangroves avoid >$80bn/yr of coastal flood losses, benefits up to 10x costs.

sources.title: A Cost Effective Solution to Reduce Disaster Losses in Developing Countries: Hydro-Meteorological Services, Early Warning, and Evacuation (Policy Research Working Paper 6058)
sources.reported_estimate: Upgrading hydro-met and EWS in all developing countries: avoided asset losses $0.3-2bn/yr, ~23,000 lives/yr ($0.7-3.5bn), wider benefits $3-30bn/yr; total $4-36bn/yr for ~$1bn/yr; BCR 4-36.

sources.title: Reviewing estimates of the economic efficiency of disaster risk management: opportunities and limitations of using risk-based cost-benefit analysis
sources.reported_estimate: Disaster risk management benefits outweigh costs on average by about four times (risk-based studies); evidence base limited.

sources.authors: Multihazard Mitigation Council, National Institute of Building Sciences
sources.title: Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves: 2019 Report (federal grants - riverine flood)
sources.reported_estimate: Federal riverine-flood mitigation grants: average BCR ~7:1 (~$82bn savings on $11.5bn); all federal mitigation grants since 1995 $27bn saving $160bn, ~6:1.

sources.authors: Hinkel, J.; Lincke, D.; Vafeidis, A. T.; Perrette, M.; Nicholls, R. J.; Tol, R. S. J.; Marzeion, B.; Fettweis, X.; Ionescu, C.; Levermann, A.
sources.title: Coastal flood damage and adaptation costs under 21st century sea-level rise
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111(9):3292-3297
sources.reported_estimate: Without adaptation 0.2-4.6% of world population flooded annually in 2100 and losses 0.3-9.3% of GDP; dike investment and maintenance $12-71bn/yr in 2100, much smaller than avoided damages.

sources.authors: Narayan, S.; Beck, M. W.; Reguero, B. G.; Losada, I. J.; van Wesenbeeck, B.; Pontee, N.; Sanchirico, J. N.; Ingram, J. C.; Lange, G.-M.; Burks-Copes, K. A.
sources.title: The Effectiveness, Costs and Coastal Protection Benefits of Natural and Nature-Based Defences
sources.reported_estimate: Salt marshes and mangroves are 2-5 times cheaper than submerged breakwaters for wave heights up to 0.5 m; coral reefs and marshes have the highest wave-reduction potential.

sources.authors: Shrader, J.; Bakkensen, L.; Lemoine, D.
sources.title: Fatal Errors: The Mortality Value of Accurate Weather Forecasts (NBER WP 31361)
sources.reported_estimate: Quasi-experimental: forecasts that under-predict temperature extremes raise mortality; 50% more accurate forecasts would save ~2,200 US lives/yr; willingness to pay $112bn for that improvement, $22bn of it for climate adaptation.

sources.title: COP27: $3.1 billion plan to achieve early warning systems for all by 2027
sources.reported_estimate: Early Warnings for All: $3.1bn of new targeted investment 2023-2027 (~50 cents per person per year); countries with limited EWS coverage have disaster mortality 8x higher.

sources.title: Adaptation Gap Report 2023: Underfinanced. Underprepared.
sources.reported_estimate: Adaptation needs of developing countries $215-387bn/yr this decade; finance gap $194-366bn/yr.

sources.title: Section 1215 | Management Costs (Disaster Recovery Reform Act of 2018)
sources.reported_estimate: HMGP management costs: 'not more than 15 percent of the total amount of the grant award', of which not more than 10% by the grantee and 5% by the subgrantee.

sources.title: Does mitigation save? Reviewing cost-benefit analyses of disaster risk reduction
sources.venue: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction 10(A):213-235
sources.reported_estimate: Many results support the economic effectiveness of DRR, but studies often lack sensitivity analysis, ignore climate change and disbenefits, and results are highly context-specific.
sources.why_excluded: Does not give a pooled ratio; used as a caution that published BCRs may be optimistic and context-dependent.

sources.authors: Ward, P. J.; Jongman, B.; Aerts, J. C. J. H.; Bates, P. D.; Botzen, W. J. W.; Diaz Loaiza, A.; Hallegatte, S.; Kind, J. M.; Kwadijk, J.; Scussolini, P.; Winsemius, H. C.
sources.title: A global framework for future costs and benefits of river-flood protection in urban areas
sources.reported_estimate: Dyke investment may be economically attractive in many regions, but not everywhere.
sources.why_excluded: No single global ratio in the abstract; supports the point that some defences fall below 1, consistent with the low end of 2 being an average rather than a floor for every project.

sources.authors: Brander, L. M.; van Beukering, P.; Nijsten, L.; McVittie, A.; Baulcomb, C.; Eppink, F. V.; Cado van der Lelij, J. A.
sources.title: The global costs and benefits of expanding Marine Protected Areas
sources.reported_estimate: Global benefits of MPA expansion exceed costs by a factor of 1.4-2.7, depending on location and extent (six scenarios).

sources.title: Expansion of Marine Protected Areas (Copenhagen Consensus assessment, 'Identifying best buys for Africa')
sources.reported_estimate: Africa, 38 coastal countries: BCR 9.2 for 10% EEZ coverage and 1.16 for 30%; MPA management ~7% of total costs, fisheries opportunity cost ~90%; 5 years to establish, benefits over a further 30 years.

sources.authors: Brander, L.; Baulcomb, C.; van der Lelij, J. A. C.; Eppink, F.; McVittie, A.; Nijsten, L.; van Beukering, P.
sources.title: The benefits to people of expanding Marine Protected Areas (summarised in WWF 'Marine Protected Areas: Smart Investments in Ocean Health')
sources.reported_estimate: BCR 3.17-19.77 across six scenarios; PV costs 2015-2050 $45-47bn (10%) and $223-228bn (30%); PV benefits $622-923bn (10%) and $719-1,145bn (30%); net benefits $490-920bn. Table 14 (PV, 3%, 2013 $bn), P2P30: management 24.374, establishment 7.854, fisheries 195.8, total 228.0, benefits 1,145.2; E2E30: management 23.768, establishment 5.980, fisheries 197.3, total 227.0, benefits 719.2.

sources.title: Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience
sources.reported_estimate: Mangroves avoid >$80bn/yr of coastal flood losses and provide $40-50bn/yr of non-market benefits; preservation and restoration benefits up to 10x costs.

sources.authors: Sala, E.; Mayorga, J.; Bradley, D.; et al.
sources.title: Protecting the global ocean for biodiversity, food and climate
sources.reported_estimate: Only 2.7% of the ocean highly protected; well-placed protection could raise catches by >8 Mt; protecting ~4% would remove 90% of carbon-disturbance risk from bottom trawling.

sources.title: Protecting 30% of the planet for nature: costs, benefits and economic implications
sources.venue: Campaign for Nature / Cambridge Conservation Initiative
sources.reported_estimate: Benefits outweigh costs at least 5:1 for protecting 30% of land and ocean; ~$140bn/yr investment needed by 2030 vs ~$24bn/yr current; +$250bn/yr output and +$350bn/yr ecosystem services.

sources.authors: Edgar, G.J. et al. (via Reef Resilience summary)
sources.title: Global conservation outcomes depend on marine protected areas with five key features
sources.reported_estimate: 87 MPAs in 40 countries: 'Only 9 of the 87 MPAs had 4 or 5 of those characteristics'; 'most of the remainder of MPAs were ecologically indistinguishable from non-MPAs'.

sources.title: Biodiversity: Post-2015 Consensus

sources.why_excluded: Combines terrestrial and marine protection in one target, so the 0.85 is not ocean-specific; the coral-reef figure (>24) is for reef-loss reduction generally, not MPAs.

sources.why_excluded: Qualitative argument without a ratio; fisheries management is outside this policy's scope, but displacement would lower the MPA ratios.

sources.title: Economic Implications of a Phased-in EV Mandate in Canada (Working Paper 2023-01; published Canadian Journal of Economics 2024)
sources.venue: University of Guelph Department of Economics / Canadian Journal of Economics
sources.reported_estimate: CGE results: parity by 2035, deadweight costs 'over $2,700 per tonne', emissions 1.3% below baseline in 2032, real GDP ~1.3% below baseline in 2030; parity by 2050, 'nearly $4,700 per tonne', emissions 3.2% below baseline, real GDP 7.0% below baseline in 2035.

sources.title: Global EV Outlook 2025 (press release: More than 1 in 4 cars sold worldwide this year is set to be electric)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: >17m electric cars sold, >20% of global sales; China >11m, almost half its market, two-thirds priced below ICE equivalents; BEVs ~20% dearer in Germany and ~30% in the US; >40% share expected by 2030.

sources.authors: Holland, S. P.; Mansur, E. T.; Muller, N. Z.; Yates, A. J.
sources.title: Decompositions and Policy Consequences of an Extraordinary Decline in Air Pollution from Electricity Generation
sources.venue: American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 12(4):244-274 (NBER WP 25339)
sources.reported_estimate: US power-plant damages fell from $245bn to $133bn a year over 2010-2017; EVs are 'now cleaner than gasoline vehicles on average, though substantial heterogeneity remains'. Update to the 2016 estimate; applies to the cleaner US grid, not to coal-heavy Asian grids.

sources.title: The Distributional Effects of US Clean Energy Tax Credits
sources.venue: Tax Policy and the Economy 30 (NBER WP 21437)
sources.reported_estimate: Top income quintile received ~90% of EV tax credits.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
Social Cost of Carbon 101
sources.reported_estimate: US IWG interim SCC $51/tCO2.

sources.title: Electric Vehicles for Everyone? The Impossible Dream
sources.reported_estimate: 'Today, the battery adds at least $10,000 to the price of an EV'; battery costs up 20% since 2021; Boston Consulting Group puts utility grid upgrade costs at $1,700-5,800 per EV ($400bn to >$1T for an all-EV US fleet); replacing ~1m US gasoline pumps needs >$100bn of superchargers; IMF projects metals at historic peaks for about a decade; EV life-cycle emissions vary widely with grid and materials.

sources.title: Economic implications of a phased-in EV mandate in Canada
sources.reported_estimate: Published version of the working paper (confirmed via Crossref): partial- and general-equilibrium modelling of Canada's 2035 ICE phase-out; if the mandate outpaces cost parity the auto manufacturing sector would likely shut down.

sources.authors: Holland, S.P.; Mansur, E.T.; Muller, N.Z.; Yates, A.J.
sources.title: Are There Environmental Benefits from Driving Electric Vehicles? The Importance of Local Factors
sources.reported_estimate: Second-best EV subsidy (= environmental benefit of an EV over a gasoline car, CO2 plus local pollution) ranges from $2,785 in California to -$4,964 in North Dakota, mean -$1,095 on the 2010-12 US grid; 91% of EV local pollution damages are exported to other states. Sets the low end.

sources.authors: Ji, S.; Cherry, C.R.; Bechle, M.J.; Wu, Y.; Marshall, J.D.
sources.title: Electric Vehicles in China: Emissions and Health Impacts
sources.reported_estimate: PM2.5 emission factors are generally lower for conventional vehicles than comparable EVs in China; primary PM2.5 health impacts per passenger-km are greater for e-cars than gasoline cars in most cities (3.6x on average).

sources.title: Global Electricity Review 2025: Major countries and regions
sources.reported_estimate: 2024 coal share of electricity generation: China 58%, India 75%, world 34%, US <15%, EU 9.8%.

sources.authors: Hagerty, J.M.; Sergici, S.; Lam, L.
sources.title: Electric Power Sector Investments of $75-125 Billion Needed to Support Projected 20 Million EVs by 2030, According to Brattle Economists
sources.venue: The Brattle Group publication summary (report: Hagerty, Sergici & Lam, 2020)
sources.reported_estimate: $75-125bn of US electric power sector investment needed for 20m EVs by 2030: generation and storage $30-50bn, T&D upgrades $15-25bn, EV chargers and customer-side infrastructure $30-50bn (1-2m public chargers). = $3,750-6,250 per EV (arithmetic).

sources.title: An Electric Vehicle-only approach would lead to the loss of half a million jobs in the EU, study finds
sources.venue: CLEPA (European Association of Automotive Suppliers) press release, 6 Dec 2021
sources.reported_estimate: EV-only phase-out by 2035: 501,000 EU supplier jobs in ICE powertrain at risk (70%, 359,000, lost in 2030-2035); 226,000 new EV-powertrain jobs; net loss 275,000 (-43%) by 2040.

sources.title: Vehicle Scrappage and Gasoline Policy
sources.reported_estimate: Scrap elasticity about -0.7; when new-vehicle standards raise used-car values and delay scrappage, 13-16% of expected fuel savings leak away through the used-vehicle market (Gruenspecht effect).

sources.title: Critical Minerals Market Review 2023: Key market trends
sources.reported_estimate: Broad-based price increases for critical minerals in 2021 and early 2022, especially volatile for nickel and lithium; market for key transition minerals doubled in five years to $320bn in 2022; clean-energy share of demand 56% lithium, 40% cobalt, 16% nickel.

sources.title: The Electric Car's Short Circuit
sources.reported_estimate: Danish EV tax exemptions cost almost EUR 6,000 per tonne of CO2 avoided vs ~EUR 5/t in the EU ETS; below ~50,000 km an EV on European power emits more lifetime CO2 than a conventional car.

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3 cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020); low-end carbon value in the cross-check.

sources.authors: Centre for Economics and Business Research (for the APPG on Fair Fuel), as reported by Forecourt Trader
sources.title: Banning sales of new ICE cars from 2030 will cost five times as much as the benefits, says report
sources.reported_estimate: UK 2030 ban: environmental benefits GBP 76bn vs costs GBP 400bn (ratio ~0.19), incl. GBP 188bn extra vehicle costs, GBP 47bn charging time, GBP 99bn electricity and charging infrastructure. Sets the high end.

sources.authors: Roland Berger for the Clean Freight Coalition (as reported by Trucking Dive)
sources.title: Electrifying trucking would cost nearly $1 trillion, study finds
sources.reported_estimate: Nearly $1 trillion for infrastructure alone: about $620bn for charging and $370bn for utility grid upgrades; about $145,000 of charging per heavy-duty vehicle; vehicle costs excluded.

sources.authors: American Transportation Research Institute (as reported by FleetOwner)
sources.title: Charging Infrastructure Challenges for the U.S. Electric Vehicle Fleet
sources.reported_estimate: All-electric US fleet would need >40% of current US generation; ~13,800 lb payload loss per truck; BEV tractor at least $380,000; 6.3-34.9 years of current world output of key minerals.

sources.title: Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024 (press release)
sources.reported_estimate: Announced projects meet 'only 70% of copper and 50% of lithium requirements in 2035' under national climate pledges.

sources.title: Regulatory Impact Analysis for rescinding the GHG endangerment finding and light-, medium- and heavy-duty vehicle GHG standards (EPA-420-R-26-002)
sources.reported_estimate: Removing the standards, 2027-2055 (2024$): scenario A1 at 3% a net cost of ~$180bn (savings $1,290bn vs costs $1,470bn); net savings of $89-680bn in the other scenario/discount-rate combinations (lower oil prices, consumers valuing only 2.5 years of fuel savings).
sources.why_excluded: Evaluates repeal of a gradual standard rather than a ban, and the visible text does not show whether forgone climate benefits are monetized; shows that the official sign depends on fuel-price and consumer-valuation assumptions.

sources.title: The Cost of Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions
sources.reported_estimate: Static cost of battery-EV subsidies $350-640/tCO2e; argues dynamic (learning) costs can be much lower than static ones.
sources.why_excluded: Prices voluntary purchase subsidies, not a binding ban; at $185 SCC it would give 0.29-0.53, inside the adopted range.

sources.authors: US Environmental Protection Agency (as summarised by NACAA; GAO)
sources.title: Multi-Pollutant Emissions Standards for Model Years 2027 and Later Light-Duty and Medium-Duty Vehicles: final rule RIA (summary)
sources.venue: NACAA summary of EPA final rule; GAO major-rule report
sources.reported_estimate: Annualized: vehicle technology $40bn, EVSE $9bn, noise/congestion $1.2bn; fuel savings $46bn, maintenance $16bn, climate ~$72bn, health $13bn; net benefits $99bn/yr (2% discount), i.e. (72+13+46+16)/(40+9+1.2) = 2.9; example pathways 35-56% BEV by MY2032. GAO (https://www.gao.gov/assets/870/868041.pdf) confirms $85bn emission benefits and $99bn net benefits.
sources.why_excluded: Government self-appraisal of a gradual, technology-neutral standard (35-56% BEV by 2032), not a 100% ban by 2030; counts private fuel savings and uses a 2% discount rate; EPA moved in 2026 to rescind it.
