sources.title: Net Zero by 2050: A Roadmap for the Global Energy Sector
sources.reported_estimate: No new ICE passenger-car sales globally by 2035; energy investment ~$5T/yr by 2030; global GDP ~4% above trend in 2030.
sources.why_excluded: Scenario projection, not a benefit-cost analysis; its GDP gain comes from an investment-led macro scenario that does not price a 2030 ban's compliance costs.

sources.title: Zero Emission Vehicle Mandate and CO2 Regulations: Joint Government Response Cost Benefit Analysis
sources.reported_estimate: 80% ZEV cars / 70% vans by 2030: PV benefits GBP 166.5bn, PV costs GBP 127.3bn incl. rebound (GBP 50.4bn excluding it), NPV GBP 39bn (range -40 to +183bn; PV costs 99-138, benefits 98-282); BCR 1.31. Costs: vehicle capital GBP 27bn, chargepoint capital GBP 11bn, opex ~GBP 2bn, congestion GBP 78bn, accidents GBP 7bn, administration <GBP 35m; grid reinforcement inside electricity price forecasts. Benefits include later BEV capital-cost savings; carbon valued at ~GBP 245/t.
sources.why_excluded: Government appraisal of its own mandate; assumes electric cars become cheaper than conventional ones and a near coal-free grid. Its administrative cost share is used in cost_components.

sources.title: Advanced Clean Fleets Standardized Regulatory Impact Assessment (Appendix C)
sources.reported_estimate: Total costs $84.6bn, savings $97.0bn, health benefits $61.7bn, BCR 1.5 (Table 40); GSP -0.12% and employment -43,138 in 2038 (Table 55).
sources.why_excluded: Regulator's appraisal of its own rule.

sources.title: Impact assessment: CO2 emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles, SWD(2023) 88
sources.reported_estimate: Manufacturer cost EUR 6,500-13,100 per vehicle in 2040; first-user net savings EUR 29,100-47,000; GDP +0.06-0.11% in 2040.
sources.why_excluded: Regulator's appraisal of its own rule.

sources.title: Costs and Benefits of the Paris Climate Targets
sources.reported_estimate: Abstract: costs of climate policy, assuming least-cost implementation, 3.8-5.6% of GDP in 2100; benefits 2.8-3.2% of GDP; Paris targets fail the cost-benefit test unless risk aversion is high and the discount rate low. Text (arXiv v1): 2 C target costs just below 4% of GDP and 1.5 C just above 5.5%; benefits ~2.8% (2 C) and ~3.1% (1.5 C) against an SSP5-8.5 baseline, 1.8% and 2.2% against SSP3-7.0; 'simple policy imperfections... would readily double the costs'; citing Riahi et al. (2022), 1.5 C would cost 0.5-6.0% of GDP in 2030 and up to 10% in 2100.

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3: cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020), yielding >3 C by 2100; 2 C limits require $158-279/t in 2020; 1.5 C 'essentially infeasible'; abatement ~1% of output for 50% cut, ~3.5% for zero emissions.

sources.authors: Nordhaus, W.D. (DICE-2007 results as tabulated by Murphy, R.P.)
sources.title: A Question of Balance: Weighing the Options on Global Warming Policies (policy table, reproduced in Murphy, 'Rolling the DICE: Nordhaus' Dubious Case for a Carbon Tax', IER 2008, Table 4)
sources.venue: Yale University Press (book); Institute for Energy Research (reproduction)
sources.reported_estimate: PV, trillions of 2005 $ (damages / abatement costs / net vs baseline): no controls 22.55 / 0.04 / 0; optimal tax 17.31 / 2.20 / +3.07; limit CO2 to 560 ppm 15.97 / 3.95 / +2.67; limit temperature to 1.5 C 9.95 / 27.08 / -14.44; Stern discounting 9.02 / 27.74 / -14.18; Gore 90% cut by 2050 10.05 / 33.90 / -21.36. Implied BCRs: 1.5 C = 12.60/27.04 = 0.47; Gore = 12.50/33.86 = 0.37; 560 ppm = 6.58/3.91 = 1.68.

sources.authors: Chirakijja, J.; Jayachandran, S.; Ong, P.
sources.title: Inexpensive Heating Reduces Winter Mortality
sources.reported_estimate: The 42% fall in relative natural-gas heating prices in 2005-2010 averted ~11,000 US winter deaths a year; higher heating prices raise winter mortality, concentrated in cardiovascular and respiratory causes.

sources.authors: Parry, I.W.H.; Williams, R.C.; Goulder, L.H.
sources.title: When Can Carbon Abatement Policies Increase Welfare? The Fundamental Role of Distorted Factor Markets
sources.venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management (1999); NBER WP 5967
sources.reported_estimate: General-equilibrium models: 'tax interactions significantly raise the costs' of carbon policies; a revenue-neutral carbon tax is efficiency-improving so long as marginal benefits are positive, but policies that do not recycle revenue into cuts in distortionary taxes lose that advantage (a non-auctioned quota needs benefits of at least $25/t carbon just to break even). Mechanism for why re-investing revenue pushes the ratio down.

sources.authors: Murphy, R.P.; Michaels, P.J.; Knappenberger, P.C.
sources.title: The Case Against a U.S. Carbon Tax (Policy Analysis No. 801)
sources.reported_estimate: Citing IPCC AR5: 2 C target costs ~4.8% of consumption vs ~2.8% of output loss avoided (implied BCR ~0.6); SCC $56/t at 2.5% vs $11/t at 5% discount; US zero emissions by 2050 lowers 2100 temperature ~0.1 C; double-dividend GDP gains rare.

sources.title: Unpacking the IPCC's Estimated Carbon Prices
sources.reported_estimate: IPCC SR1.5: 1.5 C pathways require carbon prices of $135-5,500/tCO2 in 2030 -- source of the $135 figure.

sources.authors: Parry, I.W.H.; Black, S.; Roaf, J.
sources.title: Proposal for an International Carbon Price Floor Among Large Emitters (Staff Climate Note 2021/001)
sources.reported_estimate: Closest real global proposal: differentiated price floors among large emitters (1.5-2 C requires cutting emissions by a quarter to a half this decade); allows emissions-equivalent alternatives.

sources.title: Fiscal Monitor: How to Mitigate Climate Change (October 2019), Executive Summary
sources.reported_estimate: A $75/tCO2 tax in 2030 is needed for 2 C in large emitters; the global average carbon price is currently $2/t; such a tax would raise electricity prices ~45% and gasoline ~15% cumulatively over 10 years; revenue ~1.5% of GDP in G20 countries in 2030.

sources.title: State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2024 (Executive Summary)
sources.reported_estimate: Carbon pricing covers ~24% of global emissions; prices 'continue to fall short' of Paris ambition; 1.5 C-consistent 2030 prices USD 226-385/t; 2030 range for well below 2 C USD 63-127/t; revenues exceeded USD 100bn in 2023.

sources.title: Carbon Tax and Revenue Recycling: Revenue, Economic, and Distributional Implications
sources.reported_estimate: US $50/t rising 5%/yr: $1.87T net revenue 2020-29; GDP -0.4%, -421,000 FTE jobs in isolation; payroll-tax recycling +102,000 jobs; lump-sum rebate raises bottom-quintile after-tax income 6.8%.

sources.authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, ASPE
sources.title: Standard Values for Regulatory Analysis, 2024
sources.venue: HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation
sources.reported_estimate: Value per statistical life for 2024: central $13.1m (2023 dollars).

sources.authors: Visual Capitalist (citing IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2023)
sources.title: Visualizing the $105 Trillion World Economy in One Chart
sources.venue: Visual Capitalist, summarising IMF WEO April 2023
sources.reported_estimate: World GDP ~ $105 trillion in 2023.

sources.authors: Copenhagen Consensus Center (Expert Panel: Akerlof, G.; Bhagwati, J.; Kydland, F.; Schelling, T.; Smith, V.)
sources.title: Copenhagen Consensus on Climate: Results (Expert Panel prioritised list)
sources.reported_estimate: Ranking of 15 climate responses: 1 Marine cloud whitening, 2 Energy R&D, 3 Stratospheric aerosol insertion (all 'Very Good'); $20 OECD CO2 tax 12th ('Poor'); $0.50, $3 and $68 global CO2 taxes 13th-15th ('Very Poor'). No BCRs on this page.

sources.title: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Summary for Policymakers
sources.venue: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 WGIII
sources.reported_estimate: SPM C.12.2: versus continuation of 2020 policies, global GDP in 2050 is 1.3-2.7% lower in 2 C (>67%) pathways and 2.6-4.2% lower in C1 (1.5 C, no or limited overshoot) pathways (models exclude climate damages); Table SPM.2: C1 GHG emissions in 2030 31 [21-36] GtCO2e/yr. SPM C.12: the global economic benefit of limiting warming to 2 C 'is reported to exceed the cost of mitigation in most of the assessed literature (medium confidence)'.

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(13):e2312030121
sources.reported_estimate: SCC (2019$/tCO2): C/B optimal $50 (2020), $59 (2025), $125 (2050); 2 C path $75/$89/$213; 1.5 C path $3,557/$4,185/$16,552. 1.5 C limit 'infeasible' (would need emissions near zero in 5 years: 'a deep depression (output declining by around 75%)'). Carbon prices must rise to $115 (optimal), $63 (Paris) and $200 (2 C) by 2050. C/B optimal raises wealth ~$120T, 2 C ~$107T, Paris ~$85T versus current policy; runs 'assume complete efficiency and participation'.

sources.authors: NERA Economic Consulting (for the National Association of Manufacturers)
sources.title: Economic Outcomes of a U.S. Carbon Tax (figures as summarised by the Institute for Energy Research, 26 Feb 2013)
sources.reported_estimate: Per IER summary (https://www.instituteforenergyresearch.org/regulation/new-nera-study-shows-economic-dangers-of-a-carbon-tax/): $20/t tax rising 4%/yr cuts household consumption ~$350/household by 2033; tax to reach an 80% cut from 2005 by 2053 (capped at $1,000/t) leaves GDP 3.6% below baseline in 2053, consumption -$2,680/household in 2053, worker income loss equivalent to 1.26 million jobs on average; residential electricity +42%.

sources.authors: Kreutzer, D. W. (Heritage Foundation Center for Data Analysis)
sources.title: Impacts of Carbon Taxes on the US Economy (testimony before the Senate Committee on Finance, 16 Sept 2014)
sources.reported_estimate: Heritage Energy Model, Boxer-Sanders tax ($20/t rising 5.6%/yr to $50/t by 2030): GDP -$146bn in 2030; family of four loses >$1,000/yr; >400,000 jobs lost by 2016; electricity prices +20% by 2017 and >30% by 2030; counts only the excess burden with revenue rebated. Earlier $25/t analysis: family income -$1,400/yr on average through 2035.

sources.title: What does it cost the IRS to collect taxes?
sources.reported_estimate: IRS cost of collecting $100: 36 cents in FY2024; recent peak 53 cents in FY2010. Used for the administration component (0.53% of revenue).

sources.authors: Baird, S.; Friedman, J.; Schady, N.
sources.title: Aggregate Income Shocks and Infant Mortality in the Developing World
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 93(3):847-856 (near-final version: GWU IIEP WP 2010-7)
sources.reported_estimate: 1.7 million births in 59 developing countries: a one percent decrease in per capita GDP is associated with an increase in mortality of between 0.24 and 0.40 infants per 1,000 children born (abstract; Table 2).

sources.authors: World Bank, World Development Indicators (via FRED)
sources.title: Crude birth rate and total population, low and middle income countries
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (SPDYNCBRTINLMY; SPPOPTOTLLMY)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: crude birth rate 17.84 per 1,000; population 6,722,971,301; so about 119.9 million births a year in low- and middle-income countries.

sources.title: GDP (current US$), NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, 2024
sources.reported_estimate: 2024 GDP, US$bn: US 29,298.0; EU-27 19,501.1; UK 3,695.5; Canada 2,270.1; Australia 1,757.0; Switzerland 969.9; Norway 500.9; New Zealand 261.5; Iceland 33.2; total 58,287.2 (1.99x US); world 111,669.4; low and middle income 39,490.9.

sources.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
sources.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
sources.reported_estimate: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

sources.title: False Alarm: How Climate Change Panic Costs Us Trillions, Hurts the Poor, and Fails to Fix the Planet
sources.reported_estimate: Using DICE, an optimal global carbon tax costs ~$20T and cuts damages from ~$140T to ~$100T (net benefit ~$22T; implied BCR ~2); reduces 2100 warming from ~4.1 C to ~3.75 C (7.4 F to 6.75 F). URL is a secondary summary (Shortform).
sources.why_excluded: Scores the optimal tax (~$36-48/t in 2020-2030), far below $135; a milder policy.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at 2% near-term discount rate, 3.6x the prior US value of $51 -- under this SCC a $135/t tax has BCR >1 (counter-evidence).
sources.why_excluded: Marginal-damage estimate at a 2% discount rate under which a $135 tax passes; the main mainstream counter-case, not a full-cost evaluation of a target-driven, non-rebated global tax.

sources.title: op-ed on the Copenhagen Consensus on Climate results (Forbes, 21 Sept 2009)
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Galiana & Green: about $100bn a year of non-carbon energy R&D would yield ~$11 of avoided climate damage per $1 (called conservative); reports Tol: carbon cuts to stay under 2 C avoid ~2 cents of damage per $1 spent; global carbon taxes judged 'very poor'.
sources.why_excluded: 2009-vintage estimate for drastic cuts to stay under 2 C (Tol), quoted secondhand in an op-ed; superseded by Tol's own 2023 peer-reviewed estimate, which is used instead.

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model (2 C scenario result)
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(13):e2312030121
sources.reported_estimate: A 2 C-limited path raises global wealth by ~$107T (present value) versus current policy; 'the 2 C target does pass the cost-benefit test in cases with sufficiently low discounting (2%) or the alternate damage function'.
sources.why_excluded: Reports net wealth, not separate benefits and costs, so no ratio can be taken; assumes 'complete efficiency and participation' and a carbon price path ($200/t by 2050) that reaches $135 later than 2030; the same model finds the 1.5 C path, to which $135 in 2030 corresponds in IPCC SR1.5, infeasible.

sources.title: Bag leakage: The effect of disposable carryout bag regulations on unregulated bags
sources.venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 93:254-271
sources.reported_estimate: California bag bans eliminated ~40 million lb/yr of plastic carryout bags but increased trash-bag purchases by ~12 million lb (i.e., roughly 30% of the reduction offset by weight); 12-22% of carryout bags were previously reused as trash bags

sources.authors: Bisinella, V.; Albizzati, P.F.; Astrup, T.F.; Damgaard, A.
sources.title: Life Cycle Assessment of grocery carrier bags (Environmental Project No. 1985)
sources.reported_estimate: Conventional cotton bag must be reused ~7,100 times and organic cotton ~20,000 times to match an LDPE plastic bag across all 16 environmental indicators

sources.title: Sorry, banning plastic bags won't save our planet
sources.reported_estimate: Plastic bags <0.8% of mass of ocean-floating plastic; <5% of land-based ocean plastic from OECD countries; ~70% of ocean plastics from fishing; organic cotton bag needs 20,000 reuses

sources.title: How Green Is that Grocery Bag Ban? An Assessment of the Environmental and Economic Effects of Grocery Bag Bans and Taxes (Policy Study 437)
sources.reported_estimate: Bans/taxes yield minimal environmental benefit, raise costs for consumers (esp. low-income) and impose significant enforcement costs; HDPE bags often environmentally preferable on lifecycle basis

sources.title: Five Reasons Banning Plastics May Harm the Environment and Consumers
sources.reported_estimate: China and 11 other Asian nations responsible for 77-83% of plastic entering oceans; substitutes need >100 uses to offset production impacts; bans raise business and consumer costs

sources.authors: Meijer, L.J.J.; van Emmerik, T.; van der Ent, R.; Schmidt, C.; Lebreton, L.
sources.title: More than 1000 rivers account for 80% of global riverine plastic emissions into the ocean
sources.reported_estimate: ~1,000+ rivers (mostly in Asia) account for 80% of riverine plastic emissions to the ocean

sources.title: Global Plastics Outlook: Policy Scenarios to 2060
sources.reported_estimate: Global Ambition policy package lowers global GDP ~0.8% vs baseline in 2060 (Regional Action ~0.3%), costs higher in non-OECD countries

sources.title: Single-use Plastics Prohibition Regulations (SOR/2022-138): Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement
sources.venue: Canada Gazette, Part II, Vol. 156, No. 13 (22 June 2022)
sources.reported_estimate: 10-year (2023-2032) PV costs C$1,990m vs PV monetised benefits C$616m (BCR ~0.31); annualised costs C$234m, of which government compliance and enforcement C$0.9m, business administration C$0.1m, manufacturers' forgone profit C$21m, waste management C$23m, remainder consumer substitution costs; 'around $5 per capita per year'; ~1.3 Mt plastic waste and ~22,000 t plastic pollution avoided.

sources.authors: Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra)
sources.title: Impact Assessment on the proposal to ban the supply of plastic drinking straws to the end user in England (Final, RPC-4316(3)-DEFRA)
sources.reported_estimate: 10-year PV costs £36.9-77.7m (best £54.0m) vs PV benefits £2.4-4.6m (best £3.5m); net present value best estimate -£50.5m (range -£75.3m to -£32.3m); extra CO2 from paper straws monetised as a cost; 60% of costs assumed passed to consumers.

sources.title: Talks on global plastic pollution treaty adjourn without consensus (press release, 15 August 2025)
sources.reported_estimate: INC-5.2 in Geneva (183 member states, 10 days) adjourned without agreeing treaty text; production limits among contested issues.

sources.authors: Visual Capitalist (citing IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2023)
sources.title: Visualizing the $105 Trillion World Economy in One Chart
sources.venue: Visual Capitalist, summarising IMF WEO April 2023
sources.reported_estimate: World GDP ~ $105 trillion in 2023.

sources.authors: Meng, F.; Brandão, M.; Cullen, J.M.
sources.title: Replacing Plastics with Alternatives Is Worse for Greenhouse Gas Emissions in Most Cases
sources.reported_estimate: Life-cycle comparison of 16 applications covering ~90% of global plastic volume: 'in 15 of the 16 applications a plastic product incurs fewer GHG emissions than their alternatives. In these applications, plastic products release 10% to 90% fewer emissions across the product life cycle.' Plastics are responsible for ~4.5% of global GHG emissions.

sources.title: Emissions Gap Report 2024: No more hot air ... please! (as summarised by IISD SDG Knowledge Hub)
sources.reported_estimate: Global GHG emissions set a new record of 57.1 GtCO2e in 2023 (+1.3% on 2022).

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3 cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020). Used to value substitutes' extra emissions at the high end.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at 2% near-term discount rate. Used in the low-end sensitivity.

sources.authors: Waste & Recycling Magazine (event listing of UNEP INC-5.3)
sources.title: INC-5.3: The third part of the fifth session of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee to develop an international legally binding instrument on plastic pollution
sources.reported_estimate: INC-5.3 held 7 February 2026 in Geneva as a one-day resumed session agreed by the Bureau on 30 October 2025 after the former Chair resigned; organisational only (election of officers and a new Chair), no substantive treaty negotiations.

sources.authors: Environment Agency (Edwards, C.; Fry, J. M.)
sources.title: Life cycle assessment of supermarket carrier bags: a review of the bags available in 2006 (Report SC030148)
sources.reported_estimate: Paper, LDPE, non-woven PP and cotton bags should be reused at least 3, 4, 11 and 131 times respectively to have lower global warming potential than conventional HDPE bags that are not reused (173 times for cotton if HDPE bags are reused as bin liners).

sources.authors: Franklin Associates (for the American Chemistry Council)
sources.title: Life Cycle Impacts of Plastic Packaging Compared to Substitutes in the United States and Canada: Theoretical Substitution Analysis
sources.venue: Franklin Associates, a Division of ERG
sources.reported_estimate: Substitute packaging would weigh ~4.5 times as much as the plastic packaging it replaces (US); plastic packaging global warming potential is 26.2% of substitutes' (max-decomposition case); US GWP savings of plastic vs substitutes 39.5-67.1 million tCO2e/yr; total energy demand 52% of substitutes'.

sources.authors: Trucost (for the American Chemistry Council), as reported by Recycling Today
sources.title: Plastics and Sustainability: A Valuation of Environmental Benefits, Costs, and Opportunities for Continuous Improvement
sources.venue: Recycling Today (news report of the Trucost study)
sources.reported_estimate: Environmental (natural-capital) cost of plastics in consumer goods and packaging $139bn/yr; replacing them with alternatives that perform the same function would raise environmental costs to $533bn/yr (Waste Advantage, 29 July 2016, confirms the figures are annual: https://wasteadvantagemag.com/study-finds-plastics-reduce-environmental-costs-by-nearly-4-times-compared-to-alternatives/).

sources.title: 2025 Size and Impact Report: U.S. Plastics Industry Remains Robust, Impactful, and Vital
sources.reported_estimate: US plastics industry shipments $550.7bn in 2024 ($754.5bn including suppliers); 1,066,500 direct jobs (1.71 million including suppliers).

sources.authors: IISD SDG Knowledge Hub (summarising OECD Global Plastics Outlook 2022)
sources.title: Global Outlook Details Scenarios to Decrease Plastic Pollution by 2060
sources.reported_estimate: Regional Action scenario: global GDP 0.3% lower; Global Ambition: plastics tax of USD 750/t by 2030 and USD 1,500/t by 2060 plus a 33% higher packaging tax, global GDP 0.8% lower than baseline.

sources.title: Global Issues: Population
sources.reported_estimate: World population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022 (used to scale Canada's per-capita cost).

sources.authors: Lau, W.W.Y.; Shiran, Y.; Bailey, R.M.; et al.
sources.title: Evaluating scenarios toward zero plastic pollution
sources.reported_estimate: System Change Scenario could cut ocean plastic flows >80% by 2040 with existing technology; companion Pew report claims ~$70bn savings to governments vs business-as-usual (contrasting positive estimate for a broad package, not a ban)
sources.why_excluded: Scores a broad reuse-, redesign- and recycling-led system-change package and finds net savings; not a ban on plastics, and does not net out substitutes' extra emissions.

sources.title: Turning off the Tap: How the world can end plastic pollution and create a circular economy
sources.reported_estimate: Circular shift saves ~$1.27T (costs and recycling revenues) plus ~$3.25T avoided externalities to 2040; investment $65bn/yr vs $113bn/yr under throwaway economy.
sources.why_excluded: Scores a broad reuse-, redesign- and recycling-led system-change package and finds net savings; not a ban on plastics, and does not net out substitutes' extra emissions.

sources.title: The Green New Deal: Scope, Scale, and Implications
sources.reported_estimate: $51-93 trillion over 2020-2029 (clean grid $5.4T; high-speed rail $1.1-2.5T; job guarantee $6.8-44.6T; universal healthcare $36T; green housing $1.6-4.2T); up to ~$600k per household.

sources.title: Assessing the Costs and Benefits of the Green New Deal's Energy Policies (Backgrounder No. 3427)
sources.reported_estimate: GDP loss >$15T through 2040; peak 5.2m jobs lost; $165,000 per family of four; electricity costs +30%; eliminating all US CO2 averts <0.2 C and <2 cm sea-level rise by 2100; model reached only 58% CO2 cut by 2050.

sources.title: What the Green New Deal Could Cost a Typical Household
sources.venue: Competitive Enterprise Institute study (with Power the Future)
sources.reported_estimate: Energy/transport/buildings provisions cost >$70,000 per household in year one in most studied states (>$100,000 in Alaska), ~$45,000/yr in years 2-5, >$37,000/yr thereafter. EV component: $39,500 EV at 90% financing = about $7,647 a year in loan payments for five years; grid costs drawn from AAF (Holtz-Eakin & Bosch $39,000/household), Wood Mackenzie ($4.7T incl. $700bn transmission) and Zycher (AEI).

sources.title: Costs and Benefits of the Paris Climate Targets
sources.venue: Climate Change Economics 14(4) (Special issue on reaching net zero by 2050)
sources.reported_estimate: Costs 3.8-5.6% of GDP in 2100 (optimal implementation) vs benefits 2.8-3.2% of GDP; Paris targets fail the cost-benefit test unless risk aversion high and discount rate low (implied BCR ~0.5-0.85).

sources.title: Welfare in the 21st century: Increasing development, reducing inequality, the impact of climate change, and the cost of climate policies
sources.reported_estimate: Climate damages reduce projected 21st-century welfare gain from 450% to 434%; Paris-style policy returns ~11 cents of benefit per $1 spent (BCR ~0.11) vs ~$11 per $1 for green R&D (as summarized by Codera Analytics).

sources.title: A Climate Cure Worse than the Disease
sources.reported_estimate: Paris costs $1-2T/yr (UN estimates); fully achieving pledges averts ~0.053 C by 2100; EU climate policies yield ~3 cents of long-run climate benefit per $1.

sources.authors: Morris, J.; Chen, Y.-H.H.; Gurgel, A.; Reilly, J.; Sokolov, A.
sources.title: Net Zero Emissions of Greenhouse Gases by 2050: Achievable and at What Cost?
sources.venue: Climate Change Economics (Special issue on reaching net zero by 2050)
sources.reported_estimate: Global net zero by 2050 raises mitigation costs substantially vs staggered net-zero dates; tradeoff between policy cost and probability of 1.5 C (secondary reporting cites 8-18% of GDP by 2050).

sources.title: Senate fails to advance Green New Deal as Democrats protest McConnell 'sham' vote
sources.reported_estimate: GND resolution failed 0-57 on a procedural vote needing 60; 43 Democrats voted present.

sources.authors: Chirakijja, J.; Jayachandran, S.; Ong, P.
sources.title: Inexpensive Heating Reduces Winter Mortality
sources.reported_estimate: Quasi-experimental (gas vs electric heating areas x price shocks): the 42% fall in natural-gas prices relative to electricity in 2005-2010 averted about 11,000 US winter deaths per year; elasticity of all-cause mortality with respect to heating price ~0.03 (0.057 for winter deaths from relevant causes). Authors: policymakers should consider these effects when evaluating policies that affect home energy costs.

sources.authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, ASPE
sources.title: Standard Values for Regulatory Analysis, 2024
sources.venue: HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation
sources.reported_estimate: Value per statistical life for 2024: low $6.1m, central $13.1m, high $19.9m (2023 dollars).

sources.title: How much carbon dioxide is produced when different fuels are burned? / U.S. energy-related CO2 emissions (FAQ)
sources.reported_estimate: Total U.S. energy-related CO2 emissions in 2025 were about 4,904 million metric tons (4.9 billion t).

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3 cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020). Used as low-end benefit per tonne.

sources.title: The Benefits and Costs of the Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) Program Under the 2002 Amendments
sources.venue: Mathematica Policy Research, for US Department of Labor ETA
sources.reported_estimate: Net benefit to society of TAA about -$53,802 per participant (as reported by Heritage, 'Trade Adjustment Assistance: Another Evaluation Finds the Program to Be Ineffective and Costly'); participants earned $37,133 less over four years than comparison workers (2005 dollars).

sources.title: Can Displaced Labor Be Retrained? Evidence from Quasi-Random Assignment to Trade Adjustment Assistance
sources.venue: US Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies Working Paper CES-WP-22-05
sources.reported_estimate: Quasi-random caseworker assignment: TAA-approved workers have '$50,000 greater cumulative earnings ten years out', but annual gains converge to zero by year ten; training ~$6,200 and extended UI ~$13,200 per worker; private IRR 49.5%, social IRR 0% to 9.1% depending on leakage (NBER conference draft 2018).

sources.authors: Dahl, C.; Squire, C.; Cui, R.Y.
sources.title: What is the cost of a just employment transition?
sources.venue: Center for Global Sustainability, University of Maryland
sources.reported_estimate: Across seven coal countries studied (incl. the US): rehiring support $195-784m per country (> $23,000 per worker); income compensation averages > $253,000 per worker; health support ~ $13,000 per worker.

sources.title: Countries agree $300 billion by 2035 new climate finance goal: what next?
sources.reported_estimate: COP29 New Collective Quantified Goal (24 Nov 2024): developed countries to lead in mobilising at least $300bn a year for developing countries; all actors called on to scale finance to at least $1.3 trillion a year by 2035.

sources.authors: Lee, K.; Miguel, E.; Wolfram, C.
sources.title: Experimental Evidence on the Economics of Rural Electrification
sources.reported_estimate: RCT randomising grid connections in rural Kenya: at full coverage total cost ~$55,700 vs consumer surplus ~$12,400 per community (~0.22, 'less than one quarter the costs'); no meaningful medium-run economic or non-economic impacts; authors note unmeasured long-run benefits could change the conclusion.

sources.title: The "Energy Transition" Delusion: A Reality Reset
sources.reported_estimate: Storing 12 hours of US electricity in batteries would cost about $1.5 trillion; ~$100bn of conventional backup would cover days/weeks; it costs at least $30 to store the energy of one barrel of oil in lithium batteries; EV fueling infrastructure costs 10-20x conventional for the same utility; cumulative global subsidies for biofuels, wind and solar approach ~$5 trillion.

sources.authors: Paul, M.; Darity, W.; Hamilton, D.
sources.title: The Federal Job Guarantee - A Policy to Achieve Permanent Full Employment
sources.venue: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, Full Employment Project
sources.reported_estimate: 9.7m FTE jobs x $56,000 average cost per job (wage $32,500; supplies and capital goods $11,000; employer FICA $2,500; benefits $10,000) = ~$543bn/yr gross; no administration line. AAF builds its $6.8-44.6T job-guarantee range on this per-job cost.

sources.title: Report on Progress of the WPA Program, June 30, 1938
sources.venue: US Works Progress Administration (FRASER, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis archive)
sources.reported_estimate: July 1937-June 1938: expenditures for administrative and general supervisory purposes were 4.3% of the total (general administrative 3.2%, general project supervision 1.1%); 25,531 administrative staff. Used as the administrative share of a federal job guarantee.

sources.authors: Ballard, C.L.; Shoven, J.B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States (NBER WP 1043, 1982)
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal welfare loss from raising an additional dollar of revenue is 34-48 cents (working-paper abstract); average 13-22 cents. The 0.48 figure is used for the deadweight component of the cost total.

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 81(4):674-680 (NBER WP 5055)
sources.reported_estimate: A proportional rise in all personal income tax rates involves a deadweight loss of nearly two dollars per incremental dollar of revenue. Used for the deadweight of financing at both ends of the range.

sources.title: Testimony before the US House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology (18 November 2015)
sources.venue: US House of Representatives hearing record
sources.reported_estimate: MAGICC emulator, climate sensitivity 3 C: an 80% US emissions cut by 2050 averts about 0.11 C by 2100; the 2025 US Paris target held to 2100 about 0.04 C; Clean Power Plan about 0.02 C; ~25% less at a 2 C sensitivity.

sources.title: Impact of Current Climate Proposals
sources.reported_estimate: MAGICC: US INDC reduces 2100 warming by 0.031 C; Clean Power Plan 0.013 C; EU INDC 0.053 C; China INDC 0.048 C; all Paris-era policies sustained through the century ~0.17 C.

sources.title: Census Bureau Releases New Estimates on America's Families and Living Arrangements
sources.reported_estimate: 38.5m one-person households were 29% of all US households in 2024, i.e. ~133m households (38.5/0.29). Used to scale CEI's per-household vehicle cost.

sources.title: Social Cost of Carbon: Identifying a Federal Entity to Address the National Academies' Recommendations Could Strengthen Regulatory Analysis (GAO-20-254)
sources.reported_estimate: 2020 SCC at 3%: prior global value $50/t vs domestic-only value $7/t used 2017-2020.

sources.title: GDP (current US$), NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, 2024
sources.reported_estimate: 2024 GDP, US$bn: US 29,298.0; EU-27 19,501.1; UK 3,695.5; Canada 2,270.1; Australia 1,757.0; Switzerland 969.9; Norway 500.9; New Zealand 261.5; Iceland 33.2; total 58,287.2 (1.99x US); world 111,669.4; low and middle income 39,490.9.

sources.authors: Global Carbon Project (via Our World in Data)
sources.title: CO2 emissions dataset (fossil fuels and cement), 2024
sources.reported_estimate: 2024, Mt CO2: US 4,904.1; EU-27 2,426.2; Canada 533.3; Australia 386.7; UK 312.9; NZ 32.5; Switzerland 32.1; Norway 37.2; Iceland 3.8; total 8,668.8 (1.77x US); world 38,598.6.

sources.title: 2023 Strategic Foresight Report
sources.reported_estimate: 'Additional investments of over EUR 620 billion annually will be needed to meet the objectives of the Green Deal and RepowerEU' (p. 8).

sources.title: Beyond Paris: Reducing Canada's GHG Emissions by 2030
sources.venue: Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer
sources.reported_estimate: Additional carbon pricing lowers real GDP by 0.8% in 2030; with non-price measures at minimum cost, 2030 real GDP is reduced by a total of 1.4%.

sources.title: The Seventh Carbon Budget
sources.reported_estimate: Average investment of GBP 26bn a year 2025-2050, offset by savings of around GBP 22bn a year; overall cost around GBP 4bn a year, about 0.2% of GDP (pp. 85, 88).

sources.authors: Kose, M.A.; Lakatos, C.; Ohnsorge, F.; Stocker, M.
sources.title: The Global Role of the U.S. Economy: Linkages, Policies and Spillovers
sources.venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 7962
sources.reported_estimate: A 1 percentage point increase in U.S. growth could lift growth in EMDEs by 0.6 percentage points after one year (section 4.1, Figure 8).

sources.authors: Huidrom, R.; Kose, M.A.; Ohnsorge, F.
sources.title: How Important are Spillovers from Major Emerging Markets?
sources.venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 8093
sources.reported_estimate: A 1 pp rise in EM7 growth raises other emerging and frontier market growth by 0.9 pp after three years; a G7 growth rise raises it by about 0.5 pp more (Figure 3), i.e. about 1.4 pp per 1 pp G7 shock.

sources.authors: Baird, S.; Friedman, J.; Schady, N.
sources.title: Aggregate Income Shocks and Infant Mortality in the Developing World
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 93(3):847-856 (near-final version: GWU IIEP WP 2010-7)
sources.reported_estimate: 1.7 million births in 59 developing countries: a one percent decrease in per capita GDP is associated with an increase in mortality of between 0.24 and 0.40 infants per 1,000 children born (abstract; Table 2).

sources.authors: World Bank, World Development Indicators (via FRED)
sources.title: Crude birth rate and total population, low and middle income countries
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (SPDYNCBRTINLMY; SPPOPTOTLLMY)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: crude birth rate 17.84 per 1,000; population 6,722,971,301; so about 119.9 million births a year in low- and middle-income countries.

sources.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
sources.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
sources.reported_estimate: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

sources.title: Estimating the Benefit Incidence of an Antipoverty Program by Propensity-Score Matching
sources.reported_estimate: Argentina's Trabajar public-works programme: 'The average direct gain to the participant is found to be about half the gross wage.'

sources.title: Climate change policy, market structure, and carbon leakage
sources.reported_estimate: Leakage rates 'as high as 130%', meaning 'GHG control policies in the industrialized countries actually lead to higher global emissions'; IPCC AR4 WG3 11.7.2.1 reports his range as 25-130%.

sources.authors: Böhringer, C.; Balistreri, E.J.; Rutherford, T.F. (via Harvard Belfer Center brief)
sources.title: The role of border carbon adjustment in unilateral climate policy: Overview of an Energy Modeling Forum study (EMF 29)
sources.reported_estimate: 'Leakage rates in the BAU case are between 5% and 19%, with a mean value of 12%.'

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.reported_estimate: 'The SCC in the baseline run is $66/tCO2 for the 2020 period (in 2019 international $).'

sources.title: How Do Laffer Curves Differ Across Countries?
sources.venue: Federal Reserve Board IFDP 1048 (NBER WP 17862); in Alesina & Giavazzi (eds.), Fiscal Policy after the Financial Crisis, 2013
sources.reported_estimate: Table 7 (2010 calibration): maximum additional tax revenue at the peak of the Laffer curve, as a share of baseline GDP: US 7.3% (labour taxes), 2.3% (capital), 7.4% (both); EU-14 3.0%, 0.9%, 3.1%.

sources.title: The Laffer curve revisited
sources.reported_estimate: 'The US can increase tax revenues by 30% by raising labor taxes and by 6% by raising capital income taxes. For the EU-14 we obtain 8% and 1%.'

sources.title: On the Marginal Welfare Cost of Taxation
sources.reported_estimate: 'MWC can vary from under 10 percent to more than 300 percent of marginal tax revenue.'

sources.authors: Hänsel, M.C.; Drupp, M.A.; Johansson, D.J.A.; Nesje, F.; Azar, C.; Freeman, M.C.; Groom, B.; Sterner, T.
sources.title: Climate economics support for the UN climate targets
sources.reported_estimate: Updated DICE (expert discounting, updated damages/carbon cycle) finds limiting warming below 2 C economically optimal, requiring CO2 prices >$100/t.
sources.why_excluded: Models an efficient global carbon price under expert low discounting, not the GND's mandate-and-spending design; outside the range.

sources.title: The Effects of Rural Electrification on Employment: New Evidence from South Africa
sources.reported_estimate: Household electrification 'significantly raises female employment within five years' (IV and fixed-effects estimates).
sources.why_excluded: Shows a real benefit of energy access but gives no benefit-cost ratio, and concerns a national utility rollout rather than donor clean-energy finance.

sources.authors: Galvani, A.P.; Parpia, A.S.; Foster, E.M.; Singer, B.H.; Fitzpatrick, M.C.
sources.title: Improving the prognosis of health care in the USA
sources.reported_estimate: Single-payer universal care would cut national health spending 13%, >$450bn a year (2017 dollars), and save >68,000 lives and 1.73m life-years a year (abstract read via Europe PMC, PMID 32061298).
sources.why_excluded: Used only in the high end of the range: it is a modelling estimate that assumes large administrative and price savings, and AAF's $36T outlay estimate, used for costs, does not assume such net savings; the low end excludes it.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at 2% near-term discount rate.
sources.why_excluded: Highest published social cost of carbon; the range uses DICE-2023 ($66/t) and Nordhaus ($36/t).

sources.authors: C40 Cities; Arup; University of Leeds
sources.title: The Future of Urban Consumption in a 1.5°C World (Headline Report)
sources.venue: C40 Cities report (copy hosted by Arup)
sources.reported_estimate: Ambitious 2030 targets: 0 kg meat and 0 kg dairy per person per year (current C40 averages 58 kg and 155 kg); 3 new clothing items per person per year (progressive: 8); 0 private vehicles (C40 average 240 per 1,000 people; progressive target 190); 1 short-haul (<1,500 km) return flight every 3 years per person (progressive: every 2 years), which cuts C40 residents' flight trips by about 28% against 2017. C40 consumption-based emissions 4.5 GtCO2e in 2017 (about 10% of global); 94 member cities, 523 million people in 2017. Ambitious interventions cut cumulative 2017-2050 emissions by about 32 GtCO2e (Fig. 15, by category: buildings 21->11.9, food 17.7->7.2, clothing 6.8->2.5, private transport 9.9->6.1, electronics 5->3.4, aviation 3.5->1.6). Flights 2% of C40 consumption emissions (aviation fuel combustion 66% of that, fuel extraction 18%). A 'conservative micro-rebound effect' offsets about one third of savings. Wider-benefit claims: 160,000-170,000 diet-related deaths avoided a year; residents 'save $93 billion' on clothing. States it 'does not advocate for the wholesale adoption of these more ambitious targets'. No cost or BCR estimate.

sources.title: World's major cities have not agreed to ban meat, dairy and cars
sources.reported_estimate: Confirms the ambitious-scenario figures (0 kg meat/dairy, 3 clothing items, 0 private vehicles, 1 short-haul flight per 3 years) but rates the claim that cities agreed to ban them 'False'.

sources.title: Press release: Cities from India, Philippines and United Arab Emirates join C40's global network
sources.reported_estimate: C40 'represents 500+ million people and one quarter of the global economy'. Used to scale world figures to C40 cities: 25% x ~$105T world GDP = ~$26,250bn.

sources.authors: Moreno, C.; Allam, Z.; Chabaud, D.; Gall, C.; Pratlong, F.
sources.title: Introducing the '15-Minute City': Sustainability, Resilience and Place Identity in Future Post-Pandemic Cities
sources.reported_estimate: Defines the 15-minute city as proximity planning (daily needs within a 15-minute walk/cycle); contains no travel bans, consumption caps or cost estimates.

sources.authors: Abbiasov, T.; Heine, C.; Sabouri, S.; Salazar-Miranda, A.; Santi, P.; Glaeser, E.; Ratti, C.
sources.title: The 15-minute city quantified using human mobility data
sources.reported_estimate: GPS data from 40m US devices: median resident makes only 14% of consumption trips locally; higher local usage correlates with higher experienced segregation for low-income residents.

sources.title: Some Economic Benefits and Costs of Vegetarianism
sources.reported_estimate: Demand-system estimate (Raper et al. 2002 parameters): a 1% cut in at-home meat requires compensation of ~$0.16 per household per week; eliminating at-home meat requires ~$200.48 per household per week (~$10,500/yr, 1993 $), ~$1.3T a year for US households (~$1.8T in 2006 $). Authors call the 100% figure an extrapolation 'far outside the range of data'; excludes dairy and meals away from home.

sources.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED), from US Bureau of Economic Analysis
sources.title: Gross Domestic Product, annual (GDPA)
sources.reported_estimate: US nominal GDP 2006 = $13,815.6bn. Used to express Lusk & Norwood's $1.8T (2006 $) as 13.0% of GDP.

sources.authors: Visual Capitalist (citing IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2023)
sources.title: Visualizing the $105 Trillion World Economy in One Chart
sources.venue: Visual Capitalist, summarising IMF WEO April 2023
sources.reported_estimate: World GDP ~ $105 trillion in 2023.

sources.title: Animal Production
sources.reported_estimate: Livestock supports 'the livelihoods of at least 1.3 billion people worldwide'; contributes nearly 40% of agricultural output in developed countries and 20% in developing countries.

sources.title: Trade of agricultural commodities 2005-2022 (FAOSTAT Analytical Brief 80)
sources.reported_estimate: US food (excl. fish) exports $159.6bn = 10% of world total in 2022 (so world ~ $1,596bn); meat and meat preparations = 12% of food export value (~ $191bn).

sources.authors: Moody, J.; Farr, E.; Papagelis, M.; Keith, D.R.
sources.title: The value of car ownership and use in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Discrete-choice experiments in Chicago, Dallas, Seattle and Washington DC: respondents need on average ~$11,197 to give up access to their own vehicle for one year, at least as much as the ~$9,000 average total private cost of ownership; more than half the value is non-use (flexibility, status).

sources.title: Contribution of the Automotive Industry to the Economies of All Fifty States and the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Auto industry historically 3-3.5% of US GDP; 1.7m direct employees; net employment impact of nearly 8 million jobs (~4.5% of US jobs); over $500bn a year in compensation.

sources.authors: OICA (International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers)
sources.title: Economic Contributions
sources.reported_estimate: 66m vehicles (2005) = global turnover of almost EUR 2 trillion; ~9m direct jobs, 50m+ in total; 'if auto manufacturing were a country' it would be the sixth-largest economy; over EUR 400bn of tax revenue.

sources.authors: Parry, I.W.H.; Walls, M.; Harrington, W.
sources.title: Automobile Externalities and Policies
sources.reported_estimate: Table 2 central marginal external costs (2005 $): local pollution 2.0, congestion 5.0, accidents 3.0 cents/mile (mileage-related sum 10.0); greenhouse 0.3, oil dependency 0.6 cents/mile; assumes 21 mpg.

sources.authors: US Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center (from FHWA Highway Statistics)
sources.title: Average Annual Vehicle Miles Traveled by Major Vehicle Category
sources.reported_estimate: Cars average 11,026 miles a year; light trucks/vans 11,360.

sources.title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions from a Typical Passenger Vehicle
sources.reported_estimate: A typical passenger vehicle emits about 4.6 tCO2 a year (22.2 mpg, ~11,500 miles); 8,887 g CO2 per gallon.

sources.title: Size, Sprawl, Speed and the Efficiency of Cities
sources.reported_estimate: City productivity rises with the effective size of the labour market (jobs reachable within a given travel time); a 10% rise in average commuting speed raises labour productivity by ~2.9% (as quoted in Strong Towns 2017 from a report citing the paper); a 10% rise in job-home distance cuts effective labour-market size ~11.5%. 23 French cities. Used for the slower-travel component.

sources.title: Keep Your Clunker in the Suburb: Low-Emission Zones and Adoption of Green Vehicles
sources.reported_estimate: German LEZs reduced PM10 and sped up green-vehicle adoption; back-of-envelope 'health benefits of roughly 2 billion dollars have come at a cost of 1 billion dollars' for upgrading the vehicle fleet (BCR ~2).

sources.title: Health effects of Low Emission Zones: Evidence from German hospitals
sources.venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 109:102512
sources.reported_estimate: LEZs cut annual mean PM10 by 1.3 ug/m3 (~5.8%) and NO2 by 1.6 ug/m3 (~5.3%); circulatory diagnoses fell ~1.1-1.3 percentage points (~236 cases per hospital per year), concentrated inside LEZs; no significant GDP effects; cites Rohlf et al. (2020) that health savings repay fleet-upgrade costs in 9-11 years. Effects not monetised in the paper.

sources.title: Facts & figures (Aviation: Benefits Beyond Borders 2024)
sources.reported_estimate: 2023: direct aviation GDP ~$1.1 trillion (~1% of world GDP); total impact incl. indirect, induced and tourism $4.1 trillion (3.9% of world GDP); 86.5m jobs (11.6m direct); flights emitted 882 Mt CO2 in 2023; 4.4bn passengers.

sources.title: Aviation: Benefits Beyond Borders 2024
sources.reported_estimate: Aviation sector and aviation-facilitated tourism supported a $4.1 trillion contribution to global GDP and 86.5 million jobs in 2023.

sources.authors: World Travel & Tourism Council (as reported by TravelPulse)
sources.title: Travel & Tourism Growth Outpaces Global Economy in 2025: WTTC
sources.reported_estimate: Travel & tourism contributes ~$11.6 trillion (~9.8% of world GDP) and 366m jobs (10.9% of employment) in 2025. Used only as a cross-check; air-dependent tourism is already inside ATAG's $4.1T.

sources.authors: Oxford Economics (for the U.S. Travel Association)
sources.title: The Return on Investment of U.S. Business Travel
sources.reported_estimate: Econometric model over 18 years and 14 industries: each $1 of business travel associated with $9.50 of revenue and $2.90 of profit. Not priced here because the C40 cap applies to residents' personal flights; it shows the size of losses if business flights were included.

sources.title: A case study on Germany's aviation tax using the synthetic control approach
sources.venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
sources.reported_estimate: Synthetic control: German airports had ~4 million fewer passengers a year (~2% of traffic) than without the 2011 tax, concentrated at regional low-cost airports, while most bordering airports in the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland gained passengers; 'the results are consistent with passengers engaging in cross-border substitution', so the tax 'might not be effective in curbing overall emissions from air travel'.

sources.authors: Bernardo, V.; Fageda, X.; Teixidó, J.
sources.title: Flight ticket taxes in Europe: Environmental and economic impact
sources.venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice 179:103892
sources.reported_estimate: Ticket taxes reduce flights per airline-route ~12% and CO2 ~14%; burden is higher for passengers paying low fares (regressive)

sources.authors: Lu, S. (reporting WTO World Trade Statistical Review 2023)
sources.title: WTO Reports World Textiles and Clothing Trade in 2022
sources.venue: FASH455 Global Apparel & Textile Trade and Sourcing (University of Delaware)
sources.reported_estimate: World clothing exports $576bn in 2022; textile exports $339bn; Bangladesh 7.9% of world clothing exports.

sources.authors: Hossain, S. (Dhaka Tribune, reporting WTO data)
sources.title: Bangladesh retains 2nd largest RMG exporter ranking
sources.reported_estimate: Bangladesh clothing exports $38bn in 2023 (WTO), 7.4% of world share; China $165bn (31.6%).

sources.title: Does Trade Cause Growth?
sources.reported_estimate: Geography-instrumented estimate: raising the ratio of imports plus exports to GDP by one percentage point raises income per person by between one-half and two percent (as summarised in Ossa, Univ. of Zurich lecture 'Gains from trade', 2025, https://econ.uzh.ch/dam/jcr:3e218cd0-ad31-4ecd-a862-bfff347fcae9/Topic%2003%20-%20Gains%20from%20trade%20neu.pdf).

sources.title: Trade and Income—Exploiting Time Series in Geography
sources.reported_estimate: Time-varying instrument from air-versus-sea distance (aircraft technology): 'Trade has a significant effect on income with an elasticity of roughly one-half'. Used as a cross-check on the trade-loss component.

sources.authors: UN News (reporting UNCTAD Global Trade Update)
sources.title: Global trade growth turns negative after record year: UNCTAD
sources.reported_estimate: World trade almost $32 trillion in 2022 (goods ~$25T, services ~$7T).

sources.authors: Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (as reported by The Register)
sources.title: UK gov torpedoes personal carbon credit plans (reporting Defra's pre-feasibility study of personal carbon trading)
sources.reported_estimate: Defra: 'Initial set up costs would be between £700m and £2bn. Running costs would be between £1bn and £2bn a year' for a UK personal carbon allowance scheme.

sources.authors: Management in Practice (reporting the Office for National Statistics)
sources.title: UK population hits record 61 million high
sources.reported_estimate: UK population 61.4 million (mid-2008 ONS estimate). Used to convert Defra's scheme cost to a per-person cost.

sources.authors: Fowlie, M.; Greenstone, M.; Wolfram, C.
sources.title: Do Energy Efficiency Investments Deliver? Evidence from the Weatherization Assistance Program
sources.reported_estimate: Randomized-encouragement study of ~30,000 Michigan households: upfront costs (~$4,585 per complier household) are 'about twice the actual energy savings' (~$2,349 PV); model-projected savings more than three times actual; social rate of return about -7.8% a year over 16 years with CO2 at $38/t; net cost ~$201 per ton CO2 at 3% ($285 at 7%).

sources.authors: European Commission (as summarised by the European Clean Hydrogen Observatory)
sources.title: A Renovation Wave for Europe (COM(2020) 662), policy summary
sources.venue: European Clean Hydrogen Observatory (EU) policy page
sources.reported_estimate: EUR 275bn of additional investment a year needed to reach 2030 targets; ~35 million building units renovated by 2030; renovation rate doubled from 1% to 2% a year. Against EU27 GDP of EUR 12,653bn (2020, Ricardo/EC 2021) this is 2.17% of GDP. Commission's own estimate of required spending; used as the compliance cost only, not for benefits.

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3 cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020). Used as low-end benefit per tonne.

sources.authors: US Census Bureau (as reported by The Business Standard)
sources.title: World population to be 8.09 billion on 1 Jan 2025
sources.venue: The Business Standard (reporting US Census Bureau population clock release)
sources.reported_estimate: World population ~8.09 billion on 1 January 2025. Used for C40's population share: 523m / 8.09bn = 6.5%.

sources.title: Order without Design: How Markets Shape Cities
sources.reported_estimate: Argues cities' economic value derives from large, integrated labour markets and market-driven land use; planning that fragments the labour market reduces productivity (qualitative mechanism).

sources.title: Urbanism's Newest Controversy
sources.reported_estimate: Qualitative critique: top-down planning risks inequality, freedom and surveillance concerns; quotes Glaeser that a 15-minute city is 'not really a city at all... an enclave'. No cost figures.

sources.authors: US Census Bureau (McKenzie, B.; Rapino, M.)
sources.title: Commuting in the United States: 2009 (American Community Survey Reports ACS-15)
sources.reported_estimate: Table 5, workers in metro areas: mean travel time to work 24.2 minutes driving alone, 47.8 minutes by public transportation.

sources.title: The ABC of mobility
sources.reported_estimate: 794 cities in 61 countries (~850m people): 51.4% of urban commutes are by car; 91.9% in the US and Canada; 18.8% in Eastern Asia.

sources.title: Efficient Urbanisation: Economic Performance and the Shape of the Metropolis
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Prud'homme and Lee's estimate, from French and Korean cities, of an elasticity of about 0.30 between commuting speed and labour productivity (p. 1653).

sources.authors: Baird, S.; Friedman, J.; Schady, N.
sources.title: Aggregate Income Shocks and Infant Mortality in the Developing World
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 93(3):847-856 (near-final version: GWU IIEP WP 2010-7)
sources.reported_estimate: 1.7 million births in 59 developing countries: a one percent decrease in per capita GDP is associated with an increase in mortality of between 0.24 and 0.40 infants per 1,000 children born (abstract; Table 2).

sources.authors: World Bank, World Development Indicators (via FRED)
sources.title: Crude birth rate and total population, low and middle income countries
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (SPDYNCBRTINLMY; SPPOPTOTLLMY)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: crude birth rate 17.84 per 1,000; population 6,722,971,301; so about 119.9 million births a year in low- and middle-income countries.

sources.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
sources.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
sources.reported_estimate: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

sources.title: Displacing Congestion: Evidence from Paris
sources.reported_estimate: Closing the 3.3 km Voie Georges-Pompidou cut speeds on substitute roads by more than 15%; 'The total time cost generated by the GP closure amounts to 37M EUR'; total annual cost 44M EUR (pp. 34-35).

sources.authors: Galdon-Sanchez, J.E.; Gil, R.; Holub, F.; Uriz-Uharte, G.
sources.title: Social Benefits and Private Costs of Driving Restriction Policies: The Impact of Madrid Central on Congestion, Pollution, and Consumer Spending
sources.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 21(3):1227-1267
sources.reported_estimate: Pollution -19% and congestion -16%; consumers affected reduced brick-and-mortar spending in the regulated area by 21%, partly offset by online shopping.

sources.authors: Christensen, P.; Francisco, P.; Myers, E.; Souza, M.
sources.title: Decomposing the Wedge between Projected and Realized Returns in Energy Efficiency Programs
sources.reported_estimate: 9,800+ Illinois homes, 2009-2016: 'approximately 51% of projected savings are realized for the average home'; prior studies find 38% (Michigan WAP, Fowlie, Greenstone & Wolfram 2018), 58% (Wisconsin, Allcott & Greenstone 2017) and 73% (Massachusetts). Engineering-model bias explains up to 41% of the shortfall.

sources.title: Is There an Energy Efficiency Gap?
sources.reported_estimate: Empirical work implies 'the magnitude of profitable unexploited investment opportunities is much smaller than engineering-accounting studies suggest', and much of that literature does not meet modern standards for credibly estimating the net present value of energy savings.

sources.authors: McKinsey Global Institute (as reported by Fortune)
sources.title: The net-zero transition: What it would cost, what it could bring
sources.reported_estimate: Net zero by 2050 requires capital spending on physical assets of '$9.2 trillion per year on average' (about $275 trillion in 2021-2050), 'an annual increase of $3.5 trillion from today', peaking at the equivalent of 8.8% of global GDP by 2030.

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.reported_estimate: 'The SCC in the baseline run is $66/tCO2 for the 2020 period (in 2019 international $).'

sources.authors: C40 Cities; Arup; University of Leeds
sources.title: The Future of Urban Consumption in a 1.5°C World - 'wider benefits' chapter
sources.venue: C40 Cities report (copy hosted by Arup)
sources.reported_estimate: Claims residents in all C40 cities 'could collectively save $93 billion in one year' by buying fewer clothes, that cutting flights avoids '$70 million' of air-pollution damage, and that diet change avoids 160,000-170,000 deaths a year.
sources.why_excluded: Self-assessment by the proposing network. The $93bn 'saving' counts reduced spending as a gain without subtracting the value of the forgone goods, so it is not used as a benefit; diet-related health benefits are not credited.

sources.authors: Neiva, R.; Pons, A.; Horton, G. (Ricardo); Lutz, C.; Distelkamp, M. (GWS); et al.
sources.title: Study on the taxation of the air transport sector: Final Report
sources.reported_estimate: 2030 comparison table: stepped ticket tax -> intra-EEA passengers -8.3%, total aviation CO2 -6.2%, GDP -0.06%; EUR 0.33/l fuel tax -> total aviation CO2 -3.7%, GDP -0.04%. Fuel tax net CO2 saving ~5.7 Mt (2025) and ~5.3 Mt (2050) after modal shift; GDP ~EUR 9bn (0.05%) lower by 2050 with revenue used for deficit reduction. Baselines: EU27+UK aviation GHG 192.5 Mt in 2018; EU27 GDP EUR 12,653bn in 2020 (2.7%/yr growth to 2025, then 1.1%/yr).
sources.why_excluded: Commission-funded appraisal of ticket and fuel taxes (EU self-assessment); models a tax, not a per-person flight cap, and reports small GDP effects (-0.04% to -0.06%). Only its EU GDP figure (EUR 12,653bn, 2020) is used, to express the Renovation Wave cost as a share of GDP.

sources.title: The Cost of Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions
sources.reported_estimate: Battery-EV subsidy static cost $350-640/tCO2e (Table 2).
sources.why_excluded: Prices a voluntary purchase subsidy, not a ban; the car ban is valued directly from the value of car ownership (Moody et al. 2021).

sources.title: Impacts of active travel interventions on travel behaviour and health: Results from a five-year longitudinal travel survey in Outer London
sources.reported_estimate: Mini-Holland active-travel/LTN schemes in Enfield, Kingston, Waltham Forest: BCR ~50:1 to 200:1 (health), ~GBP 4,800 health benefit per adult over 20 years (per press coverage of the paper) -- counter-evidence for the non-coercive component.
sources.why_excluded: Voluntary low-traffic and active-travel schemes in Outer London (health BCR ~50-200): shows the non-coercive 15-minute-city planning component can pay, but it does not price car bans or consumption caps.

sources.authors: Keen, M.; Parry, I.; Strand, J.
sources.title: Planes, ships and taxes: charging for international aviation and maritime emissions
sources.reported_estimate: A ~$25/tCO2 fuel charge would raise ~$12bn/yr from aviation; welfare gains from correcting aviation's tax anomalies may be as large as the environmental gains (implies positive net benefits for a moderate Pigouvian tax).
sources.why_excluded: Models a moderate (~$25/t) Pigouvian charge on untaxed international aviation fuel, not a flight limit or high ticket tax; finds it welfare-improving.

sources.authors: Parry, I.; Strand, J.; Keen, M.
sources.title: The (non-) taxation of international aviation and maritime fuels: Anomalies and possibilities
sources.reported_estimate: $25/t CO2 illustrative charge (~$12bn/yr aviation revenue); 'the welfare gains from our suggested charges may be as large as those from environmental improvement, especially for aviation'
sources.why_excluded: Same moderate Pigouvian fuel-charge framing as Keen, Parry & Strand (2013); not a cap.

sources.title: Schiphol: krimpen of verduurzamen? (distance-based aviation tax package)
sources.venue: Social cost-benefit analysis commissioned by KLM, Schiphol and BARIN
sources.reported_estimate: Environment-and-noise package (distance-based aviation tax, fewer night flights, clean-fuel subsidies) has NPV +EUR 9.1bn to +EUR 43.9bn to 2050, positive in all 60 sensitivity runs.
sources.why_excluded: A differentiated tax-and-technology package rather than a flight limit; shows a well-designed aviation levy can pass a cost-benefit test.

sources.title: Climate Emergency, Urban Opportunity
sources.reported_estimate: Urban low-carbon measures: US$1.83 trillion invested a year 2020-2050 (about 2% of 2018 world GDP), with annual savings of US$2.80 trillion in 2030 and US$6.98 trillion in 2050; NPV US$23.9 trillion at 3.5% (p. 68).
sources.why_excluded: Covers cities' sector (production-side) actions, which are scored under the Green New Deal entry rather than with the consumption caps. Its savings are engineering projections: measured programmes realise about 38-73% of projected energy savings, 51% on average in the largest study (Christensen et al. 2023; Fowlie, Greenstone & Wolfram 2018), and Allcott & Greenstone (2012) find profitable efficiency opportunities much smaller than engineering-accounting studies suggest. At 51% realisation the projected $2.80tn of 2030 savings become about $1.43tn, below the $1.83tn a year of investment, a net cost of about $0.4tn a year; at 38%, savings of $1.06tn leave a net cost of about $0.77tn. McKinsey (2022) puts total net-zero capital spending at $9.2tn a year, $3.5tn above today's, peaking at 8.8% of world GDP in 2030.

sources.title: Changing the urban design of cities for health: The superblock model
sources.reported_estimate: 503 Barcelona superblocks could prevent 667 premature deaths a year (95% CI 235-1,098), worth EUR 1.7bn a year; implementation cost not estimated.
sources.why_excluded: Health impact of street redesign only, without the consumption caps or implementation costs.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at 2% near-term discount rate.
sources.why_excluded: Highest published social cost of carbon ($185/t); the range uses DICE-2023 ($66/t) as the upper carbon value.

sources.title: Technology-led Mitigation (Third Copenhagen Consensus: Climate Change Assessment Paper)
sources.venue: Copenhagen Consensus Center; final version in Lomborg (ed.), Global Problems, Smart Solutions: Costs and Benefits (Cambridge University Press, 2013)
sources.reported_estimate: Increased low-carbon energy R&D would yield benefits 'ranging from 3 to 11 times higher than cost, depending on rate of success and time horizon'.

sources.title: op-ed on the Copenhagen Consensus on Climate results (Forbes, 21 Sept 2009)
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Galiana & Green: about $100bn a year of non-carbon energy R&D would yield ~$11 of avoided climate damage per $1 (called conservative); reports Tol: carbon cuts to stay under 2 C avoid ~2 cents of damage per $1 spent; global carbon taxes judged 'very poor'.

sources.authors: Copenhagen Consensus Center (Expert Panel: Akerlof, G.; Bhagwati, J.; Kydland, F.; Schelling, T.; Smith, V.)
sources.title: Copenhagen Consensus on Climate: Results (Expert Panel prioritised list)
sources.reported_estimate: Ranking of 15 climate responses: 1 Marine cloud whitening, 2 Energy R&D, 3 Stratospheric aerosol insertion (all 'Very Good'); $20 OECD CO2 tax 12th ('Poor'); $0.50, $3 and $68 global CO2 taxes 13th-15th ('Very Poor'). No BCRs on this page.

sources.authors: Rosegrant, M. W.; Wong, B.; Sulser, T. B.; Dubosse, N.; Lybbert, T. J.
sources.title: Benefit-Cost Analysis of Increased Funding for Agricultural Research and Development in the Global South
sources.reported_estimate: BCR 33; costs $61bn NPV ($5.2bn/yr); benefits $2.1 trillion; +10% ag output, -35% hunger, -16% food prices, +4% per capita income over 35 years.

sources.authors: Alston, J. M.; Andersen, M. A.; James, J. S.; Pardey, P. G.
sources.title: The Economic Returns to U.S. Public Agricultural Research
sources.reported_estimate: Average own-state BCR 21:1, 32:1 including interstate spillovers; real IRR 9-10%.

sources.authors: Alston, J. M.; Pardey, P. G.; Rao, X.
sources.title: Payoffs to a half century of CGIAR research
sources.reported_estimate: Overall BCR on the order of 10:1 on ~$60bn PV of CGIAR investment.

sources.authors: Glennerster, R.; Emerick, K.; Krahn, A.; et al.
sources.title: The Return to Investing in Climate-Resilient Crops
sources.venue: Market Shaping Accelerator, University of Chicago (draft report)
sources.reported_estimate: Adoption-based advance market commitment (pull prize) for heat-resilient crops: BCR 8.7-22.6 (West African maize), 10.4-25.7 (East African sorghum), 24.3 for a $250m multi-target fund.

sources.title: An Analysis of Climate Engineering as a Response to Climate Change (Copenhagen Consensus on Climate: Climate Engineering Assessment)
sources.reported_estimate: Stratospheric aerosol insertion: ~$230bn cost, BCR ~15:1; marine cloud whitening: ~$5.8bn cost, ~$20 trillion benefits, BCR ~3,448:1.

sources.title: Climate Engineering (Third Copenhagen Consensus: Climate Engineering Assessment)
sources.reported_estimate: Climate-engineering R&D program 'on the order of a billion dollars'; each $1 could create ~$1,000 of benefits.

sources.authors: Kremer, M.; Levin, J.; Snyder, C. M.
sources.title: Advance Market Commitments: Insights from Theory and Experience
sources.reported_estimate: $1.5bn pneumococcal AMC: ~150 million children immunized in 73 countries, ~700,000 lives saved, ~$83 per DALY averted; diffusion ~5 years faster than rotavirus vaccine without an AMC.

sources.authors: Brunt, L.; Lerner, J.; Nicholas, T.
sources.title: Inducement Prizes and Innovation
sources.reported_estimate: RASE prizes 1839-1939: doubling a cash prize raised entries 6.4-14% and renewed (high-quality) patents 4-7%; each extra medal raised high-quality patents 20-44%.

sources.title: Innovation Inducement Prizes: Connecting Research to Policy
sources.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management 31(3):752-776
sources.reported_estimate: Literature review prompted by the America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 (all federal agencies may offer prizes): success of prizes is hard to judge and 'careful empirical evaluations of innovation inducement prizes are needed'.

sources.authors: Jones, B. F.; Summers, L. H.
sources.title: A Calculation of the Social Returns to Innovation
sources.venue: NBER Working Paper 27863 (published in Innovation and Public Policy, Goolsbee & Jones eds., 2022)
sources.reported_estimate: Average social benefit-cost ratio of innovation investment ~13.3 at baseline; ~5.3 under conservative assumptions (IRR ~27%).

sources.authors: Ozawa, S.; Clark, S.; Portnoy, A.; Grewal, S.; Brenzel, L.; Walker, D. G.
sources.title: Return On Investment From Childhood Immunization In Low- And Middle-Income Countries, 2011-20
sources.reported_estimate: Net return of 16 times costs (cost-of-illness approach) and 44 times costs (full-income approach) for 10 childhood vaccines, including pneumococcal, in 94 LMICs, 2011-20.

sources.authors: Bays, J.; Goland, T.; Newsum, J.
sources.title: Using Prizes to Spur Innovation
sources.reported_estimate: Ansari X Prize: $10M purse induced >$100M in team spending and >$1.5bn subsequent investment; large prizes tripled to $375M over a decade; only 23% of sponsors evaluate impact.

sources.title: McKinsey partners with Stripe, Alphabet, Shopify, and Meta on $925 million carbon removal commitment
sources.reported_estimate: Frontier: a $925M, eight-year advance market commitment guaranteeing future demand for permanent carbon removal to expand supply.

sources.title: XPRIZE Makes History, Awards $100M Prize for Groundbreaking Carbon Removal Solutions
sources.reported_estimate: $100M XPRIZE Carbon Removal (Musk Foundation-funded) awarded in April 2025.

sources.title: Mission Innovation Phase 2: More Failed Aspirations to Fight Climate Change
sources.reported_estimate: Mission Innovation 1.0 (2015-2020), 19 members: public clean-energy RD&D rose from $21.08bn to $26.8bn (+16%) against a pledge to double; only the UK doubled; six countries cut spending.

sources.title: Harvard Has Halted Its Long-Planned Atmospheric Geoengineering Experiment
sources.reported_estimate: Harvard halted the SCoPEx stratospheric experiment after years of opposition.

sources.authors: Olson, S. (interview with Erika Wagner, X Prize Foundation)
sources.title: X-Prize director describes incentive prizes
sources.reported_estimate: 'The rough rule of thumb is that the operational costs are equal to the prize costs': a $10M prize implies ~$20M total spending (research, infrastructure, judges, staff, media).

sources.authors: Nextgov (reporting the White House OSTP report on federal prize competitions)
sources.title: White House discloses administrative costs for innovation contests
sources.reported_estimate: USDA video challenge: ~$97,000 administration vs $9,000 prizes; CDC flu app: $59,611 vs $35,000; VA Blue Button: $30,614 staff costs vs $50,000 prizes.

sources.authors: Goes, M.; Tuana, N.; Keller, K.
sources.title: The Economics (or Lack Thereof) of Aerosol Geoengineering
sources.reported_estimate: Complete substitution of aerosol geoengineering for CO2 abatement fails a cost-benefit test over a wide range of scenarios, driven by termination risk and damages from geoengineering itself (as summarised in Bickel & Agrawal 2013).
sources.why_excluded: Peer-reviewed finding that substituting aerosol geoengineering for CO2 abatement fails a cost-benefit test in many scenarios; it concerns deployment, not research, and is answered by Bickel & Agrawal (2013). It is one reason the 1,000:1 research figure is treated as contested.

sources.title: Reexamining the Economics of Aerosol Geoengineering
sources.reported_estimate: Reframing Goes et al.: geoengineering may pass a cost-benefit test over a wide range of the scenarios Goes et al. considered (abstract; no single BCR in abstract).
sources.why_excluded: Reply to Goes et al. finding that geoengineering may pass a cost-benefit test; it gives no research-specific ratio, so it is used only as context.

sources.title: A Perspective Paper on Climate Engineering (Copenhagen Consensus on Climate)
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Bickel & Lane's BCRs as ~25:1 (stratospheric aerosols) and ~5,000:1 (marine cloud whitening); criticises them as 'precision without accuracy', citing Goes et al.'s contrary result.
sources.why_excluded: Critique of the Bickel & Lane ratios ('precision without accuracy'); used as context for the contested geoengineering figure, not as a separate estimate.

sources.title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from U.S. Appropriations Shocks
sources.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Working Paper 2305 (rev. 2024); later American Economic Review
sources.reported_estimate: Returns on nondefense government R&D of 140-210%; government-funded R&D accounts for about one-fifth of business-sector productivity growth since WWII.
sources.why_excluded: Returns of 140-210% to government (grant/appropriation) R&D: shows public R&D also pays well; not a prize mechanism and not privately funded.

sources.authors: Diamond, R.; McQuade, T.; Qian, F.
sources.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco
sources.reported_estimate: Treated landlords cut rental supply 15%; tenant mobility down ~20%; NBER version: 5.1% citywide rent rise.

sources.authors: Diamond, R.; McQuade, T.; Qian, F.
sources.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco (NBER conference draft)
sources.reported_estimate: Covered tenants gained $7.621bn cumulative 1995-2012 ($423m/yr; $3,100-5,900 per person per year), about one third of it landlord buyout transfers; citywide rent +7% and $5bn welfare loss to all renters, 'almost as large' as tenant gains.

sources.title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul? The Redistribution of Wealth Caused by Rent Control
sources.reported_estimate: St. Paul 2021 law cut property values 6-7% ($1.57bn); 67% direct capitalisation, 33% (at least $518m) deadweight externalities; higher-income tenants gained most, lower-income owners lost most.

sources.authors: Autor, D. H.; Palmer, C. J.; Pathak, P. A.
sources.title: Housing Market Spillovers: Evidence from the End of Rent Control in Cambridge, Massachusetts
sources.reported_estimate: Decontrol in 1995 explains about a quarter of Cambridge's $7.8bn residential appreciation 1994-2004, mostly on never-controlled properties.

sources.authors: Glaeser, E. L.; Luttmer, E. F. P.
sources.title: The Misallocation of Housing Under Rent Control
sources.reported_estimate: An economically and statistically significant fraction of New York City apartments is misallocated across demographic groups under rent control; dollar figures are in the NBER working-paper version (w6220), listed separately.

sources.title: Rent control effects through the lens of empirical research: An almost complete review of the literature
sources.reported_estimate: Rent controls are effective at slowing rent growth in controlled units but bring wide-ranging adverse effects for society as a whole.

sources.title: Rent Control (Feb 7, 2012)
sources.venue: Kent A. Clark Center for Global Markets, Chicago Booth
sources.reported_estimate: 0 strongly agree, 1 agree, 3 uncertain, 20 disagree, 13 strongly disagree (33/37 = 89% disagree) that rent limits improved affordable housing.

sources.title: National Rent Caps (Jul 23, 2024)
sources.venue: Kent A. Clark Center for Global Markets, Chicago Booth
sources.reported_estimate: A 5% cap on corporate landlords: 80.5% disagree it would make middle-income Americans substantially better off (2.4% agree); 68.3% agree it would substantially reduce apartments for rent (7.3% disagree). 41 responses.

sources.authors: Elmendorf, C. S.; Nall, C.; Oklobdzija, S.
sources.title: What State Housing Policies Do Voters Want? Evidence from a Platform-Choice Experiment
sources.venue: Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy 5(1) (SSRN 4811534)
sources.reported_estimate: National survey of ~5,000 urban and suburban voters: homeowners and renters alike support price controls; Cato (Bourne 2024) reports over 85% supported capping rents.

sources.title: Uh Oh, There's High Public Support for Price Controls
sources.reported_estimate: Over 85% of respondents in Elmendorf et al. supported capping rental prices.

sources.authors: City and County of San Francisco, Rent Arbitration Board
sources.title: Rent Arbitration Board FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 Budget Memo
sources.venue: City and County of San Francisco
sources.reported_estimate: Proposed FY2024-25 budget $13,827,383 (FY2025-26 $14,386,934); 50 FTE; funded by the Rent Board fee (up to $64/unit proposed for FY2025-26); 219,125 dwelling units and 13,138 SRO guest units billed (projected FY2023-24).

sources.authors: City of Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board
sources.title: FY 2024-2025 Budget, Staffing Model, and Expenditure Level (Item 7C, 20 June 2024)
sources.venue: City of Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board
sources.reported_estimate: FY2024-25 expenditure budget $8,332,918; ~29-30 FTE; registration fee $344 per fully covered unit and $212 per partially covered unit; ~5,700 partially covered units; $6.88m fully-covered fee revenue implies ~20,000 fully covered units.

sources.authors: New York State Homes and Community Renewal, Office of Rent Administration
sources.title: Office of Rent Administration 2025 Annual Report
sources.reported_estimate: ORA has 350 staff across six offices administering 1,064,049 registered rent-stabilized units (registration year 2025); no budget figure published.

sources.title: Quarterly Residential Vacancies and Homeownership, Second Quarter 2026 (press release)
