sources.venue: U.S. Census Bureau, Housing Vacancy Survey
sources.reported_estimate: Estimated 46,827 thousand renter-occupied housing units in Q2 2026 (Table 3; MOE +/-335 thousand).

sources.authors: Glaeser, E. L.; Luttmer, E. F. P.
sources.title: The Misallocation of Housing Under Rent Control (NBER Working Paper 6220)
sources.reported_estimate: Best estimate of the cost of New York rent control from misallocating rental apartments: $200 per apartment a year; lower bound from bedrooms and rent/own choice more than $40 per regulated or owned apartment; correcting for unobservables and other attributes gives $200-2,000 per apartment, $300m-$3bn a year for 1.5 million apartments (authors call the top 'perhaps unrealistic'). Data: 1993 NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey vs 1993 American Housing Survey.

sources.title: A Review of Empirical Evidence on the Costs and Benefits of Rent Control
sources.reported_estimate: Table 1: Olsen (1972) NYC 1968 subsidy $406 a year, tenant benefit $213, transfer efficiency 0.52; Mildner (1987 data) landlord cost of subsidy $122/month for controlled units, -$14 for stabilized, efficiency 0.65; other studies 0.45-0.99. Early (2000): controls raise uncontrolled rents 12% and 'the average benefit to tenants in regulated units was negative'. Gyourko & Linneman (1990): Manhattan units under old controls had 'a 9 percent higher probability of being in unsound condition'. Glaeser & Luttmer: misallocation DWL 'from USD 200 to USD 2,000 per apartment per year'.

sources.title: Out of control: What can we learn from the end of Massachusetts rent control?
sources.reported_estimate: As summarised by the NMHC review (Sturtevant 2018): rent control had little effect on new construction but was associated with owners converting rental units to condominiums, keeping thousands of units off the Boston-area rental market; controlled buildings were of lower quality. No dollar estimate used here.

sources.title: Rent Control, Rental Housing Supply, and the Distribution of Tenant Benefits
sources.reported_estimate: As reported by Turner & Malpezzi (2003): using 1996 NYC data, controls raised uncontrolled rents by 12% and the average benefit to tenants in regulated units was negative (abstract not available; figures read from the review).

sources.title: The Impacts of Rent Control: A Research Review and Synthesis
sources.venue: National Multifamily Housing Council Research Foundation
sources.reported_estimate: Summarises Glaeser & Luttmer (15-21% of NYC renters in units larger or smaller than they would choose without controls), Sims (2007) condominium conversion, Early (2000) higher uncontrolled rents leaving controlled tenants worse off, Navarro (1985) Cambridge administration ~$40 per unit, Peat Marwick (1988) NYC property-tax loss ~$370m a year.

sources.authors: Favilukis, J.; Mabille, P.; Van Nieuwerburgh, S.
sources.title: Affordable Housing and City Welfare
sources.reported_estimate: Calibrated NYC model: affordability policies (including rent control) have substantial insurance value, and targeting the neediest can yield substantial net welfare gains despite supply and misallocation costs.
sources.why_excluded: A calibrated structural model of well-targeted affordability policy, not an estimate of actual rent caps; its gains depend on targeting that real rent-control programmes lack (see Ahern & Giacoletti on who benefits). Shown as the main counterpoint.

sources.authors: Diamond, R.; McQuade, T.; Qian, F.
sources.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality (NBER w24181 abstract)
sources.reported_estimate: Rent control offered large benefits to covered tenants; welfare losses could be mitigated if rent-increase insurance were provided as government social insurance rather than a landlord mandate.
sources.why_excluded: Supports the tenant-insurance rationale, but the authors' remedy is a different, tax-funded policy; the gross tenant benefits it reports are already in the ratio's numerator.

sources.authors: Albrecht, B. C.; Tabarrok, A.; Whitmeyer, M.
sources.title: Chaos and Misallocation under Price Controls
sources.reported_estimate: 1973-74 US gasoline controls: ceiling 20% below baseline, 9% shortfall; Harberger triangle ~2.0% of spending; misallocation 2.2-17.7% of spending (1.09-8.75x the triangle); cites Frech & Lee and Deacon & Sonstelie finding queuing costs could exceed the entire rent transfer.

sources.authors: Frech, H. E. III; Lee, W. C.
sources.title: The Welfare Cost of Rationing-By-Queuing Across Markets: Theory and Estimates from the U.S. Gasoline Crises
sources.reported_estimate: Estimates the welfare cost of improper allocation across markets in the 1973-74 and 1979 gasoline crises (queuing costs could exceed the transfer, per Albrecht et al.).

sources.title: The Allocative Cost of Price Ceilings in the U.S. Residential Market for Natural Gas
sources.reported_estimate: Allocative cost of natural-gas price ceilings averaged $4.6bn a year 1950-2000 (peak $6.4bn in 1980), roughly tripling earlier net welfare loss estimates; MacAvoy's DWL $10.5bn/yr 1968-77.

sources.authors: Blinder, A. S.; Newton, W. J.
sources.title: The 1971-1974 Controls Program and the Price Level: An Econometric Post-Mortem
sources.reported_estimate: Nixon controls cut the non-food, non-energy price level 3-4% by Feb 1974, but catch-up after April 1974 left it only 0-2% below the no-controls path; decontrol explains most of 1974's double-digit core inflation.

sources.authors: Cavallo, A.; Cavallo, E.; Rigobon, R.
sources.title: Prices and Supply Disruptions during Natural Disasters
sources.venue: Review of Income and Wealth 60: S449-S471
sources.reported_estimate: After the 2010 Chile and 2011 Japan earthquakes, goods available fell 32% and 17% while prices stayed stable for months (sellers fearing 'customer anger').

sources.title: Price Gouging (May 2, 2012)
sources.venue: Kent A. Clark Center for Global Markets, Chicago Booth
sources.reported_estimate: Connecticut SB 60 anti-gouging bill: 1 strongly agree, 2 agree, 6 uncertain, 15 disagree, 5 strongly disagree, 3 no opinion (20 of 29 taking a position = 69% against).

sources.title: Election Economic Policy Ideas (Sept 10, 2024)
sources.venue: Kent A. Clark Center for Global Markets, Chicago Booth
sources.reported_estimate: As tallied by Cato (Bourne, Sept 13 2024): 88% agree widespread price controls create substantial distortions (99% confidence-weighted); 77% agree little evidence that price gouging causes high grocery prices, 0% disagree.

sources.authors: Oil & Gas Journal (reporting CRA International study for ACCF)
sources.title: ACCF: Price-gouging legislation could be costly
sources.reported_estimate: A federal price-gouging law in force after Katrina/Rita would have caused about $1.9bn of welfare losses (Sept-Oct 2005).

sources.title: Voters Support a Progressive Agenda Focused on Lowering Costs and Taking On Corporations
sources.venue: Data for Progress blog (1,085 likely voters, Apr 17-20, 2026)
sources.reported_estimate: 65% support cracking down on grocery store price gouging.

sources.authors: General Social Survey / ISSP Role of Government (SDA codebook)
sources.title: PRICECONGOVTS: government responsibility to keep prices under control
sources.reported_estimate: 32.1% definitely should, 41.8% probably should (73.9% total), pooled across years.

sources.authors: Bleiberg, R. M. (reporting J. T. Dunlop, Cost of Living Council)
sources.title: Farewell to Wage and Price Controls
sources.reported_estimate: Per Dunlop, the 'five freezes and phases, stretching over more than two and a half years, cost the taxpayer nearly $200 million and U.S. industry an estimated $721 million to $2 billion'; other sources put the cost to industry at about $2bn a year, or perhaps $5bn for the whole period.

sources.authors: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
sources.title: Gross Domestic Product, annual (GDPA)
Administration and Judicial Review of Economic Controls
sources.reported_estimate: Qualitative: Phase II enforcement would need 'far more enforcement personnel than the Administration has thus far provided'; no cost figures.

sources.title: The Welfare Costs of Rationing by Waiting
sources.reported_estimate: Under gasoline price controls with rationing by waiting, the value of time in queues plus the waste from buying more per purchase may exceed the rent transferred from suppliers to consumers; 'Rent seeking exhausts an estimated 116 percent of the rent transferred.'

sources.title: The Welfare Costs of Price Controls for Cars and Color Televisions in Poland: Contrasting Estimates of Rent-Seeking from Recent Experience
sources.reported_estimate: Colour televisions with rent dissipation: welfare cost 0.46% of GDP, 112% of Polish producers' sales, about ten times the Harberger triangle (rent rectangle 116bn zlotys, triangle 14bn). Cars without dissipation: 0.29% of GDP, 36% of producers' sales.

sources.title: The Two-Price System: U.S. Rationing During World War II
sources.venue: The Independent Institute (28 April 2009; also published in The Freeman)
sources.reported_estimate: The Office of Price Administration imposed 259,966 sanctions between 11 Feb 1941 and 31 May 1947; one in fifteen businesses was charged with illicit transactions and one in five warned; 2,000-5,000 investigators and 500-1,000 attorneys; substantial black-market shares in beef and gasoline (no percentage given).

sources.title: Targeted Price Controls on Supermarket Products
sources.reported_estimate: Argentina 2007-15: controlled goods stayed available (no evidence of shortages), but effects on aggregate inflation were temporary and firms introduced new, higher-priced varieties.
sources.why_excluded: Shows narrow, negotiated supermarket controls need not cause shortages, which argues the low end overstates harm for mild controls; but it gives no welfare estimate and found only temporary price effects, so it cannot set either end of the ratio.

sources.authors: Office of the New York State Attorney General, Economic Justice Division
sources.title: Price Gouging Economics and Price Volatility I (staff report)
sources.reported_estimate: Argues gouging laws are 'profit controls', not price controls, since short-run supply is inelastic; cites >97% of survey respondents viewing rationing as fair; gives no welfare estimate and rejects a ~$2bn cost study's method.
sources.why_excluded: A policy argument without any quantified welfare effect; it does not supply a number that could enter the ratio. Kept as the main argument for the policy.

sources.title: EconLib post on price controls and the 1979 gasoline shortage (date not checked)
sources.reported_estimate: 1979: average price ~80c, DOE market-clearing estimate $1.00, effective price including waiting time ~$1.20 per gallon.
sources.why_excluded: Blog-level arithmetic; used only as a cross-check on the low end, not as its basis.

sources.title: Drastic Measures: A History of Wage and Price Controls in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: History of US controls from colonial times to 1971-74, covering black markets and enforcement; argues controls can sometimes have a net positive effect, in particular that temporary controls may reduce the unemployment and lost output that usually accompany disinflation.
sources.why_excluded: Argues temporary controls can lower the output cost of disinflation, which would raise the high end in that setting; it gives no welfare estimate per $1 transferred that could enter the ratio, and the policy here is not tied to a disinflation programme.

sources.authors: Bombardini, M.; Gonzalez-Lira, A.; Li, B.; Motta, C.
sources.title: The Increasing Cost of Buying American
sources.reported_estimate: Current final-goods rules created up to ~100,000 jobs (99,901 in Table 2) at a welfare cost of $111,500-137,700 per job ($132,142 baseline); removing them raises US welfare 0.092%; tightening input rules adds 41,300 jobs at $154,000-237,800 per job; federal procurement ~$400bn/yr; scant evidence of effective industrial policy.

sources.title: The high taxpayer cost of 'saving' US jobs through 'Made in America'
sources.venue: PIIE Trade and Investment Policy Watch
sources.reported_estimate: US procurement tariff equivalent 26.0%; 5.6% cost premium; ~$94bn a year extra taxpayer cost (2017); 358,360 jobs 'saved'; over $250,000 per job; very little reaches workers.

sources.title: Buy American (Nov 15, 2011)
sources.venue: Kent A. Clark Center for Global Markets, Chicago Booth
sources.reported_estimate: Buy American mandates significantly raise US manufacturing employment: 0 strongly agree, 4 agree, 9 uncertain, 15 disagree, 4 strongly disagree (59.4% disagree, 12.5% agree of 32).

sources.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, ranging 17-56 cents (as summarised by Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.reported_estimate: A proportional rise in all personal income tax rates causes deadweight loss of nearly $2 per extra $1 of revenue.

sources.authors: Hinrich Foundation / TradeVistas (Lincoln Park Strategies poll)
sources.title: Buy American poll: public opinion
sources.reported_estimate: 75% support requiring the federal government to buy from domestic suppliers whenever possible (48% strongly).

sources.authors: Alliance for American Manufacturing (Mellman Group and Public Opinion Strategies)
sources.title: Americans want action to rebuild America
sources.venue: Alliance for American Manufacturing (1,200 likely 2020 voters; field date not stated)
sources.reported_estimate: 80% favour requiring taxpayer-funded infrastructure to use American-made goods (Republicans 88%, Democrats 75%).

sources.authors: General Social Survey / ISSP Role of Government (SDA codebook)
sources.title: AIDINDUSGOVTS: government responsibility to provide industry with the help it needs to grow
sources.reported_estimate: 22.8% definitely should, 47.4% probably should (70.2% total), pooled across years.

sources.title: Buy America Requirements for Manufactured Products (final rule, 90 FR 2932, 14 Jan 2025)
sources.reported_estimate: Annualized costs $61m-$942m; extra material costs $41m-$980m a year; additional $22m a year administrative costs to recipients of FHWA assistance and $167,000 a year for FHWA.

sources.title: Department of Transportation, Federal Highway Administration: Buy America Requirements for Manufactured Products (B-337017, major rule report)
sources.reported_estimate: Costs FY2026-35 $545m-$8,466m at 2% (annualized $61m-$942m); +$167,000/yr FHWA administrative costs; +$22m/yr administrative costs to recipients; benefits not quantified.

sources.title: Notice N 4510.892: Apportionment of Federal-aid Highway Program Funds for Fiscal Year 2025
sources.reported_estimate: Total FY2025 apportioned Federal-aid highway programs: $55,697,254,881.

sources.title: Federal Contracting: Opportunities Exist to Improve the Reporting of Waivers to Domestic Preference Laws (GAO-24-106166)
sources.reported_estimate: 17 agencies reported 745 waivers as of June 2023; OMB and GSA had not agreed on resource needs for the waiver website; no administrative cost figures.

sources.title: Federal Acquisition Regulation: Amendments to the FAR Buy American Act Requirements (final rule, FAR Case 2021-008)
sources.reported_estimate: About 8,800 respondents affected; 'the cost impact of this rule is not significant'; no new recordkeeping requirements; proposed domestic-content reporting collection withdrawn (no burden hours).

sources.authors: Bombardini, M.; Gonzalez-Lira, A.; Li, B.; Motta, C.
sources.title: The Increasing Cost of Buying American (local employment estimates)
sources.reported_estimate: A one-standard-deviation rise in procurement per worker (~$2,947) raised local manufacturing employment by 0.47 percentage points of the working-age population over five years.
sources.why_excluded: Shows the rules do move jobs into procurement-heavy places, which is the policy's stated aim; but jobs are inputs, not net welfare, and the same paper's welfare accounting (used in the ratio) already counts them.

sources.authors: Alliance for American Manufacturing (Mellman Group and Public Opinion Strategies)
sources.title: Americans want action to rebuild America
sources.reported_estimate: Industry-sponsored polling framing domestic content as job creation; no cost or welfare estimate.
sources.why_excluded: Advocacy source with no quantified benefits; used only for the popularity figure.

sources.title: Costs of Suspending Student Loan Payments and Canceling Debt
sources.reported_estimate: Cancellation of up to $10,000 ($20,000 for Pell recipients) costs about $400bn in present value; payment pause Sept-Dec 2022 $20bn.

sources.title: Biden's Student Loan Forgiveness: Budgetary Costs and Distributional Impact
sources.venue: Penn Wharton Budget Model brief (Aug 26, 2022; corrected Oct 4, 2022)
sources.reported_estimate: Cancellation $469-519bn over FY2022-31; with forbearance and new IDR ~$605bn static, >$1T with higher IDR take-up; about two-thirds of forgiveness benefits to households earning <=$88k; top 5% ~0%.

sources.title: The Distributional Effects of Student Loan Forgiveness
sources.reported_estimate: Full or partial forgiveness is regressive in present value: the top decile benefits as much as the bottom three deciles combined; enrolling eligible households in income-driven repayment is cheapest and most progressive.

sources.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, range 17-56 cents (per Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.reported_estimate: Deadweight loss of nearly $2 per extra $1 of revenue from a proportional rise in all personal income tax rates.

sources.authors: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.title: Biden v. Nebraska, No. 22-506
sources.reported_estimate: 6-3: the HEROES Act does not authorise the roughly $430bn mass cancellation plan.

sources.authors: Catherine, S.; Perez Clanton, M.; Yannelis, C.
sources.title: The Distributional Effects of Student Loan Forgiveness: An Update on SAVE and the COVID-19 Moratorium
sources.reported_estimate: Income-driven repayment expansions are more progressive than universal forgiveness but may raise moral hazard at the school level.

sources.title: Cooperative Election Study 2024 Common Content
sources.reported_estimate: Item CC24_323f 'Forgive up to $20,000 of student loan debt for each person': 55.1% support (weighted by commonweight, researcher-computed from the CES microdata; ~60,000 respondents).

sources.title: Student Debt Relief for the William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan Program ... (notice of proposed rulemaking, 89 FR 27564, 17 April 2024), Regulatory Impact Analysis
sources.reported_estimate: Net budget impacts of the waivers sum to ~$147bn (e.g., $62.1bn, $27.2bn, $17.1bn, $13.8bn, $11.0bn, $8.6bn, $7.6bn); one-time administrative expenses ~$13.0m for systems and contractors plus $18.0m for assigned-loan waivers; paperwork compliance for guaranty agencies and commercial FFEL holders $12.06m (annualized, 2%); one-time federal admin $3.4m annualized.

sources.title: Student Loans: Education Should Proactively Manage Fraud Risks in Any Future Debt Relief Efforts (GAO-24-107142)
sources.reported_estimate: Cites CBO's ~$430bn of relief to more than 31 million borrowers; identifies fraud-risk management as an implementation cost for any future relief; no administrative cost figure.

sources.authors: Chen, J.; Smetters, K. (Penn Wharton Budget Model)
sources.title: Biden's New Income-Driven Repayment ('SAVE') Plan: Budgetary Cost Estimate Update
sources.reported_estimate: SAVE 10-year cost: $342bn with no behavioural change; $391bn with a conservative borrowing increase; $475bn medium; $559bn with maximum borrowing increase; 'future student borrowers have the incentive to increase their federal student loan borrowing'.

sources.authors: NBC Boston / CNBC (reporting Sallie Mae, How America Pays for College 2024)
sources.title: Student loan forgiveness expectations may fuel more borrowing, expert says
sources.reported_estimate: 49% of families borrowed for college in 2023-24 (41% the year before); 48% of student borrowers expect their debt to be forgiven; the article notes no causal link has been established.

sources.authors: Lucca, D. O.; Nadauld, T.; Shen, K.
sources.title: Credit Supply and the Rise in College Tuition: Evidence from the Expansion in Federal Student Aid Programs
sources.venue: Review of Financial Studies 32(2): 423-466 (FRBNY Staff Report 733)
sources.reported_estimate: About 60 cents of each $1 increase in subsidised loan maximums passes through to tuition; used to describe where induced borrowing goes, not added separately.

sources.authors: Di Maggio, M.; Kalda, A.; Yao, V.
sources.title: Second Chance: Life without Student Debt
sources.reported_estimate: Borrowers whose private student loans were voided (chain-of-title failures) cut debt 11%, had 24% fewer delinquent accounts, moved and changed jobs more, and earned about $3,000 more over three years.
sources.why_excluded: Positive behavioural effects of relief, but from defaulted private loans of a small group via a legal accident, not a broad federal programme; the implied extra tax revenue is small relative to the cost, so it is noted but not added to the ratio.

sources.authors: Dinerstein, M.; Yannelis, C.; Chen, C.-T.
sources.title: Debt Moratoria: Evidence from Student Loan Forbearance
sources.reported_estimate: The 2020 payment pause led borrowers to take on more mortgage, auto and card debt rather than avoid delinquency, concentrated among non-delinquent borrowers.
sources.why_excluded: Evidence on the payment pause, not cancellation; suggests relief went mostly to already-solvent borrowers but gives no welfare number.

sources.authors: Social Security and Medicare Boards of Trustees
sources.title: Status of the Social Security and Medicare Programs: A Summary of the 2026 Annual Reports
sources.venue: Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary
sources.reported_estimate: OASDI 75-yr actuarial deficit 4.42% of taxable payroll; HI 0.56%; OASI depletion Q4 2032, OASDI Q3 2034 (83% payable), HI Q2 2033 (89% payable); OASDI annual deficit 0.8% of GDP in 2026 rising to 2.4% by 2085; 2026 OASDI cost $1,697bn (5.3% of GDP); Medicare 4.1% of GDP in 2026.

sources.title: Trustees Report One-Pager Placemat 2026
sources.reported_estimate: 75-yr deficit 4.42% of payroll, up from 3.82% in 2025; closing it needs a 31% income increase or 25% benefit cut; costs $1.61T (2025) to $2.49T (2034).

sources.title: Raising the Ages of Eligibility for Medicare and Social Security
sources.reported_estimate: FRA 67 to 70 cuts Social Security spending ~13%; Medicare age 65 to 67 cuts Medicare ~5%; raising the FRA to 70 or early age to 64 enlarges workforce and economy by slightly more than 1% in the long term.

sources.authors: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget
sources.title: Raising Eligibility Ages Is Good for the Budget...and the Economy
sources.reported_estimate: Reporting CBO: all three age changes make GDP about 2% larger by 2035 and 3% by 2060; revenue gain roughly 0.5% of GDP in 2035 per CBO's rule of thumb.

sources.title: Raise the Full Retirement Age for Social Security (Options for Reducing the Deficit: 2025 to 2034)
sources.reported_estimate: FRA to 70 for those born 1981+: outlays down $94.7bn over 2025-34; 75-yr OASDI balance improves from -1.5% to -1.0% of GDP (-4.3% to -2.9% of payroll).

sources.title: Labor supply effects of the recent social security benefit cuts: Empirical estimates using cohort discontinuities
sources.reported_estimate: Mean retirement age of affected cohorts rose by about half as much as the 1983-law increase in the normal retirement age.

sources.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue (range 17-56 cents), per Fullerton & Henderson 1987 (NBER w2353).

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.reported_estimate: Nearly $2 of deadweight loss per extra $1 of revenue from a proportional rise in income tax rates.

sources.authors: YouGov for Blueprint and The Liberal Patriot
sources.title: TLP / Blueprint poll: Biden and Trump economic proposals
sources.reported_estimate: 'Protect Medicare and Social Security from funding cuts or increases in the age of eligibility': net support +72.

sources.authors: General Social Survey / ISSP Role of Government (SDA codebook)
sources.title: AIDOLDGOVTS: government responsibility to provide a decent standard of living for the old
sources.reported_estimate: 46.2% definitely should, 41.3% probably should (87.5% total), pooled across years.

sources.authors: Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary
sources.title: Administrative Expenses as a Percentage of Total Cost (OASI, DI, OASDI)
sources.reported_estimate: CY2025 administrative expenses: OASDI $6,952m, 0.4% of total cost (OASI 0.3%, $4,308m; DI 1.6%, $2,644m).

sources.title: Medicare's Financial Status (R43122, updated 27 July 2026)
sources.reported_estimate: Table 1: HI administrative expenses $5.9bn in CY2025 against total HI expenditures of $444.2bn (about 1.3%, calculated from the table).

sources.title: Social Security and the Evolution of Elderly Poverty
sources.venue: In Auerbach, Card & Quigley (eds), Public Policy and the Income Distribution, Russell Sage Foundation (NBER w10466)
sources.reported_estimate: Elasticity of elderly poverty with respect to Social Security benefits is roughly unitary; cutting benefits would significantly raise elderly poverty.
sources.why_excluded: Measures a real benefit (poverty reduction) that a distribution-weighted analysis would add; the dashboard values transfers at $1 per $1 without weights, so it informs who_benefits rather than the ratio.

sources.authors: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget
sources.title: Raising Eligibility Ages Is Good for the Budget...and the Economy
sources.reported_estimate: Raising the early eligibility age to 64 changes Social Security spending little but adds output.
sources.why_excluded: The output gain from later retirement is partly offset by lost leisure, which is a private choice; only the tax (fiscal-externality) share is counted in the ratio, so the GDP figure itself is not used.

sources.authors: Clemens, M.A.; Montenegro, C.E.; Pritchett, L.
sources.title: The Place Premium: Bounding the Price Equivalent of Migration Barriers
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 101(2):201-213 (IZA DP 9789, 2016)
sources.reported_estimate: For prime-age, low-skill (9-12 yrs schooling) males, lower bound on the US/home real-wage ratio for identical workers: Mexico 2.557, Guatemala 2.617, median country 3.95, population-weighted average 5.65. Lower bound on absolute gain (PPP$/yr, 2000 Census data): Mexico >10,523, Guatemala >9,347, median country 13,600, weighted average 13,710.

sources.title: Open Borders
sources.reported_estimate: Net gains from removing immigration restrictions are 'about the same as the gains from a growth miracle that more than doubles the income level in less-developed countries'.

sources.title: Globalization, Brain Drain, and Development
sources.reported_estimate: Survey finding: high-skill emigration 'need not deplete a country's human capital stock' and 'can generate positive network externalities'. Effects on sending countries depend on context. Used to set the brain-drain term to zero for low-skill flows.

sources.title: Remittances Slowed in 2023, Expected to Grow Faster in 2024 (Migration and Development Brief 40)
sources.reported_estimate: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries reached $656bn in 2023, more than FDI and ODA. Mexico received $66.2bn (+7.8%). Treated as part of the migrant's earnings, not added separately.

sources.title: An Update to the Demographic Outlook, 2025 to 2055
sources.reported_estimate: Net immigration is 1.6m lower in 2025 and 0.96m lower in 2026 than in the January 2025 projection, mainly because of executive actions. The 2025 reconciliation act (P.L. 119-21) alone means 320,000 fewer people in the Social Security area population in 2035, from the removal of 290,000 immigrants. Used for the low-end enforcement cost: $170.7bn / 320,000 = $533,400 per person.

sources.title: Mass Deportation: Devastating Costs to America, Its Budget and Economy
sources.reported_estimate: One-time removal of 13.3m people costs at least $315bn (arrests $89.3bn, detention $167.8bn, legal processing $34.1bn, removal $24.1bn). 1m deportations a year costs about $88bn/yr ($88,000 each, all-in), or $967.9bn over about a decade. GDP would fall 4.2-6.8%.

sources.authors: Edelberg, W.; Veuger, S.; Watson, T.
sources.title: Macroeconomic Implications of Immigration Flows in 2025 and 2026: January 2026 Update
sources.reported_estimate: Net migration -295,000 to -10,000 in 2025 and -925,000 to +185,000 in 2026. US GDP growth lower by 0.2-0.3 pp in 2025 and 0.1-0.3 pp in 2026. Consumer spending $40-60bn lower in 2025 and a further $10-40bn lower in 2026.

sources.title: Economics and Emigration: Trillion-Dollar Bills on the Sidewalk?
sources.reported_estimate: Removing all barriers to labour mobility would raise world GDP by about 50-150% (Table 1: 67-147%); even partial removal yields gains of 0.6-55% of world GDP, one to two orders of magnitude more than freeing goods and capital flows. Used as the world-GDP upper bound, which is consistent with but not added to the per-migrant arithmetic.

sources.authors: di Giovanni, J.; Levchenko, A.A.; Ortega, F.
sources.title: A Global View of Cross-Border Migration
sources.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 13(1):168-202 (NBER WP 20002)
sources.reported_estimate: Quantitative multi-country model: in the long run natives in main receiving countries gain about 5-10% in welfare from observed migration (product variety); short-run average effect close to zero; remittance-receiving countries gain about 10%. Not added, to avoid double counting with Allen et al. Signals that the native-loss term is conservative.

sources.authors: Allen, T.; Dobbin, C. de C.; Morten, M.
sources.title: Border Walls (NBER Working Paper 25267, Nov 2018, revised May 2024)
sources.reported_estimate: 2006-10 wall (548 extra miles) cost $2.3bn plus $0.45bn maintenance 2007-15 (GAO lifetime maintenance about $1bn); reduced migration by about 311,000 (95% CI about 219,000-378,000); high-skill US workers lose $21/yr (0.04%), low-skill US workers gain $9/yr (0.02%).

sources.authors: Clemens, M.A.; Lewis, E.G.; Postel, H.M.
sources.title: Immigration Restrictions as Active Labor Market Policy: Evidence from the Mexican Bracero Exclusion
sources.reported_estimate: Excluding almost 500,000 Mexican bracero farm workers in 1964 did not raise native farm wages; the authors cannot reject zero change in agricultural wages and employment, because farms adopted labour-saving technology and switched crops.

sources.authors: East, C.N.; Luck, P.; Mansour, H.; Velasquez, A.
sources.title: The Labor Market Effects of Immigration Enforcement
sources.reported_estimate: Secure Communities lowered employment of low-skill noncitizens and of citizens in middle and high-skill occupations: about 178 fewer employed citizens per 100,000, about 1.5 citizen jobs lost per noncitizen job lost, and about 600,000 fewer employed male citizens nationally; small, imprecise positive effect on low-skill citizens.

sources.authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (Blau, F.D.; Mackie, C., eds.)
sources.title: The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration
sources.reported_estimate: Wage effects on natives very small over 10+ years; 75-year fiscal impact generally positive at federal level and negative at state/local level; first generation less fiscally favourable than natives, second generation the most favourable; results hinge on how public-goods costs are allocated.

sources.title: Do Immigrants Cost Native-Born Taxpayers Money?
sources.reported_estimate: NAS 75-year NPV of one additional immigrant including descendants: +$259,000 if public goods are not charged to the immigrant, +$173,000 if they are.

sources.title: Every Immigrant Without High School Degree Will Cost Taxpayers $640,000
sources.reported_estimate: From the NAS report: 75-year NPV net fiscal cost of a nonelderly adult immigrant without a high school diploma = $231,000 (current plus second generation); about $640,000 in undiscounted future outlays (author's own extrapolation). Used as the fiscal benefit at the HIGH end.

sources.authors: Nowrasteh, A.; Eckhardt, S.; Howard, M.
sources.title: The Fiscal Impact of Immigration in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Replicates and updates the NAS model. High-school-dropout immigrant arriving at 25: NPV +$216,000 excluding descendants and +$57,000 including descendants (Cato model), against -$32,000 / -$177,000 for native-born dropouts. Used as the forgone fiscal contribution, a cost, at the LOW end.

sources.title: Yes, Immigration Hurts American Workers
sources.reported_estimate: Immigration surplus about $50bn/yr; about $500bn/yr redistributed from competing native workers to employers; fiscal burden at least $50bn/yr; net effect on natives' total wealth 'barely' changed.

sources.title: National Academy of Sciences Study of Immigration: Workers and Taxpayers Lose, Businesses Benefit
sources.reported_estimate: Reading of NAS: immigration surplus $54.2bn/yr (0.31% of native income); native wage losses $493.9bn and business gains $548.1bn; annual fiscal burden up to $299bn.

sources.title: Comparing DHS Component Funding, FY2025: In Brief (R48115)
sources.reported_estimate: Net discretionary: CBP $19.62bn (FY2024 enacted and FY2025 CR); ICE $9.56bn (FY2024) and $10.04bn (FY2025 CR). CBP total budget authority FY2024 $22.67bn.

sources.title: What's in the Big Beautiful Bill? Immigration and Border Security Unpacked
sources.reported_estimate: H.R. 1 provides $170.7bn of extra immigration and border enforcement funding through 30 Sept 2029, including $46.6-51.6bn for the wall and CBP facilities, $45bn for ICE detention and $29.9bn for enforcement and removal. Lines: DOJ (immigration judges, prosecutions) $3.3bn; border processing $2.1bn (treated as admin); DHS reimbursement fund $10bn; states $13.5bn; DOD $1bn.

sources.title: ICE and Customs and Border Protection Budgets to Exceed $200 Billion
sources.reported_estimate: OBBBA gave DHS $170bn through Sept 2029; the 2026 Secure America Act added $70bn more; ICE and CBP had $118bn unspent as of April 2026.

sources.title: Women in the Labor Force: A Databook, Table 8 (2009 annual averages, ages 25-64, by educational attainment)
sources.reported_estimate: Civilian labour force aged 25-64, 2009 (thousands): total 126,247; less than high school 11,401; high school no college 36,159; some college/associate 35,291; bachelor's or higher 43,397. Used to weight Allen et al.'s per-worker effects.

sources.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
sources.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
sources.reported_estimate: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

sources.title: Effects of the Immigration Surge on the Federal Budget and the Economy
sources.reported_estimate: An extra 8.7 million net immigrants over 2021-26 lowers federal deficits by $0.9T over 2024-34 (revenues +$1.2T, mandatory outlays +$0.3T; discretionary about +$0.2T not included) and raises nominal GDP by $8.9T. CBO expects state and local costs to exceed revenues but did not estimate them.
sources.why_excluded: Federal budget only, mostly mandatory spending, and covers all recent immigrants rather than the low-skill unauthorized flows that enforcement targets. It points the same way as the low end.

sources.authors: Stanford News Service (on Allen, Dobbin & Morten 2018 version)
sources.title: Border wall came at high cost, low benefit to U.S. workers, Stanford study finds
sources.reported_estimate: 2018 version: wall cost $2.3bn (about $7 per US resident); cut Mexican-born workers by 0.6% (about 83,000); low-skill US workers +$0.36/yr, high-skill -$4.35/yr; a 25% cut in US-Mexico trade costs would cut migration more and benefit workers in both countries.
sources.why_excluded: Superseded by the 2024 revision, which is the version used. On the 2018 numbers the labour-market term is smaller (-$0.33bn/yr) but has the same sign.

sources.title: How CBO Analyzes the Costs of Proposals for Single-Payer Health Care Systems That Are Based on Medicare's Fee-for-Service Program (Working Paper 2020-08)
sources.reported_estimate: Across five illustrative single-payer options in 2030: national health expenditures change by -$0.7T to +$0.3T; federal subsidies rise by $1.5T to $3.0T; coverage nearly universal.

sources.title: The Costs of a National Single-Payer Healthcare System
sources.reported_estimate: M4A (S. 1804) adds about $32.6T in federal spending 2022-31 (10.7% of GDP in 2022, about 12.7% in 2031); assumes provider payments more than 40% below private rates; doubling all projected federal income-tax revenue would be insufficient.

sources.title: Understanding CBO's Medicare for All Cost Estimates
sources.reported_estimate: CBO Option 5 (closest to current proposals) raises federal costs about $3.0T in 2030; Option 3 $1.77T, Option 4 $2.40T; 2030 NHE baseline $6.6T; demand rises about 11-12% under both CBO and Blahous.

sources.authors: Blumberg, L.J.; Holahan, J.; Buettgens, M. et al. (Urban Institute, with Commonwealth Fund)
sources.title: Comparing Health Insurance Reform Options: From 'Building on the ACA' to Single Payer
sources.reported_estimate: Enhanced single payer: covers everyone; national health spending +$720bn in 2020; federal spending +$2.8T in 2020, $34T over 10 years. Single-payer 'lite': national spending -$209.5bn (-6%), federal +$1.5T in 2020.

sources.authors: Galvani, A.P.; Parpia, A.S.; Foster, E.M.; Singer, B.H.; Fitzpatrick, M.C.
sources.title: Improving the prognosis of health care in the USA
sources.reported_estimate: Single payer (S. 1804) saves about 13% of national health expenditure, more than $450bn a year (2017 USD), and prevents more than 68,000 deaths and 1.73 million life-years lost a year.

sources.authors: Miller, S.; Johnson, N.; Wherry, L.R.
sources.title: Medicaid and Mortality: New Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
sources.reported_estimate: ACA Medicaid expansions cut annual mortality among affected near-elderly adults by 0.132 percentage points (9.4%); CBPP summary: at least 19,200 deaths averted among 55-64-year-olds in expansion states 2014-17.

sources.authors: Ballard, C.L.; Shoven, J.B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal welfare loss from raising an additional $1 of revenue is 34-48 cents; 34 cents used here.

sources.authors: Institute for Clinical and Economic Review
sources.title: 2023 Value Assessment Framework
sources.reported_estimate: Health-benefit price benchmarks set at $100,000 and $150,000 per QALY or evLYG gained; used to value life-years.

sources.title: The Opportunity Costs of Socialism
sources.reported_estimate: If 'Medicare for All' were financed through higher taxes, 'GDP would fall by 9 percent, or about $7,000 per person in 2022'; programme financed with about $2.4T in 2022; funding it from existing spending would require cutting more than half the federal budget.

sources.authors: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
sources.title: Gross Domestic Product, annual (GDPA)
sources.reported_estimate: Nominal GDP 2025: $30,861.3bn.

sources.title: The Private Cost of Public Queues for Medically Necessary Care, 2024
sources.reported_estimate: 1,209,194 Canadians waiting for treatment in 2023; lost time valued at almost C$3.5bn (about C$2,871 each) counting working hours only, or C$10.6bn (about C$8,730 each) counting all hours except eight hours of sleep a night.

sources.title: Waiting Your Turn: Wait Times for Health Care in Canada, 2024 Report
sources.reported_estimate: Median wait from GP referral to treatment 30.0 weeks in 2024 (27.7 in 2023; 9.3 in 1993, 222% longer now); about 1.5 million procedures awaited.

sources.title: Testimony before the House Committee on Rules, Hearing on H.R. 1384, the Medicare for All Act of 2019 (30 April 2019)
sources.venue: U.S. House of Representatives, Committee on Rules
sources.reported_estimate: Added federal costs $32.6-38.8T over 2022-31; the $32.6T lower bound assumes savings 'without regard for any accompanying adverse effects this might have on health care access, timeliness or quality'; first-dollar coverage induces 11% additional demand for the privately insured and 16% for the uninsured; lowering provider payments to Medicare rates saves $5.307T; 'We do not know how providers would respond to payment reductions of this magnitude'.

sources.authors: World Bank via Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED); U.S. Census Bureau via FRED; Board of Governors via FRED
sources.title: Population, Total for Canada (POPTOTCAA647NWDB); Population (POPTHM); Canada / U.S. Foreign Exchange Rate, annual (AEXCAUS)
sources.reported_estimate: Canada population 2023: 40,049,088; US population Aug 2026: 343,008 thousand; 2023 average exchange rate 1.3494 Canadian dollars per US dollar.

sources.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
sources.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
sources.reported_estimate: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

sources.title: How Do Laffer Curves Differ Across Countries?
sources.venue: Federal Reserve Board IFDP 1048 (NBER WP 17862); in Alesina & Giavazzi (eds.), Fiscal Policy after the Financial Crisis, 2013
sources.reported_estimate: Table 7 (2010 calibration): maximum additional tax revenue at the peak of the Laffer curve, as a share of baseline GDP: US 7.3% (labour taxes), 2.3% (capital), 7.4% (both); EU-14 3.0%, 0.9%, 3.1%.

sources.title: The Laffer curve revisited
sources.reported_estimate: 'The US can increase tax revenues by 30% by raising labor taxes and by 6% by raising capital income taxes. For the EU-14 we obtain 8% and 1%.'

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.reported_estimate: 'The relative deadweight loss caused by increasing existing tax rates is substantially greater and may exceed $2 per $1 of revenue.'

sources.title: On the Marginal Welfare Cost of Taxation
sources.reported_estimate: 'MWC can vary from under 10 percent to more than 300 percent of marginal tax revenue.'

sources.authors: Finkelstein, A.; Taubman, S.; Wright, B.; et al. (Oregon Health Study Group)
sources.title: The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment: Evidence from the First Year
sources.reported_estimate: Lottery-based RCT: Medicaid raised insurance by about 25 pp, raised use of care, and cut out-of-pocket costs and medical debt; better self-reported health. Later follow-up (Baicker et al. 2013) found no significant change in measured physical-health markers over two years.
sources.why_excluded: Randomized evidence on covering low-income adults, not a cost estimate for single payer. It suggests mortality gains as large as Galvani's are uncertain; used as context only.

sources.title: Medicaid Expansion Has Saved at Least 19,000 Lives, New Research Finds
sources.venue: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities
sources.reported_estimate: At least 19,200 deaths averted among 55-64-year-olds in expansion states 2014-17; about 15,600 premature deaths in non-expansion states.
sources.why_excluded: Summary of Miller et al.; covers Medicaid expansion for one age band, not single payer.

sources.title: The Pros and Cons of a Guaranteed National Income (Policy Analysis No. 773)
sources.reported_estimate: Poverty-level UBI ($12,316 each) costs ~$4.4T/yr, >4x current welfare spending (~$3.4T gap after replacing all programs); 1968-80 NIT experiments reduced work effort (wives/single mothers -17% hours, husbands -7%).

sources.title: Universal Basic Income, In Perspective
sources.reported_estimate: Yang $1,000/month per adult ~ $2.544T/yr (56% increase in federal spending; ~74% tax increase); $10,000/yr variant adds ~$1.07T net; high implicit marginal tax rates for $15k-$55k earners.

sources.title: Universal Basic Income: Debate and Impact Assessment (WP/18/273)
sources.reported_estimate: Framework: UBI outcomes hinge on coverage, generosity, progressivity and financing (no single cost figure in abstract).

sources.title: A Unified Welfare Analysis of Government Policies
sources.reported_estimate: MVPFs for 133 US policies: Negative Income Tax experiment MVPF = -0.01 (partly due to reduced earnings of children in adulthood, per Price & Song 2018); tax credits and cash welfare to low-income households range from negative values to 1.20 (EITC 1.12-1.20); unemployment insurance 0.43-1.03; housing vouchers 0.65-0.91.

sources.authors: Ortiz, I.; Behrendt, C.; Acuña-Ulate, A.; Nguyen, Q.A.
sources.title: Universal Basic Income proposals in light of ILO standards: Key issues and global costing (ESS Working Paper No. 62)
sources.venue: International Labour Office, Social Protection Department
sources.reported_estimate: Global UBI at the national poverty line costs on average 39.4% of GDP (all persons at 100%) or 32.7% (children at 50%); low-income countries 62.3-79.1% of GDP; high-income countries 27.4-29.9%.

sources.authors: Visual Capitalist (citing IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2023)
sources.title: Visualizing the $105 Trillion World Economy in One Chart
sources.venue: Visual Capitalist, summarising IMF WEO April 2023
sources.reported_estimate: World GDP ~ $105 trillion in 2023 (IMF WEO April 2023 projection).

sources.authors: Vivalt, E.; Rhodes, E.; Bartik, A.W.; Broockman, D.E.; Miller, S.
sources.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States (NBER WP 32719)
sources.reported_estimate: RCT, $1,000/month for 3 years: 'For every one dollar received, total household income excluding the transfers fell by at least 21 cents, and total individual income fell by at least 12 cents'; individual income excl. transfers -$1,900/yr; participation -4.2 pp; no improvement in job quality; well-being gains faded after year one. (OpenResearch Unconditional Income Study, Illinois and Texas, 1,000 treated vs 2,000 controls receiving $50/month; NBER abstract: non-transfer individual income -$1,900/yr, participation -4.2 pp, 1-2 fewer hours/week.)

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 81(4):674-680 (NBER WP 5055)
sources.reported_estimate: Deadweight loss could be as much as 30% of revenue; 'A marginal increase in tax revenue achieved by a proportional rise in all personal income tax rates involves a deadweight loss of nearly two dollars per incremental dollar of revenue.' Used as the high excess-burden case for financing a UBI.

sources.authors: Ballard, C.L.; Shoven, J.B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: CGE model of the US tax system: 'The marginal welfare loss to consumers from raising an additional dollar of revenue is in the range of 34 cents to 48 cents' (working-paper abstract). Used as the low (mainstream) excess-burden case.

sources.title: Universal Basic Income: A Dynamic Assessment (NBER WP 27351; published AER 114(1), 2024)
sources.reported_estimate: GE-OLG model with human capital: a labour-tax-financed UBI ($5,500 per adult, 2000 dollars, in the WP version) raises the average labour tax from 22% to ~27.8%; steady-state GDP falls 12.9% (capital stock -20.2%); 'all future generations ... would be willing to sacrifice over 9% of consumption' to avoid it, though current adults gain 1.2%.

sources.title: More Americans oppose than favor the government providing a universal basic income for all adult citizens
sources.venue: Pew Research Center Short Reads (19 Aug 2020)
sources.reported_estimate: Public support 45%: 45% favour vs 54% oppose a federal $1,000/month guaranteed income for all adult citizens (American Trends Panel, n=11,001, 27 Jul-2 Aug 2020); Democrats 66% favour, Republicans 78% oppose.

sources.authors: Basic Income Earth Network (reporting Dalia Research)
sources.title: Survey of 11,000 Europeans finds 68% would vote for basic income
sources.reported_estimate: Public support 68%: 68% of 11,021 respondents aged 14-65 in all 28 EU states (March 2017) would vote for a basic income in a referendum, up from 64% in 2016; 24% against; MoE +/-1.1%.

sources.title: Where your donations go
sources.reported_estimate: 'In the last 3 years, 74% of dollars went to our large transfer programs, where ~80% was delivered as cash, with the rest covering the cost of getting it there'; Mozambique start-up ~60% efficiency, later USAID programmes ~75%.

sources.title: GiveDirectly (November 2020 version)
sources.reported_estimate: 'The proportion of total expenses that GiveDirectly has delivered directly to recipients is approximately 83% overall.'

sources.authors: Caldes, N.; Coady, D.; Maluccio, J. A.
sources.title: The Cost of Poverty Alleviation Transfer Programs: A Comparative Analysis of Three Programs in Latin America (FCND Discussion Paper 174; published in World Development 34(5), 2006)
sources.venue: IFPRI FCND Discussion Paper / World Development
sources.reported_estimate: Steady-state cost-transfer ratios (non-transfer cost per unit transferred): PROGRESA 0.041, PRAF 0.068, RPS 0.212; programme-life averages including set-up: PROGRESA 0.106, PRAF 0.499, RPS 0.629.

sources.authors: Vivalt, E.; Rhodes, E.; Bartik, A. W.; Broockman, D. E.; Miller, S.
sources.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States (NBER Working Paper 32719)
sources.reported_estimate: 1,000 treated receive $1,000/month vs 2,000 controls at $50/month for three years: individual income excluding transfers -$1,900/yr (preferred); household income excluding transfers -$4,215/yr (raw survey) or -$3,228 (adjusted); 'For every dollar received, total household income excluding the transfers fell by about 28 cents, and total individual income fell by around 16 cents'; participation -4.2 points; partners reduce hours about as much as participants.

sources.title: How Do Laffer Curves Differ Across Countries?
sources.venue: Federal Reserve Board IFDP 1048 (NBER WP 17862); in Alesina & Giavazzi (eds.), Fiscal Policy after the Financial Crisis, 2013
sources.reported_estimate: Table 7 (2010 calibration): maximum additional tax revenue at the peak of the Laffer curve, as a share of baseline GDP: US 7.3% (labour taxes), 2.3% (capital), 7.4% (both); EU-14 3.0%, 0.9%, 3.1%.

sources.title: The Laffer curve revisited
sources.reported_estimate: 'The US can increase tax revenues by 30% by raising labor taxes and by 6% by raising capital income taxes. For the EU-14 we obtain 8% and 1%.'

sources.title: On the Marginal Welfare Cost of Taxation
sources.reported_estimate: 'MWC can vary from under 10 percent to more than 300 percent of marginal tax revenue.'

sources.authors: VATT Institute for Economic Research; Kela (Hamalainen, K. et al.)
sources.title: Results of the basic income experiment: small employment effects, better perceived economic security and mental wellbeing
sources.venue: VATT / Finnish Ministry of Social Affairs and Health press release on final evaluation
sources.reported_estimate: 2017-18 pilot (unemployed recipients): ~6 more days employed in Nov 2017-Oct 2018 vs controls (78 days avg); small employment effect; better self-reported wellbeing.
sources.why_excluded: Two-year pilot for 2,000 unemployed people with no tax financing; says nothing about labour supply or tax costs of a universal program.

sources.authors: Egger, D.; Haushofer, J.; Miguel, E.; Niehaus, P.; Walker, M.W.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Effects of Cash Transfers: Experimental Evidence From Kenya
sources.reported_estimate: ~$1,000 transfers to 10,500 households (15% of local GDP): local transfer multiplier ~2.4, minimal inflation, large spillovers to non-recipients -- counter-evidence for low-income settings.
sources.why_excluded: Local spending multiplier of a one-off, donor-funded transfer in poor Kenyan villages; not a welfare BCR and not a permanent tax-financed universal payment.

sources.authors: Banerjee, A.; Faye, M.; Krueger, A.; Niehaus, P.; Suri, T.
sources.title: Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya
sources.venue: Working paper (15 Sept 2023), NBER conference draft
sources.reported_estimate: GiveDirectly UBI RCT in 295 villages (about 23,000 adults treated): $0.75/day per adult for 12 years (long-term arm), 2 years (short-term) or about $500 lump sum. After about 2 years: enterprises +14%, net enterprise revenues +52%; no fall in total household labour (shift from wage work to self-employment); consumption +5% (n.s.); depression down in all arms; lump sum had economic effects as large or larger. No formal cost-benefit analysis.
sources.why_excluded: Donor-funded transfers into very poor Kenyan villages, with no tax financing and no excess burden. It shows that UBI-style payments do not cut work in that setting, but it is not a tax-financed global programme.

sources.authors: Muralidharan, K.; Niehaus, P.; Sukhtankar, S.
sources.title: Identity Verification Standards in Welfare Programs: Experimental Evidence from India
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 107(2) (NBER WP 26744, 2020)
sources.reported_estimate: Biometric (Aadhaar) verification reforms in India's PDS reduced corruption but 1.5-2 million beneficiaries lost access at some point; adverse effects driven mainly by how the transition was managed

sources.title: Identification for Development (ID4D) overview brochure
sources.reported_estimate: ~40% of adults 15+ in surveyed low-income countries lack ID; 45% of poorest quintile vs 28% richest; 45% of women vs 30% of men; robust ID systems 'have the potential to produce substantial savings in the public sector' (no dollar figure)

sources.title: The New National ID Systems (Policy Analysis No. 831)
sources.reported_estimate: National ID infrastructure (REAL ID, E-Verify, facial recognition) enables government tracking; California REAL ID compliance >= $220m initial; Pennsylvania $27m year one then $17-20m/yr

sources.title: National ID Systems (Chapter 21, Cato Handbook for Policymakers, 8th ed.)
sources.reported_estimate: REAL ID delivers 'negligible national security gains at a significant cost in terms of personal privacy'; national employment-verification system ~$20bn initial plus hundreds of millions per year

sources.title: Digital ID Isn't for Everybody, and That's Okay
World population to reach 8 billion on 15 November 2022
sources.reported_estimate: World population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022.

sources.authors: Muralidharan, K.; Niehaus, P.; Sukhtankar, S.
sources.title: Identity Verification Standards in Welfare Programs: Experimental Evidence from India (NBER WP 26744; RESTAT 107(2):372-392, 2025) - randomized ABBA results
sources.reported_estimate: Randomized rollout of mandatory Aadhaar-based biometric authentication (ABBA) in Jharkhand's food-ration program: 'leakage increased insignificantly by Rs. 14 per ration card x month'; ABBA 'did not decrease (and if anything slightly increased) government spending'; 'overall transaction costs across the government, dealers, and beneficiaries increased by Rs. 13.6 per ration card per month ... a non-trivial 7.8% increase'; beneficiaries' own costs +Rs 7 (17% of control mean); unseeded households lost Rs 49/month (12.6%); nearly 300,000 people lost access to benefits.

sources.authors: Muralidharan, K.; Niehaus, P.; Sukhtankar, S.
sources.title: Building State Capacity: Evidence from Biometric Smartcards in India
sources.reported_estimate: RCT across 157 subdistricts (19m people): 'the investment was cost-effective, as time savings to NREGS beneficiaries alone were equal to the cost of the intervention'; per Ideas for India summary: time savings Rs 26 crore vs cost Rs 24 crore; NREGS leakage reduction Rs 197 crore (~8x cost); pensions leakage reduction Rs 20 crore vs Rs 14 crore cost.

sources.authors: Muralidharan, K.; Niehaus, P.; Sukhtankar, S. (Ideas for India summary)
sources.title: Building state capacity for better programme implementation: Lessons from the Andhra Pradesh Smartcard Programme
sources.reported_estimate: NREGS: time-savings value Rs 26 crore vs programme cost Rs 24 crore; leakage reduction Rs 197 crore, 'eight times the cost'; SSP leakage reduction Rs 20 crore vs Rs 14 crore cost. (Undated; references a July 2014 IGC Delhi lecture.)

sources.authors: Office for Budget Responsibility (reported by The Register)
sources.title: UK digital ID plan gets a price tag at last - £1.8B
sources.venue: The Register (28 Nov 2025), reporting OBR Economic and Fiscal Outlook
sources.reported_estimate: OBR provisional forecast: national digital ID costs £1.8bn over three years (£0.5bn resource, £1.3bn capital), about £0.6bn a year; no offsetting savings yet identified; target to issue IDs to all legal residents by Aug 2029.

sources.title: Do you support or oppose the proposal to introduce a digital ID card system in Britain?
sources.reported_estimate: Public support 42%: 14% strongly and 28% somewhat support; 15% somewhat and 30% strongly oppose (45% oppose); 14% don't know; n=4,920 GB adults.

sources.title: 57% of Britons support national ID card scheme, but have significant concerns over data security and implementation
sources.reported_estimate: Public support 57% for a national identity card scheme, but only 38% support vs 32% oppose a digital ID card when asked after pros and cons; n=1,116 GB adults, 18-21 July 2025.

sources.title: Government drops mandatory digital ID for right to work
sources.reported_estimate: UK government abandoned compulsory digital ID for right-to-work checks; refocus on voluntary use for public services; OBR cost up to £1.8bn over 3 years disputed by government.

sources.title: Burnham to scrap digital ID to focus on cost of living in 'reset of priorities'
sources.reported_estimate: Incoming PM Andy Burnham to scrap the UK all-adult digital ID programme; support had collapsed after the 2025 announcement and right-to-work use had already been made voluntary.

sources.authors: World Bank (Koshy, T.; Jayaram, P.; Menon, R.; Jain, N.; Prajapat, U. [Ernst & Young]; Chandra, K.)
sources.title: Understanding Cost Drivers of Identification Systems
sources.reported_estimate: Citing Gelb & Diofasi Metz (2018): building a foundational ID likely costs a low-income country ~0.6% of GDP; enrolment and credential issuance ~$4-11 per registrant; recurrent costs ~0.06-0.1% of GDP in a few countries; staff often >80% of annual costs; Aadhaar iris capture added ~Rs 4.40 ($0.06) per enrolment.

sources.authors: Visual Capitalist (citing IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2023)
sources.title: Visualizing the $105 Trillion World Economy in One Chart
sources.reported_estimate: World GDP about $105 trillion in 2023 (IMF WEO April 2023).

sources.authors: White, O.; Madgavkar, A.; Manyika, J.; Mahajan, D.; Bughin, J.; McCarthy, M.; Sperling, O.
sources.title: Digital identification: A key to inclusive growth
sources.reported_estimate: 'Good' digital ID (consent-based, privacy-protecting) could unlock value equal to 3-13% of GDP by 2030 (~6% emerging, ~3% mature economies); ~1bn people lack legal ID; risks include surveillance and exclusion (contrasting positive estimate)
sources.why_excluded: Consultancy projection of potential value from consent-based, privacy-protecting 'good' ID; not an evaluation of a mandate.

sources.reported_estimate: Alcohol excise tax increases: cost below I$0.10 per capita; under I$100 per healthy life year gained in all settings

sources.title: Effects of beverage alcohol price and tax levels on drinking: a meta-analysis of 1003 estimates from 112 studies
sources.reported_estimate: Mean price/tax elasticities: beer -0.46, wine -0.69, spirits -0.80, total alcohol -0.51; heavy drinking -0.28

sources.authors: Copenhagen Consensus Center (Post-2015 Consensus expert panel)
sources.title: Post-2015 Consensus: smart development goals (presentation of benefit per dollar by target)
sources.reported_estimate: Health: Increase tobacco prices 125% $22 per $1 (panel figure)

sources.title: Universal health coverage and intersectoral action for health: key messages from Disease Control Priorities, 3rd edition
sources.reported_estimate: Fiscal policies 'most prominently involved large increases in excise taxation of tobacco, with emerging evidence on taxation of alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages'; 40x30 goal likely missed without substantial excise tax action

sources.authors: Disease Control Priorities (Watkins, D.A.; et al.)
sources.title: CCC replication repository: new_inputs/PINandCosts0625.csv; '3. Cost calcs_bca.Rmd'; '4. BCR tables and figures.R'; Figures/clinical_full_2023_2030*.csv
sources.reported_estimate: Clinical unit costs carry a 'Cost adjustment' multiplier of 1.17 (community platform), 1.25658 (health centre) or 1.48824 (first-level hospital), i.e. a 17% above-facility markup plus ancillary costs; intersectoral policies carry 1.0. Policy unit costs per capita (2017 US$): tobacco tax 0.004, alcohol tax 0.004, salt policy 0.0351. PV 2023-30 at 8% (LIC+LMC): tobacco tax gross benefits $51.31bn, incremental cost $0.0453bn, forgone surplus $0.462bn; alcohol tax $2.935bn, $0.0286bn, $0.0264bn; salt $15.61bn, $0.414bn, $0.0156bn. Code sets forgone surplus = 0.9% (tobacco/alcohol) and 0.1% (salt) of gross benefits.

sources.title: WHO technical manual on tobacco tax policy and administration
sources.reported_estimate: Cost-of-collection ratio (recurrent tax-administration budget per 100 units collected, 2015, IMF survey): low-income 1.3, lower-middle-income 1.6, upper-middle 0.9, high-income 0.9. California tax stamps: US$0.42 per 1,000 (traditional), US$4.77 (first high-tech), US$8.20 (encrypted).

sources.title: Confronting Illicit Tobacco Trade: A Global Review of Country Experiences
sources.venue: World Bank (WBG Global Tobacco Control Program)
sources.reported_estimate: Global tobacco tax revenue loss from illicit trade US$40-50bn a year, about 600bn sticks or 10% of global consumption; tax increases do not necessarily lead to substantial illicit trade. UK: illicit-strategy enforcement staff spending by HMRC and the Border Agency about GBP90m a year (plus GBP209m start-up investment in 2000); 1999 illicit loss GBP2.5bn = 25% of tobacco revenue (implies ~GBP10bn revenue). Georgia: secure tax-stamp system cost EUR5 per 1,000 stamps, borne by industry from 2018. Australia: A$7.7m enforcement funding attached to 2016/17 excise increases.

sources.authors: World Health Organization; United Nations Development Programme
sources.title: Non-communicable disease prevention and control: a guidance note for investment cases (WHO/NMH/NMA/18.97)
sources.venue: WHO/UNDP (UN Interagency Task Force on NCDs)
sources.reported_estimate: In WHO NCD return-on-investment cases, clinical interventions are costed as drug/supply costs plus related health-system costs; policy interventions are costed as 'programme costs, defined as costs incurred at the administrative level outside the point of delivery' (OneHealth Tool / WHO NCD Costing Tool).

sources.authors: Watkins, D.; Ahmed, S.; Pickersgill, S.
sources.title: Best Investments in Chronic, Noncommunicable Disease Prevention and Control in Low- and Lower-Middle-Income Countries
sources.reported_estimate: Tobacco tax BCR 620 (LICs) to 1,300 (LMCs) with no forgone consumer surplus
sources.why_excluded: Assumes smokers lose no welfare from smoking less. Watkins et al. keep a forgone-consumer-surplus charge in their headline figure, and this analysis follows them to stay conservative, so 1,300 is not used as the high end.

sources.title: Poor Smokers, Poor Quitters, and Cigarette Tax Regressivity
sources.reported_estimate: Whether cigarette taxes are regressive depends on the burden measure; under every measure they heavily burden poor smokers who do not quit
sources.why_excluded: Does not dispute the BCR. It qualifies the distributional finding: net health and financial gains are pro-poor (GTEC 2018), but poor continuing smokers bear a real burden. Recorded here so the 'pro-poor' label is not overstated.

sources.authors: Copenhagen Consensus Center (Hall, A.; Horton, S.)
sources.title: Deworming: best practice paper (Copenhagen Consensus guide to giving)
sources.reported_estimate: 'each dollar spent results in about $6 of benefits' for preschool children; 'up to 60 times' the costs in high-infection areas.

sources.authors: Ahuja, A.; Baird, S.; Hicks, J.H.; Kremer, M.; Miguel, E.
sources.title: Economics of Mass Deworming Programs (DCP3 Vol. 8, Ch. 29)
sources.reported_estimate: Long-run benefits 'more than 100 times the cost'; annualised internal rate of return 32-51%; under $0.3bn a year to treat most of 870 million at-risk children (pp. 417-419).

sources.authors: Hamory, J.; Miguel, E.; Walker, M.; Kremer, M.; Baird, S.
sources.title: Twenty-year economic impacts of deworming
sources.reported_estimate: 'annualized social internal rate of return is 37%'; social NPV US$ PPP 230.71 (earnings) to 467.90 (consumption) at a 10% discount rate.

sources.authors: Baird, S.; Hicks, J.H.; Kremer, M.; Miguel, E.
sources.title: Worms at Work: Long-run Impacts of a Child Health Investment
sources.reported_estimate: Ten-year follow-up of the Kenyan Primary School Deworming Project: higher earnings, hours and meals for treated children as adults (basis of DCP3 return figures).

sources.title: Soil-transmitted helminth infections (fact sheet)
sources.reported_estimate: WHO recommends periodic preventive chemotherapy (deworming) for children in endemic areas.

sources.authors: Taylor-Robinson, D.C.; Maayan, N.; Soares-Weiser, K.; Donegan, S.; Garner, P.
sources.title: Deworming drugs for soil-transmitted intestinal worms in children: effects on nutritional indicators, haemoglobin, and school performance
sources.reported_estimate: Mass treatment shows little or no effect on many nutrition, haemoglobin and school outcomes.
sources.why_excluded: Covers short-run outcomes; the range uses long-run trial and Copenhagen estimates.

sources.title: Post-2015 Consensus: Population and Demography Assessment
sources.reported_estimate: 'Achieve universal access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services by 2030, and eliminate unmet need for modern contraception by 2040 which will return $120 for every dollar spent.'

sources.title: Why Family Planning Is a Smart Investment
sources.reported_estimate: Kohler & Behrman: ~$3.6bn/yr to serve 214 million women; 640,000 fewer newborn deaths, 150,000 fewer maternal deaths a year; $40 per $1 on health alone; demographic dividend $288bn/yr; $120 per $1 in total. Donor FP funding ~$1.27bn in 2017.

sources.authors: Madise, N.; Nandi, A.; Wong, B.; Razvi, S.
sources.title: Achieving Maternal and Neonatal Mortality Development Goals Effectively: A Cost-Benefit Analysis
sources.reported_estimate: Figure 3 (55 LICs/LMICs, 8% discount): BEmONC+FP 87; BEmONC alone 83; CEmONC 65; entire continuum of care 36; family planning alone 22; antenatal 7; periconceptual 6. Headline package: +$3.2bn/yr, $278bn/yr benefits plus $25bn/yr demographic dividend; 1.20m newborn and 161,000 maternal deaths averted per year at full scale. Family planning in Table 2: 68.6m extra women covered at unit costs $2.89 drugs + $2.14 staff + $0.65 hospital + $0.75 supervision.

sources.authors: Amporfu, E.; Arthur, E.; Novignon, J.; Wong, B.
sources.title: Costs and Benefits of Family Planning in Ghana (Ghana Priorities)
sources.venue: Copenhagen Consensus Center / National Development Planning Commission, Ghana
sources.reported_estimate: 8% discount: +10 pp contraceptive prevalence, married women BCR 33.6; unmarried women 29.3; compulsory comprehensive adolescent SRH education 2.3.

sources.title: Family Planning and Women's and Children's Health: Long-Term Consequences of an Outreach Program in Matlab, Bangladesh
sources.reported_estimate: Quasi-experimental comparison of Matlab programme vs comparison villages: ~17% lower fertility sustained about two decades, with better women's health and child outcomes.

sources.title: Contraception as Development? New Evidence from Family Planning in Colombia
The Economic Consequences of Reproductive Health and Family Planning

sources.authors: Duflo, E.; Dupas, P.; Kremer, M.
sources.title: The Impact of Free Secondary Education: Experimental Evidence from Ghana
sources.reported_estimate: Randomized secondary-school scholarships for 2,064 youths, 12 years of data: higher attainment, knowledge, skills and preventive health behaviour; reduced female fertility; earnings gains for women. (Sub-policy evidence.)

sources.authors: Duflo, E.; Dupas, P.; Spelke, E.; Walsh, M.
sources.title: Intergenerational Impacts of Secondary Education: Experimental Evidence from Ghana
sources.reported_estimate: RCT with 15-year follow-up: scholarships delay fertility, reduce unwanted pregnancies; 'Under-one mortality is reduced by half'; children's test scores +0.24 SD by age five; 'a conservatively estimated US$4.1 in benefits for each US$1 the policy would cost the government in the long run'. (Sub-policy BCR.)

sources.authors: Duflo, E.; Dupas, P.; Spelke, E.; Walsh, M. (VoxDev column)
sources.title: Subsidising secondary education has huge benefits for this generation and the next
sources.reported_estimate: Four years of senior high school cost ~$505 per woman including forgone wages; benefits 6-56x cost overall and 10-110x when targeted at girls; children of female recipients have 45% lower under-3 mortality. (Sub-policy.)

sources.title: Multigenerational Benefits to Secondary Schooling in Ghana (evaluation summary)
sources.reported_estimate: SHS enrolment 75% (scholarship) vs 19%; graduation 73% vs 45%; +1.26 years of secondary education; female recipients' earnings 20-30% higher from 2020-2023. (Sub-policy.)

sources.title: Post-2015 Consensus: Gender Equality (targets summary)
sources.reported_estimate: 'Programs increasing the number of years of education and increasing the age at marriage can return $5 for every dollar spent'; SRH access returns $120 (Kohler & Behrman). (Sub-policy.)

sources.title: Post-2015 Consensus: Education (targets summary)
sources.reported_estimate: 'Ensure secondary school completion has a benefit of $4 for every dollar spent.' (Sub-policy.)

sources.title: Progress on girls' access to education: What the new UNESCO data reveals
sources.reported_estimate: 122 million girls out of school worldwide.

sources.reported_estimate: Harmonized standard cost-recovery (indirect cost) rate of 8 per cent on other-resources (earmarked donor) contributions; 7 per cent for thematic contributions.

sources.authors: Sully, E.A.; Biddlecom, A.; Darroch, J.E.; et al.
sources.title: Adding It Up: Investing in Sexual and Reproductive Health 2019 - Methodology Report
sources.reported_estimate: Total cost = direct costs + 'programs and systems costs' (indirect markups) covering program management, staff supervision, monitoring and evaluation, human resources development, transport, health education and outreach, infrastructure, commodity supply systems and health information systems.

sources.title: Desired Fertility and the Impact of Population Policies
sources.reported_estimate: Argues that women's desired fertility, not contraceptive access, explains most cross-country differences in fertility, implying a smaller fertility (and demographic-dividend) effect of supply-side family planning.
sources.why_excluded: No BCR. Its argument bears mainly on the demographic-dividend part of the 120 figure, which is why the low end rests on Madise et al.'s 22, well below it.

sources.authors: Amporfu, E.; Arthur, E.; Novignon, J.; Wong, B.
sources.title: Costs and Benefits of Family Planning in Ghana: adolescent SRH education
sources.reported_estimate: Compulsory comprehensive adolescent sexual and reproductive health education: BCR 2.3.
sources.why_excluded: Different intervention (school curriculum, not contraceptive supply); not part of this policy.

sources.title: Advancing Social and Economic Development by Investing in Women's and Children's Health: A New Global Investment Framework

sources.why_excluded: Far broader package (all women's and children's health, ~$30bn/yr) than facility obstetric/newborn upgrades; lower average return expected for a broader package.
